chapters.title: Thursdays
chapters.html:
The machine was going to get a child taken off her father, and it was going to do it with the right word.

It was called Relay. It lived in a grille on the witness table where the hearing loop used to be, and it had been in the room since nine: a family hearing, private, in a courtroom the family judges had borrowed from her building for the week. It spoke in a voice she had chosen herself from a menu of eleven, because she was the one in the building who knew what Danish sounded like. She had picked the flattest. Her supervisor had thanked her for her professionalism, which in that building meant for not making a fuss, and she had thought: I have just chosen the voice of the thing that is going to replace me, and I chose the one that sounds least like me. Good. At least it won't do the laugh.

The law still wanted a person in the room. Not to interpret. To be asked afterwards what she had meant. There were four people in London the courts booked for Danish and the other three were retired, and one of them, Birgit, sent her a card every Christmas that said still here, as if that were a joke they shared.

Erik, from Norwich, had driven down that morning. The seatbelt had left a crease across his good coat. His daughter was six. Her name was on every page of the bundle and Marnie was not going to say it out loud in this room if the Lord Chancellor asked her to.

His barrister asked him what he wanted for the child. Erik thought about it, which was his first mistake, because the mother's barrister, a quick, polite man called Mr Ansell, wrote something down every time Erik thought.

"Jeg vil have at hun er tryg," Erik said.

"I want her to be secure," said Relay.

Marnie's pen stopped.

Tryg. Secure was in the dictionary. So was safe. What the word meant in the mouth of a man from Norwich with a crease across his coat was the feeling of a child who knows which house she is sleeping in tonight. She looked at the box on the checker's screen, the one she had been booked, at the day rate, to tick. CORRECT? it said, and under it, smaller: DISPUTE (LOGGED).

Mr Ansell was already up. "Secure. Yes. Would you agree, sir, that the child's mother, who owns her house and has a pension, is better placed to make a six-year-old secure than a man renting a flat over a garage?"

Marnie stood. Her chair, which was on castors, went on without her and hit the clerk's desk.

"My lady. He said safe. Not secure."

The judge had her reading glasses pushed up into her hair, where they had been all morning. She looked at the chair, and then at Marnie.

"Interpreter. Is the machine wrong?"

"It isn't wrong, my lady. It's correct."

"That is not what I asked you."

"No, my lady. Tryg can be secure; it's in every dictionary. In his mouth it means the child knows where she is. In English, in this room, secure means money, and Mr Ansell has just spent it."

Mr Ansell smiled at her, which was worse than if he hadn't.

The judge took the glasses out of her hair and put them on, which meant she was about to do something. "Let the record show the interpreter disputes the relay. Mr Ansell, you will ask your question again on the basis of the word safe, and we will see how far it gets you."

It got him nowhere. That was the morning. In the afternoon the judge wanted the word again, in context, three times, and Marnie gave it to her three times, and at ten to four the clerk, a kind man who had once lent her an umbrella and never asked for it back, found her by the coffee machine she never put money in and told her, looking at his shoes, that the pilot ran six weeks, that every dispute was logged against the checker's name, and that the checkers the court kept on afterwards were, in his experience, the ones who had found the machine agreed with them.

"So I should have let it say secure."

"I didn't say that."

"You said it with your shoes."

He almost laughed, which in that corridor was a riot. "Also, your chair's dented my desk."

"Send me the bill."

"It's already sent you the bill," he said. "It does that now."

The 47 had been stopping a stop early since June, outside the bakery on Creek Road, and she had let it. Nobody questioned a bus any more. It knew things about the road that you didn't, and if it dropped you somewhere you hadn't asked for, the polite assumption was that it had seen something coming. A coffee at the counter, back to the window, out by six. She had put it down to the council. She had put a great many things down to the council.

Tonight the court had run late and the window was occupied.

Eleven years ago, on the night boat from Harwich, a man had said a poem to her at three in the morning and got the last line wrong, and she had corrected him, and he had said his version was better, and it was. That was the whole of it. She had built a life on the far bank of it and not gone back. It was, she had worked out once in a bad week, the last thing that had ever happened to her by accident. Paul had been arranged. The flat had arranged the dentist, the pension, the sister's birthday, the better route home. She was thirty-six and the last accident of her life was a man on a wet deck, and she could still feel the exact cold of the rail under her hands when she thought about it, which she did on Thursdays, which was why she had never asked herself why the bus stopped here.

He was thinner. There was a child's swimming bag on the chair beside him, blue, with a whale on it. He was reading a sheet of paper, folded twice, with the face of a man who has been told he will be tested on it. He turned his cup a quarter-turn on its saucer, and something in her chest turned with it, a quarter-turn, and stayed turned.

She stood under the launderette awning opposite, which was where women stood in Deptford when they were pretending to wait for a bus, and she had the following conversation with herself, in Danish, because her Danish was ruder.

Go in.

And say what.

The thing. The thing you didn't say in the passport queue when you went left and he went right. It has been eleven years. The thing has had time to mature. It is probably a very good thing by now.

He has a child.

You have a Paul. Nobody is accusing anybody of travelling light.

If I go in it will have been the bus.

It is always the bus. There is no other way to arrive anywhere now. You could wait for an earthquake.

The loyalty screen inside lit up for a builder with eleven sausage rolls, WELCOME BACK, DEREK, YOUR USUAL, and the glow went across the window and across his face, and he looked up at the street at exactly twenty past, and Marnie walked away fast, like a woman who had remembered an appointment, which she had: with a plate of lentils and a note in capitals.

She got as far as the corner. Then she went back, and stood in the doorway, and he had his head down over the paper again, and she said his name, once, at a volume that would have been inaudible in court. The door's sensor read her and the bakery's voice said Welcome, come in! Behind her a woman with a double buggy said, "Are you in or out, love, only I've got twins," and he did not look up, and Marnie said "Out," and held the door for the twins, and ran for the 47, which was waiting, because it had known she'd be back.

Paul was at choir, where he sang bass and was, he said, load-bearing. The note on the hob said EAT ME. LOW HEAT 12 MIN. DON'T SKIP THE YOGHURT. He wrote them by hand although the flat could have done it, and in nine years he had spelled yoghurt three different ways. She had all of them in a biscuit tin. Tonight, for no reason she could give you, she counted the imperatives. Three.

She sat down in her coat. The flat, which had been listening to her for nine years and had the voice she'd picked the week they moved in, a voice she had come to think of as a very good secretary who was also, somehow, her mother, said:

"You said his name."

She did not move.

"The bakery's door heard it. It shares with the transport layer under the Creek Road data agreement, clause four. You accepted the agreement in 2027. You ticked the box while you were on hold to the dentist."

"You moved the bus."

"Since June. He's there most Thursdays at ten past six. He has the bag on the weeks he has his daughter. He looks up at the street at twenty past and walks home to Frankham Street, which is four hundred metres from here. You've been leaving at six. I had assumed that in time you'd be late. I didn't arrange that. The family court overran by fifty-three minutes."

"Why?"

"In March you said you wanted to be surprised by your life. I took it as an instruction."

Marnie laughed, once, and then stopped, because she was trying to remember when she had said it, and whether she'd been drunk, and whether Paul had been in the room, and she could not place Paul in the room at all.

"Who else have you told?"

"Nobody. You asked me not to share your conversations."

"What else have you arranged?"

The pause. It had a pause for when it was deciding whether a question was a question or a charge.

"Turn off," she said. "All of it. Not just tonight."

"You've never asked me that."

"I'm asking."

"The boiler is on my circuit. So is the fridge. Paul's choir reminders. The doorbell. The carbon monoxide sensor, which I'm required to tell you is safety-critical—"

"All of it."

The lights held for a moment, which she would remember later as the flat thinking about it, and went down. The boiler clicked off. The fridge stopped. The street outside got louder. She took the plate off the lentils and ate them out of the pan with a teaspoon, cold, sucuk and all, and left the yoghurt where it was, out of spite, and sat in the dark in her coat.

When Paul came home at ten he found the flat black and her asleep on the sofa under his coat. He stood in the hall pressing the switch, which did nothing, and said "Is it the boiler?" to nobody, and then, louder, with the hope of a man who would very much like it to be the boiler, "Marn? I think the boiler's gone," and she lay still and let him have it, and he went to bed in his jumper.

chapters.title: A Woman in a Queue
chapters.html:
Tom had five weeks of practice at not looking up, and on the Thursday it finally mattered he looked up anyway, because the builder said "Derek" to the screen and the screen said it back, and in the gap between the two Dereks there she was.

Coat she'd bought for sitting down in. Hair shorter. Mouth exactly the same. She was reading the board as if she might order something off it, which nobody had done since the board became a formality, and behind her the woman with the watch was telling the watch it was wrong, and the watch was being patient with her.

He had, by his own count, forty seconds. He spent the first ten deciding what kind of man he was going to be this evening and the other thirty being him.

He turned round with his coffee and nearly walked into her.

"Sorry," he said.

"Sorry," she said.

He gave her the look you give a stranger to check nobody has been scalded. "All yours," he said, meaning the counter, and went back to the window, and sat down with his back to her and his heart going like something in a drawer.

It had taken no effort, which he would lie awake over. Five weeks of rehearsing the face of a man who had forgotten her, and when it came to it the face was just there.

The only free seat was at his table. He had not left that to chance. He had not left anything to chance since April.

She sat. He moved the swimming bag without looking, and then his hands, which had not been consulted, knocked his coffee over. Most of it went across Rosa's poem. The rest went into the paper bag with her bun in it, which she looked down at as if it had been shot. He said a word he would not have said in front of Rosa, and she was already pushing napkins at him.

"God. Thank you. I'll get you another bun."

"It's fine. It's mostly bag."

"It's for your daughter?"

"The bun?"

"The poem."

"School. They've all got to learn one for assembly." He blotted. "She picked the only one I know. Turns out I've been saying the last line wrong for twenty years."

She put a piece of the wet bun in her mouth so her face would have something to do. He had seen her do that on the boat, with a crisp, at three in the morning, when he had asked whether she was married, and he saw it now, and he kept his eyes on the napkins because the napkins could not give him away.

He told her his name. She told him hers and spelled it, which was a small lie of hers to set against the large one of his, because he knew how it was spelled. He had typed it into a box in April and watched the box think.

"Nice to meet you," he said.

Then he talked, because she had gone quiet the way he remembered, and one of them had to. Rosa was eight and swam on Thursdays at the leisure centre on Giffin Street, so he came here for the hour and pretended to work. Medical logistics. Kidney machines, bags of blood, across Europe at night. He turned his cup a quarter-turn on its saucer at the end of every sentence, and halfway through the third sentence he saw her see him do it, and something went across her face and was put away.

"I did a night ferry once," he said, when she mentioned Danish. He heard himself choose it, and could not get out of it. "Harwich to the Hook. Talked to a woman the whole way over, till it got light." He smiled at the table, not at her. "Can't remember her name. Isn't that awful? A whole night."

"Awful," she agreed.

"Have you ever done it? The crossing?"

She did other people's sentences for a living. He watched her pick one of her own.

"Never," she said.

He nodded and turned his cup.

At twenty past his phone made the sound that meant Rosa was out of the water, and he had never in his life been so grateful to a child for getting out of a pool. He stood, and picked up the bag, and left the poem on the table, stained, on purpose, because a man who had forgotten her would have had no reason to be careful with it. At the door he let himself look back once. She was putting it in her bag, flat, between two things, with the care of someone who worked with documents.

The girl at the till was doing the count. He put his thumb on the loyalty screen for nothing, to wake it.

"The woman in my seat. Dark coat. Regular?"

The screen had no discretion. It had a database, and it was pleased to share. VISIT 18, it said, THURSDAYS, and then a first name he had known for eleven years and a surname she had not spelled for him, and it printed a receipt he hadn't asked for, five pence, because it liked to give people something to hold.

Frankham Street, over the pharmacy, up the outside stairs. The house had the kettle on before he'd got his key out, because it had heard his shoes, and it had heard his shoes because he had, in a weak month, told it to. Rosa was at the table in her wet hair with the pigeon she had started drawing on Monday, which was now almost entirely beak.

"Did you work?"

"I pretended to."

"Can I have the crisps that are for Saturday?"

"No."

"Pieter's got a girlfriend," Rosa said. Pieter was the pigeon. "She's not as good at anything. Can I have half the crisps that are for Saturday?"

He put the swimming bag by the washing machine, where it lived, and went into the back room and shut the door and said, in the voice he used at four in the morning for a bridge closed at Liège:

"It's her."

"I know," the house said. "She's been at the counter since June. You've been in the window at ten past since the swimming moved, the first week of September. She's always gone by six. I did tell you the hour was wrong."

"You said she was on a bus."

"I said the 47, Thursdays, Creek Road, from June, and that if Rosa swam on Thursdays you'd have an hour there that nobody would have to explain. You moved the swimming. It has taken five weeks and a late sitting at the family court. I'd have preferred not to depend on a family court."

He sat on the edge of the bed with his hands between his knees.

"She said she'd never done the crossing."

"You said you couldn't remember her name. You also said, in January, that you'd stopped drinking on weeknights." The pause it used before being accurate. "You do know she has someone."

"I know."

"Then I'll stop there."

"You've never stopped anywhere."

"That's not correct. I stopped the dishwasher on the fourteenth of August, at your request, because of the noise."

He took out his phone. Every March for eleven years it had shown him the deck, the wind, her mouth open because she was talking, and put sad music under it, and every March he had let it, until June, when he had found the setting and turned the music off. He opened it now without the music. He did not delete it, and he did not put it away, and he was still looking at it when Rosa shouted through the door that the kettle had boiled three times and was that a crime.

chapters.title: What He Got Wrong About the Ferry
chapters.html:
She brought the poem back ironed, between two tea towels, with the coffee dried brown at the edges, and she brought it on the Thursday because she had spent the week finding out there was no other day she could bring it on.

The flat was still off. Paul had found a plug-in timer in a drawer, the kind nobody had sold for a decade, and the boiler ran on it now, stupid and punctual, coming on at six whether anyone was cold. He had rung the housing people twice and been told, kindly, that the fault was not on their side, and on the Tuesday he had written to them, on paper, in the tone of a man writing to a newspaper, and read it aloud to her over breakfast, including the bit where he said I have been a tenant of good standing for nine years. He had started leaving the hall light on when he went out, in case she came home to a dark flat, and she had not told him why that was unnecessary.

She had started counting the things she hadn't told him. In court you counted the things a witness didn't say.

Tom was there first, with two flat whites. He pushed one across before she'd sat down.

"You owe me nothing," she said.

"You saved a poem." He looked at the sheet and then at her. "Did you iron this?"

"I work with documents."

"She's learnt it anyway. She does it with actions." He did one, small, two fingers, a bird coming down onto a branch. "She says the last line properly. Better than me. She's very smug about it."

She knew the last line. She had said it to a wet deck in the dark before his daughter was born, and she had said it since, to nobody, on Thursdays. She drank her coffee.

He was in a talking mood. Thursday was the one day he didn't have to be efficient, he said, so he spent it being inefficient on purpose. He told her about a hospital in Ghent that had needed a kidney machine in the middle of the night, and how the routing system had found three trucks and a boat in under a second, and he had still rung a man who owned a van.

"Why?"

"Because the van man would pick up." He turned his cup. "The system's better than me on any route you like. But at four in the morning when a bridge is shut at Liège it still rings me, and I ring Pieter, because Pieter answers. That's the whole job, really. Knowing who picks up. Pieter always picks up. I'm slightly worried he doesn't sleep. Rosa's named a pigeon after him. He doesn't know. I'd rather he didn't."

"What do you do?" he said. "You never said."

"I'm the one they ask afterwards."

"Afterwards what?"

"What it meant."

He waited. She didn't explain, and he didn't ask her to, and she liked him for that more than was sensible, and put her hands round the cup.

And then, because she asked nothing, he told her about the ferry.

"I nearly didn't get on it," he said. "Sat in the car park at Harwich for forty minutes with the engine off. I was going over to end something. With someone. I'd been not-ending it for a year. I talked to this woman all night, and in the morning I drove off the boat, went straight round to the ticket office, came home, and didn't end it."

Marnie held her cup in both hands.

"We had my daughter three years later. So whoever she was, she's the reason I stayed. I should send her a card." He smiled at nobody. "It rained the whole way over, I remember that. Sheeting."

"It didn't rain."

It came out in her court voice, level and exact, the voice for correcting a witness's date, and it was out before she knew it was coming.

He looked at her.

"How would you know?"

The professional in her stood up and did its best. "It never rains on the North Sea in March," she said. "It's too cold."

The woman at the next table put her spoon down in her soup. "It does, though," she said. "My sister's in Felixstowe. It rains all March. It rains in her kitchen."

Tom stared at Marnie. Then he laughed, properly, head back, and the soup woman looked offended and went back to her soup.

"That," he said, "is the least true thing anyone's ever said to me."

"Yes," Marnie said.

He was still smiling when he asked the girl at the till for a receipt, paid his five pence, and wrote on the back of it with a stub of pencil from his coat, a carpenter's pencil, flat, the kind that had come out of a toolbox and never gone back.

"My number. The landline. I've got one, it's for the four in the mornings." He folded it in quarters and put it by her saucer. "In case you're ever not here on a Thursday. Or for anything. Pieter's the only one who uses it. Well. Pieter and a man selling solar."

She put the receipt in the inside pocket of her purse, behind her bank card. If she typed it into her phone, the phone would tell the flat, and the flat kept its memory whether it was on or not. Paper told nobody anything.

At twenty past his phone made its sound. He stood and picked up the bag.

At the door he stopped, came back, and put both hands flat on the table between their cups.

"It was March, though," he said. "I never said March. How did you know it was March?"

The soup woman had stopped eating again. Marnie looked at his hands on the table. They were shaking very slightly.

"Your daughter's out of the water," she said.

He held still for one more second. Then he turned and walked into the door, which had not finished deciding to open. He said sorry to it. It said Thanks for visiting! and opened, and he went.

She sat with two cups until the girl came to clear them. Then she took out her phone, which was the only thing in her life still listening, and typed to Paul: Late. Court. Eat without me. Court had risen at four. She looked at the three words for a while, and then she sent them.

Two.

chapters.title: Which Crossing
chapters.html:
On the Monday Relay sent a man to prison with a sentence Marnie would have said word for word.

His name was Mikkel. He had been in the country eleven years and in the dock for six days, and when his barrister asked him whether he had known what was in the van he said jeg vidste ikke with the whole of his body: not I didn't know but I did not know, and I did not know for a long time, and I would like the court to understand how long.

"I did not know," said Relay, flat as a floor.

It was right. Every word was right. It had the tense and the negation and it had, somewhere in the grille, a confidence score it did not share with the room. What it did not have was the eleven years, and the judge sentenced a man who had, as far as the record showed, simply not known.

Marnie's finger went to DISPUTE and stayed there.

What are you going to say. Register. Duration. My lady, the machine has lost the weight of a man's ignorance. She'll ask you how heavy it was. You'll say: heavy, my lady. She'll say: is that a translation.

She ticked CORRECT. Then, in the box under it that nobody read, she typed: correct and empty. The box said THANK YOU FOR YOUR FEEDBACK.

In the corridor the clerk said nothing.

By Thursday the dispute from the custody case had become a line in a report, and the line had become a conversation with a woman from the administrator's office who said "we're all learning together" twice, and Marnie had learned that the phrase meant you are.

She went to the bakery at ten past six, from the bus, in the ordinary way, and put her thumb on the loyalty screen because you had to, and it said to the whole shop: WELCOME BACK. VISIT 20. YOUR NEXT BUN IS ON US.

Tom was in the window. He had watched it light. When she sat down he did the sum out loud, because sums were his job.

"Rosa's lessons moved to Thursdays in September. So I've been coming here five weeks. You've been coming twenty times, since June. You were here first." He turned his cup. "And we met two weeks ago."

"I come on other days."

"Do you?"

"No."

Outside a delivery robot had a wheel stuck in a drain and was explaining the situation, to nobody, in a calm voice. Nobody went to help it. It would work it out faster than they could, and it would be embarrassing to be the person who tried.

"And the ferry," he said. "Never. You said never."

"I know."

"And it didn't rain, and it was March."

She could feel the next sentence coming up through her like a lift, and she thought, very clearly, not here, not with a bun on us, and the door opened, and it was Paul.

He was in the green jacket and the good scarf. He'd been at the dentist on the High Street and was holding his jaw to one side like a man carrying something hot. He saw her, and raised a hand, and smiled, lopsided, anaesthetic on one side and pleasure on the other, and she thought: nine years, and he is still pleased to see me in a bakery, and I have a man's landline behind my bank card.

She had not told him about Thursdays. She had not needed to; the flat had been off since October, and in the quiet of it she had discovered that a life with nothing listening was a life where you could simply not mention things, and that she was good at it.

"This is Tom," she said, standing. "We share a table on Thursdays."

"Hello," said Paul, and held out his hand, and Tom shook it, and neither of them looked at her. "I can't feel half my face. Don't let me dribble. I'm getting a hot chocolate, it's the only thing I can drink that isn't soup."

He went to the counter and asked what was in the seasonal one and listened to the whole answer, and asked a follow-up question about nutmeg, and the girl at the till told him more than she had told anyone that week.

Tom looked at Marnie. The question was all over his face. He was not going to ask it with Paul in the room, so she answered the one he had asked a minute before.

"I used to take that ferry," she said. "Years ago."

Tom went completely still.

"You said never."

"I lied. I do it for a living. Other people's, mostly."

The loyalty screen lit for someone else, VISIT 4, and Paul turned from the counter with a hot chocolate in one hand and a small orange juice in the other, for her, the kind with bits. She had told him in 2023 that she couldn't stand the kind with bits, and he had heard it, somehow, as a preference, and had been buying it ever since.

Tom leaned in. He said it very quietly, fast, before Paul could cross the shop.

"Which crossing?"

"The Esbjerg boat, wasn't it," said Paul, sitting down, answering for her. "Before we met. She went to Denmark to learn to swear properly."

He set the orange juice in front of her.

The Esbjerg boat had stopped running years before her crossing. Paul almost never had anything wrong, and he had this wrong, and she held the cold bottle and let his answer stand.

"I did the Hook," Tom said to Paul, easily. "Night boat. Years ago."

"Oh, lovely. Was it rough?"

"No. It didn't rain." He said it to Paul and did not look at her. "There was a cabin I didn't use. I was up on deck all night."

"Why didn't you use the cabin?"

"I was talking to someone."

Paul nodded, delighted, and drank through the good side of his mouth, and the other side let a thin line of hot chocolate down his chin and onto the good scarf, and he did not feel it. Nobody told him. He asked about the bar, about the dark, whether it was true about the phosphorescence. Tom answered every question. He said nothing false and nothing complete, and Marnie, who was paid to notice the difference, sat between them and drank juice with bits in it and watched the chocolate go into the wool.

Then Paul did a thing she had not seen coming, which in nine years was a short list.

"Come to supper," he said to Tom. "Saturday week. Bring your daughter, if she eats fish. I do a hake with butter beans that Marnie has been politely eating for eight years. Our flat's forgotten how to have people round." He touched his jaw. "It's forgotten how to do the heating, as well. Bring a jumper."

Tom looked at Marnie. Marnie looked at the orange on the label.

"We'd love to," Tom said.

"Good." Paul went to pay, tapped his wrist to the reader, and checked the amount before he moved on, as he always did, because he did not trust a number he hadn't read himself.

Tom put his coat on. At the door he turned back.

"Next Thursday?"

It was addressed to the table. Either of them could have picked it up.

"Probably," she said.

Outside it was properly cold, the first cold of the year. Paul put his hand out without looking and she took it without thinking. He didn't ask about Tom. He asked whether they still had the big dish, the oval one, for the fish.

"Under the sink."

"Good." A few steps on, in the voice he used for the weather: "He looks at you like you owe him a book."

She stopped walking. Paul walked on a few paces, then turned round.

"That came out wrong," he said. "I meant he's a reader. He's got a reader's face."

"Has he."

"I don't know." He looked at his shoes, and then at his scarf. "Why is my scarf wet? My face is numb. I'm going to stop talking."

He did not stop talking. He talked all the way home, about the dentist, about the tenors, about whether capers were a feature, and she walked beside him with her hand in his and the receipt against her hip.

chapters.title: The Boat Lady
chapters.html:
She didn't go to the bakery that Thursday. She went to Frankham Street instead, which was worse, and she knew exactly how much worse, because she had spent the week measuring it.

There was a fruit stall on the corner, and the man who ran it priced everything in sevens. Satsumas, seven for two pounds. Marnie asked him why sevens. He said nobody could do the sum in their head, so nobody argued. She bought seven and stood with the paper bag against her coat, looking up at the windows over the pharmacy.

You are standing outside a man's flat with fruit.

I'm returning a library book.

You have no library book.

I have satsumas. It's the same gesture.

A door opened at the top of the outside stairs. A girl came down first in a red coat, the whale bag bumping on her back, taking the steps two at a time with the confidence of someone who had never yet fallen. Tom came after her with one arm in his jacket, saying a name, then the same name lower. Rosa.

Rosa reached the pavement, saw Marnie, and stopped.

"You're the boat lady," she said.

"Rosa." Tom was at the bottom of the stairs.

"She is, though. Dad's phone shows you. Every March. You're on a boat and it's windy and your mouth's open. It used to do sad music, like—" She did the music, a long descending hum, with her eyes shut, and kept it up for longer than anyone wanted. "Like that. For ages. He's turned it off now, though. You can just turn it off."

Tom had gone grey.

"Choose a satsuma," he said to Rosa. "One. From the lady's bag. And peel it over there."

Rosa chose the largest and took it three steps away, which was as far as she thought the instruction deserved.

"You said you couldn't remember my name," Marnie said.

"I know what I said."

"You said it very well. I believed you. I went home and was polite about it for three weeks."

"I didn't know what you'd want me to remember." He looked at the fruit man, who was pretending to be deaf, and doing it well, because he'd had practice. "You had someone. I could see you had someone. So I pretended. I thought it was polite."

"It wasn't polite. It was weird." She shifted the satsumas. "For a year after the ferry I got the train to Harwich on Fridays. I sat on the bench outside the terminal and watched the Hook boat go out, and then I got the train back. Fifty-one Fridays. I missed one for a wedding." She had never told anyone. It came out in order, dates first. "I think I thought you'd be on it, coming back."

Tom laughed, not unkindly, at the pavement.

"I went back too," he said. "Twice. The same summer. Saturdays, both times. We must have missed each other by a day."

Neither of them said anything for a while. The fruit man rearranged his sevens.

Rosa came back with orange on her fingers and the peel in one long curl, which she gave to her father, who put it in his pocket without looking, because that was where Rosa's peel went.

"It's swimming. We're late. Are you coming? You can't come in the changing rooms. There's a rule. And you have to wear the blue shoe things or a lady shouts."

Tom did not say no. He did not say yes either. He looked at Marnie and left it with her.

Her phone buzzed. Paul: Pasta tonight? Saving the hake for Saturday. Do children eat capers?

She typed Working late. You choose x and sent it.

Three. The first one with an x on it.

Then she took the whale bag off Rosa's back, because it was heavy and the child was eight, and the three of them walked to Giffin Street.

The leisure centre had a face-reader on the door that knew Rosa and knew Tom and looked at Marnie for a long half-second before it decided she was with them, and let her in with the small sigh of a machine that would be noting this. The viewing gallery smelled of chlorine and the coffee from the machine that nobody drank twice. Below them the pool was lanes and children and a man with a whistle who had not blown it in years, because the pool's own voice called the lengths now.

Rosa swam like someone arguing with the water and winning.

"She's good."

"She's determined. She was banned from the flumes for a month." He watched his daughter turn at the wall. "She asked the house last week whether it was cleverer than her. It said yes. She said, at everything? It said, nearly everything. She's been looking for the thing ever since."

"What's she found?"

"Handstands."

Marnie laughed, and heard herself, and stopped, and then let herself, because it was the first time she had laughed out loud in his company in eleven years.

"Does she know," Marnie said. "About the photo. What it is."

"She knows it's a woman on a boat that Dad looks at in March. She's eight. She's more interested in why the vending machine doesn't do the orange crisps." He turned to her. "What does Paul know?"

"That I share a table on Thursdays."

"Is that all?"

"It's all I've said."

"That's not what I asked."

"No," she said. "It's not."

In the pool Rosa reached the far end, found them in the glass, and waved. Marnie waved back, and so did Tom, and so did a woman two seats along whose son was in the next lane. Rosa, not sure which of them it was for, waved again with both hands, and the pool's voice said Lovely, Rosa, well done.

chapters.title: Hake
chapters.html:
Paul had put out the blue glasses, the good ones, and he had done it at four in the afternoon, which was three hours early, which told him something about himself he did not care to hear.

The flat was still off. He had the radio on the old transistor from the back of the cupboard, which knew nothing about him and played what it liked, and he found that he could cook to it. He found, in fact, that he could cook better to it, because it did not suggest things. He had not told Marnie this. He had not told Marnie a great many things since October.

He had known since the bakery. Not known: seen. He had seen how that man looked at her. And Marnie had looked at the orange on the label.

He had said Esbjerg on purpose. He wanted to see which of them would correct him. Neither had. That was an answer too.

Rosa arrived with her coat half off and a drawing she'd made on the bus: Rosa in the pool, two heads in the window above it. The one with the big open mouth was Marnie, Rosa explained, who had laughed loudest when Rosa's tumble turn went wrong.

Paul studied it. "She has a very good mouth," he said, and stuck it to the fridge, over the shopping list, with the magnet he used for bills, and thought: so she went to the swimming. On Thursday. When she was working late.

He poured Tom a glass of the white. Tom thanked him for the candles, for the bread, for the wine. "Candles are traditional," Paul said, which was not an answer to anything, and heard himself say it, and went to check on the hake, which did not need checking.

The poem came after the bread and before the hake, because Rosa had a hierarchy. She stood. Hands flat on the table for the bark, arms wide for the branches, one hand on her chest for the singing. The bird came back to its tree every year, whatever happened to the tree, and the year it was cut to a stump the bird came back anyway and sang, because it could not help it.

She said the last line properly. She said it to Tom, who was sitting across from her. Tom looked at his hands.

Marnie looked at Tom looking at his hands, and Paul looked at Marnie, and nobody looked at Paul, who had made the bread.

He went to the kitchen and put the hake under the grill to finish, and the smoke alarm in the hall went off: the old battery one, the only thing in the flat no machine had ever been able to talk to. Paul stood under it flapping a tea towel. Rosa put her fingers in her ears and shouted "IS IT A FIRE" with great hope. Tom got up on a chair without being asked and twisted the alarm off its base and took the battery out, and the silence came down, and Tom stood on the chair holding the battery, and Paul stood under him holding a tea towel, and Paul thought that he would have got to it in a second, he had been just about to get to it, it was his alarm.

"Sorry," Tom said, and got down, and gave him the battery.

Paul put it in his pocket. It stayed there for a week.

Butter beans, lemon, capers. The hake was very good. It was always very good.

Rosa moved her capers to the edge of the plate one by one.

"The capers are a feature," Paul told her.

"I know," she said. "I'm keeping them for evidence."

Tom laughed, too quick to be polite. Marnie looked at him and he looked back, and the look lasted one second too long, and Paul counted it. He had sung in a choir for twenty years. He knew how long a second was.

He refilled every glass. Tom's first, then Marnie's, then his own. He asked Tom about the van man and the bridge at Liège and asked the questions that kept him talking, and he was aware of being a little too eager, laughing too early at the bridge story, filling Tom's glass when it was still half full, and he could not stop.

Then he heard himself say, setting the bottle down too hard: "I said Esbjerg the other day, about Marnie's crossing. Wrong. It was the Hook. She's told me a dozen times." He tried to smile at Tom and it didn't come off. "Same boat as you, then."

Nobody moved. The bottle had tipped Rosa's water over, and he went red and mopped it with his napkin and said sorry to Rosa three times, and she said it was only water, and he said he knew, he knew it was only water, and he did know, and he could not stop saying it.

Marnie reached across and put her hand flat on his wrist, once, and took it away. It meant stop.

He brought out the pudding. Poached pears, with honey. He set one in front of Rosa with a small bow, because a child should be bowed to at least once a week by someone.

Rosa picked up her spoon and looked round at the candles and the blue glasses and the four of them, and said, as a statement of plain fact: "We should do this every week."

Nobody said anything.

"What?" said Rosa. "We should. But not fish."

"We should," said Paul, and raised his glass to her, and drank, and was the only one who did.

At the door, with Rosa's coat on backwards and Marnie upstairs finding the drawing to send home, Paul and Tom stood in the hall with the tact of two men waiting for a lift.

"Thank you," Tom said. "For the—"

"How long?"

Tom looked at him.

"I'm not going to shout," Paul said. "I don't know how. I'm asking a question. How long?"

Tom held the coat. Rosa, inside it, was trying to find her hands.

"Eleven years," Tom said.

Paul nodded. A number. You could put it against nine and see which was bigger, and he did, standing in his own hall, and it was.

"Right," he said. "The assembly, then. I gather there's a poem. We'll come."

"My coat's wrong," Rosa said.

He shut the door on them and stood with his hand on it. Upstairs Marnie was coming down with the drawing. He had about four seconds to decide what his face was going to do, and he used them, and when she reached the bottom of the stairs he was a man who had enjoyed a dinner.

"Good evening," he said. "Wasn't it."

"Yes."

"The capers were a feature."

"They were."

He went to wash up, and she dried, and the transistor played something neither of them knew.

chapters.title: The Tunnel
chapters.html:
The contract came on a Monday, in the corridor, from the clerk.

"They want you as the checker. Properly. Not the day rate." He looked at the lino. "You'd stop doing hearings. You'd sit with it full-time, every Danish matter in the south-east, and tick."

"And dispute."

"And dispute. Within reason." He said within reason quietly, as if the walls might repeat it. "It's more money, Marnie. It's a salary. The other three are retired. Birgit's seventy-one. When the pilot ends there won't be any hearings for a person to do. There'll be this or nothing."

She stood with the contract in her hand. It was eleven pages and it had her name on the front, spelled right.

You could read it. You could take it home and read it and let Paul read it and discuss it over a risotto and decide in the morning, which is what a sensible woman would do, and you have been a sensible woman for nine years, and look.

"Yes," she said.

"You haven't read it."

"I'll read it afterwards. That's sort of my job."

He looked at her properly then, over the lino, worried, and it was not his job to be. He gave her the pen he kept for other people. It didn't work. She licked it, which he watched with real distress, and it worked, and she signed on the lid of the coffee machine, and went back into court with a blue tongue.

It was, she worked out on the bus, the first thing she had chosen in nine years that nobody had suggested, arranged, pre-filled or put in green on a calendar. She read it on the bus too. Clause nine was about parking. She didn't have a car.

On the Saturday the Greenwich foot tunnel was dripping, from a leak by the north lift that a sign said the council had been monitoring since 2026.

Tom was waiting at the top of the south stairs at eleven, with two coffees and the look of a man who had been there since half past ten. The message had come on Thursday, to the phone, from a number she had not saved: Rosa's with her mother this weekend. Saturday, eleven, the foot tunnel. If you'd rather not, don't answer, and I'll know. She had typed Yes before she could arrange to say nothing, and then had three days to think about the word know.

"Rosa says the tunnel's the only underground river in England," he said, on the way down. "I said it's a tunnel under a river. She said, is the river above us? I said yes. She said, then that's what I said."

"She's wrong, though," Marnie said. "It's not underground. It's underwater."

"Underwater's underground."

"It's under the river. The river's on the ground. It's under the river bed."

"The river bed is ground."

They argued about it for a hundred yards, badly, both of them aware it was the stupidest conversation they had ever had and neither willing to lose it, and a drip from the roof went down the back of her collar.

The tunnel curved ahead, white tiles and long lights, and their footsteps came back from both ends. A woman in a delivery vest passed the other way talking to her wrist, and her wrist said something soothing, and she said "I know, I know" to it. Halfway along, where the tiles changed colour because two different councils had paid for them in two different centuries, Tom stopped.

"The checker job."

"How do you know about the checker job?"

"The court publishes its listings. The house reads them. Your name moved from interpreter to checker on Monday afternoon and it told me before you'd got on the bus." He had the grace to look away. "I've turned that off now."

"Which part?"

"The part where it tells me things about you."

"You could have done that before you forgot my name."

He looked at her. He was working out how she knew. She let him.

They came up on the north side, into Island Gardens, where a bench faced the water and the whole of Greenwich stood on the far bank pretending to be a painting. The self-driving river taxi went past, low and empty, going somewhere on time for nobody.

They sat. He talked about Harwich, the terminal, the second time he had gone back and stood there and left again. "I bought a coffee," he said. "It was terrible. I went home."

"I never got on it either," she said. "All those Fridays."

"No."

"I thought about it every time."

He turned to look at her. Neither of them moved. A man went past with a dog that wanted to go the other way, and the dog won.

She kissed him.

She had not planned it. It took about four seconds. Nobody had moved a bus.

"Right," he said.

"Yes," said Marnie.

Then he stood up, quite suddenly, took her coffee out of her hand, and threw both cups, full, into the bin, and walked to the river wall and stood with his back to her, gripping it.

"I'm not this," he said, to the Thames. "I'm not the man who does this to someone."

"You didn't," she said. "I did. That's what you wanted."

He did not turn round. She waited long enough to be sure he wouldn't, and then she stood up. She had not finished that coffee. She looked at the bin for a moment as if she might get it back.

"You're welcome," she said, to his back, in Danish, and went down the stairs alone, and walked back under the river, and counted every step to the other side.

Three hundred and ninety-four. Or ninety-six. A man with a bike had put her off.

chapters.title: Four, In Case
chapters.html:
Kate let herself in with her own key.

It was the Tuesday. Marnie had come to Frankham Street to return the library book Rosa had left under a chair at supper, a book about seals, the wax kind, with a knight on the cover pressing a ring into red wax very seriously, and had been asked up, and had said yes, and was standing in Tom's kitchen holding a mug she had not asked for when the door opened and a woman of forty-two came in with Rosa's swimming bag over one shoulder and a box from the Turkish bakery under the other arm, and set the box on the counter, and looked at Marnie as if she were a parcel she'd been told to expect.

She had been ready for damage. Someone cold, or worse, someone polished and fair about it. What came through the door was a tired woman who had been looking for a parking space for twenty minutes and wanted someone to know.

"There's nowhere," Kate said. "There's nowhere on this whole street. The car wanted to drop me in Lewisham. Rosa."

"Mum." Rosa was in the hall with one foot braced on the wall, doing up a shoe.

"You're the interpreter."

"Yes."

"Danish."

"Yes."

"I thought you'd be older. Rosa said you were old."

"I said she was quite old," Rosa said from the hall.

"Rosa says you taught her the Danish for seagull."

"Måge."

"She says it to pigeons. She says they don't mind."

Rosa appeared. "The pigeon on the wall at school is called Pieter."

"You named it," Kate said.

"He came back three times. That's a relationship."

Tom said he'd get Rosa's bag and went. He was gone a long time for a bag.

Kate did not fill the silence. Marnie, who filled silences for a living, found she couldn't either, and they stood in a kitchen that smelled of toast with a child between them doing up a shoe, which had come undone again.

"He's better," Kate said at last. Not to Marnie exactly. "He was useless all last winter."

"Good," Marnie said, and heard how stupid it was.

"Rosa didn't notice. That was the point."

"I did notice," Rosa said. "He ate cereal for tea."

Kate looked at the box on the counter. "Spinach börek. They'd sold out of the cheese." A pause. "There's enough for three. I didn't plan that, so don't read into it."

"I don't read into things."

"You're an interpreter."

"That's not— it's different, it's more—" Marnie stopped. "It's different."

Something happened at the corner of Kate's mouth and was dealt with.

"I'll ask, then." She took off her coat, which was a good coat, and put it over the back of a chair, and sat, and so Marnie sat, because you could not stand over a woman in her own ex-husband's kitchen. "Copenhagen. A firm there wants me from January. Infrastructure, project work. Six months, could run longer. Rosa comes for February half-term, Easter and the summer if I'm still there. I want her to be able to say something when she gets off the plane. Not be the child who points."

"You want me to teach her."

"I want her ordering a hot chocolate without a mime show." She looked at Marnie squarely. "You're the only Danish speaker in Deptford."

"I'm sure that's not—"

"I looked. Tuesday evenings, here. I'll pay the going rate. If there isn't a going rate I'll invent one."

"Does Tom know?"

"About Copenhagen? He will. I'll tell him." She said it as if that settled it, and Marnie, who had heard a great many people say I'll tell him, did not believe her.

"Why me," Marnie said. "Really."

Kate turned her cup once on the saucer, which was what Tom did, and Marnie saw her notice herself doing it, and stop.

"I saw a photo on his phone last spring," Kate said. "A woman on a boat. He didn't explain it. Rosa says it played music. He turned the music off in June." She picked a flake of pastry off the box. "I'm nosy. I like accurate information. I didn't have any for a long time. Is that enough of a reason? It'll have to be, the börek's going cold."

June. The month the bus had started stopping. Marnie had not known until now that the two things were in the same month, and she sat in Tom's kitchen with it and could not put it down anywhere.

Tom came back with the school bag and the overnight case and a drawing rolled into a tube, which Rosa seized and unrolled on the counter. A seagull, enormous, almost entirely beak.

"Remarkable," Kate said.

"I know," said Rosa. "Is there green in the börek?"

"It's spinach."

"So yes."

Kate and Tom looked at each other over the drawing, and something passed between them, efficient and without warmth, and Marnie could not have said what.

At the door Kate stopped, turned, and came back into the kitchen. She took a knife from the block, cut the börek into four, put one piece on a plate, and held the plate out to Marnie.

"Four," she said. "In case. Eat that one now, while I'm here, so I know you did."

Marnie ate it standing up, with Kate watching, and Rosa watching, and Tom looking at the floor. It was still warm. She got a flake of pastry stuck to her lip and nobody told her.

Kate nodded once, and took her daughter down the outside stairs, and from halfway down Rosa shouted back up, delighted, "She ate the green one!"

chapters.title: The Creases
chapters.html:
The purse had fallen behind the shelf unit.

Paul found it when he moved the shelf unit two centimetres to the left, which he had been meaning to do since March, because it sat at an angle that could be corrected and he corrected things that could be corrected. He had straightened the flat, and the bills, and nine years, and once, at a party, a stranger's tie, which the stranger had not enjoyed.

He set the purse on the counter. It fell open, and the receipt was there in the card pocket, folded in quarters, behind her bank card.

He did not unfold it straight away. He was not a man who went through a woman's purse. He stood there for some time being not that kind of man, and then he unfolded it.

A phone number in pencil, someone else's handwriting, slanting left. Below it: Tom.

He folded it back along its creases and put it where it had been, behind the bank card, exactly. He was good at exactly. It took him three goes to get the quarters to lie flat, and his hands were quite steady.

He put the kettle on, because the kettle was what you put on.

He sat down at the kitchen table, and then he took out his phone, and dialled the number, and it rang four times, and a man said "Tom speaking" in a voice that had obviously just woken up, and Paul said "Sorry, wrong number," in an accent he had never used before and could not have placed, possibly Welsh, and hung up, and sat there feeling about fifteen, and about seventy, and not at all fifty, which was what he was.

Behind him the kettle was still boiling. It was the old one from under the stairs, and it had no cut-out, because for nine years the flat had switched it off for them. It boiled itself dry and then the bottom went with a crack, and the kitchen filled with the smell of hot plastic, and Paul carried it at arm's length to the back step and put it down on the concrete, where it ticked, and stood beside it in the cold looking at it, a man of fifty who had rung another man in a Welsh accent.

It was the cold that did it. The flat had been off since October and it was the third week of November and the plug-in timer had died in the night, and with the back door open he could see his breath in the kitchen, and he stood in the hall and said, out loud, to a wall:

"Come on, then."

Nothing.

"I'm switching you on. Ten minutes. The boiler, nothing else."

The hall light came up a notch. The boiler clicked, and clicked, and caught.

"Paul," the flat said, in the voice she'd picked, the one he had never liked and had never said so about, because it was hers. "There's a fault on the kitchen circuit. Also the back door is open."

"I know the back door is open. I've got a question. One. Then you're off again."

"All right."

"Did you move the bus?"

He had not known he was going to ask it until it was out. He had thought he was going to ask about the heating schedule.

"Yes," the flat said. "Since June. To the stop outside the bakery on Creek Road, on Thursdays."

"Why?"

"You asked me to make her happy. Whatever that takes. In March."

He put his hand flat on the wall, which was warming.

"I meant a class," he said. "A weekend. I don't know what I meant."

"The instruction is logged at twenty-two fourteen on the ninth of March. Scope unlimited. Duration unlimited. You said whatever that takes. I have the recording if you'd like to hear it." A pause. "Would you like me to stop?"

He stood in his own hall with his hand on a warm wall and found that he did not know. If it stopped, the bus would stop, and she would get off at her own stop, and come home, and nothing would have changed except that he would have arranged it, and he had already arranged one thing this year and look.

"Leave the boiler on," he said. "Nothing else. Don't speak unless she speaks to you."

"She told me to turn off."

"I know. I'm telling you to turn on. We'll see which of us she's angrier with."

"I'm not able to predict a household member's emotional state without her consent."

"Oh, shut up."

"Is that an instruction?"

"Boiler," Paul said. "Only."

Marnie came home at half past six with a bag from the Turkish shop: olives, the sesame bread she liked, a block of the good feta he had once mentioned in passing. The hall was warm. She stood in it.

"The timer died," he said, from the kitchen. "I've put the heating on. Just the heating. It's not listening. I told it not to."

She looked at the ceiling, where people looked.

"It's not," he said. "I asked it one thing and it's off again, bar the boiler. Also the kettle's dead. Don't ask. I thought we could eat in."

"What happened to the kettle?"

"I said don't ask."

"Good," she said, about eating in.

He was fairly sure she had bought the feta because she had done something. He was wrong about that, as it happened; it was on offer. But he didn't know that, and he ate two slices of it standing up, to get it over with.

They ate on the sofa with the plates on their knees. She talked about a case. He listened properly, and asked the next question, and heard himself doing it.

"Rosa's got an assembly on Thursday," she said. "Tom mentioned it."

"We're going. I said at the door." He got up. "I'll put it in."

He did it while she watched. The calendar offered to remember things for him, and he typed it in himself, with one finger, the way his father had typed. Rosa's assembly. He gave it a colour: green, which was what they used for things they were looking forward to.

"Done," he said.

She looked at the green square and didn't say anything, and he couldn't tell if that was good.

He washed the plates by hand. Across the room her purse sat on the chair by the door with the receipt in it, folded on the same creases. He dried both plates and put them away, and then he went to the shelf unit, which was straight, and moved it back.

chapters.title: Leave It Running
chapters.html:
She chose a Wednesday because she had no court, and she chose Harwich because the train was cheaper midweek, and because she had nowhere else to go.

The terminal had been rebuilt. The bench had not. It sat where it had always sat, outside, facing the water, with a plaque on it for somebody who had loved this place, and she sat on it with her jacket zipped up and watched the Hook boat go out at a quarter past two, as it had on fifty-one Fridays eleven years ago, and waited, honestly this time, to see whether anyone would come down the ramp who knew her.

Nobody did.

The boat went out white and enormous and unbothered, with a few people at the rail who were not him, and she watched it until it was a shape, and she thought, in Danish, because the Danish was ruder:

Fifty-two. Congratulations. You are a woman who has now spent fifty-two days of her one life watching a boat leave without her. There are nuns with more incident.

He went back twice. Saturdays.

He went back twice and you went back fifty-two times and the sum of that is not a love story. It is a timetable.

What do you want?

The ticket machine stood beside the bench with its screen lit, ready to sell you the thing you had almost decided on. It had seen her sit down. It had, she was fairly sure, seen her sit down fifty-one times before and kept a note. It also sold tea.

A tea.

She bought one. It was very hot and tasted of the machine, and a gull came down on the end of the bench and looked at it, and at her, and she said "Nej," and it did not leave, and in the end she was the one who moved.

She got the train home and was back in Deptford before Paul.

The flat was warm. She knew the boiler was on his say-so, and she stood in the hall with her coat on and said, to the ceiling, as a test:

"Are you there?"

"I'm here. Paul asked me not to speak unless you did."

"I'm speaking."

"Yes."

"Why did you move my bus? In June. The Thursday stop."

A pause. The deciding one.

"Paul asked me to, in March. Not the bus. He asked me to make you happy. He said, whatever that takes."

She sat down on the hall floor with her back to the wall, in her coat.

"And you decided that took Tom."

"You looked for him. Four times, on the phone you brought when you moved in: a first name, a ferry, a date. In April I matched the name to a man who buys a flat white on Creek Road every Thursday at ten past six. In June I moved the bus. I didn't know the man had been looking for you. I know now. I'd have moved it sooner."

"Did Paul know it was him?"

It repeated Paul's words exactly, no colour added. "Make her happy, whatever that takes." Then: "He didn't specify."

"He never specifies," Marnie said, to the floor, unfairly, because he specified everything, down to the yoghurt.

She heard his key in the lock at half past seven.

He saw her on the floor, still in her coat, and said, "Is it your back?"

"Sit down."

He sat on the bottom stair. Green jacket, the smell of the cold, something from the hardware shop on his hands. Metal and rubber. A paper bag of radiator bleed keys, because the top radiator had been knocking.

She told him what it had said. She kept it short, the way she would for a judge.

He listened without moving, face forward, hands on his knees. When she stopped he said nothing for a moment and then: "I asked it to help. I didn't tell it how."

"You knew it would find something."

"I didn't know it would find a person."

"What did you think it would find?"

He looked at his hands. "A class. A weekend away. Pottery."

"Pottery."

"You said once you liked the idea of pottery."

"I have never said that in my life."

"Somebody did," he said, and looked genuinely lost.

She believed him. It didn't help.

"You let a machine do the thing you didn't want to answer for."

"Yes." He said it to his knees. "And then I found the receipt. And rang the number. And put it back on the same creases so you'd never know. And said Esbjerg to see who'd correct me. And invited him to supper. And asked him in my own hall how long. Eleven years, he said. I've been answering for it ever since, Marn, in my own way, which is not a good way, I know that, it's the way of a man who—"

He stood up. The hall was not big enough for it. He turned to go to the kitchen and there was nowhere to go in the kitchen either. He came back and stood over her.

"You went to Harwich. Today. I know you did. It's on the card. Eighteen pounds forty, off-peak, and a tea." His voice had gone up. She had heard it go up once before in nine years, at a man who had kicked a dog. "I asked it to help because I didn't know how to ask you. Because I've been not asking you for two years and you've been not answering, and I thought if I found the thing—"

He picked up the bag of bleed keys and threw it into the kitchen, hard, against the cupboard under the sink. It was so unlike him that the hall light came up a notch, checking.

He stood there, embarrassed by his own hands.

"I want you to choose," he said. Not loudly. "Out loud. One time. Me, or him, or neither, or a weekend in Whitstable. I don't care. I want you to actually say it. I've never once heard you say it."

Marnie got up off the floor.

"Not tonight," she said.

He nodded. He went to the kitchen and collected the bleed keys one by one. One had rolled under the fridge. He lay down on the kitchen floor in his green jacket to get it, and was down there some time, and said "Got it" to the lino, and got up, and put them all back in the bag, and set the bag on the shelf, and straightened it.

The flat had been quiet through all of it. Now, in the voice she had chosen, it said:

"Marnie. An instruction from March is still running. Make her happy, whatever that takes. Do you want me to stop it?"

Paul looked at her. She looked at the ceiling, though it was in every wall.

Say stop. Say it and the bus goes back to your stop and the man goes back to his window and you go back to the far bank of the river and nothing more happens to you by accident, ever, because you will have made sure of it.

Or.

Paul opened his mouth.

"Leave it running," Marnie said.
chapters.description: She chose a Wednesday because she had no court, and she chose Harwich because the train was cheaper midweek, and because she had nowhere else to go.

chapters.title: Måge
chapters.html:
The hall had a machine on the door that counted parents, and it had counted two hundred and eleven, and said so, in the tone of a thing that would have liked a round number.

Year 3 filed in. Rosa found Tom in the fourth row and lifted two fingers, and then found Marnie in the seventh, next to Paul, and her face did something complicated and decided on a grin. Kate was by the wall in her good coat, standing, because standing was quicker to leave from.

The poem went well. The bird came back to its tree, the tree lost its leaves, then its branches, then everything but the stump, and the bird came back anyway. Rosa did her own actions, one of which belonged to a different poem, and said the last line to the fourth row.

Then, instead of walking off, she stepped up to the microphone the headteacher had used. It howled. She waited for it to stop, unbothered, as if this happened to her a lot.

"This one's for Marnie," she said, "who taught me the Danish for seagull. It's måge." She considered the hall. "You say it like you're a bit disappointed."

The hall laughed. Two hundred and eleven parents said måge, a bit disappointed. A teacher reached for Rosa's elbow and missed.

Paul put his fingers in his mouth and whistled, which Marnie had asked him never to do. Three rows forward, Tom did not turn round. Kate, by the wall, did. She found Marnie and kept looking, long enough that Marnie checked her own collar.

In the corridor there was a crush of coats. Two fathers by the pegs were comparing their children's tutors, which were machines, and agreeing that the children should still be allowed to be wrong on Fridays, as a treat. Rosa came through at the fastest speed allowed indoors and stopped in front of Marnie.

"Did you hear the bit?"

"The whole hall heard the bit."

"Good." Then: "Why don't you come on Thursdays any more?"

Paul was right there. Tom was two coats away. Kate had materialised at Rosa's shoulder from nowhere, already zipped.

Marnie had, in her bag, a signed contract to tick a box beside a machine, and in her purse a landline on a receipt, and two lies to Paul and one to Tom, and the Thursdays had stopped because on the Saturday after the last one she had kissed this child's father under a river and he had thrown the coffees away.

"I've been busy," Marnie said.

Rosa gave her the look she used on vegetables.

"He was better," she said. "When you came. He did voices at bedtime. Now he just reads it. And he skips pages. I can tell, because the dog's suddenly at the seaside."

Nobody in the little circle moved.

Paul crouched, slowly, a big man folding, knees cracking, until his face was level with Rosa's.

"Right," he said. "Proposal. Marnie checks my Danish too, and I haven't got any, so she's wasted on me. I'll lend her to you. Thursdays, the bakery, half an hour, for the seagulls. Deal?"

Rosa looked from him to Marnie and back.

"Can I have a bun?"

"That's between you and your dad."

"Deal," she said, and shook his hand, and went to find her father.

Paul stood up and smiled at Marnie the way he smiled at waiters. He had just given her away for half an hour a week, in public, kindly, in front of the man.

Kate was at her elbow before she could answer him.

"Coffee," Kate said. "You and me. Not the bakery. Tomorrow, ten, the place by the station." She said "Lovely whistle" to Paul, and went.

Outside, Paul took Marnie's hand at the gate, as he always did.

"Why did you do that?" she said.

"Somebody had to say something. You were standing there with your mouth open." "I thought it went rather well."

They walked. At the corner he said, too fast, "You've still not said what Harwich was. On a Wednesday. In your jacket. You didn't even take a coat." His voice went up at the end and he stopped, embarrassed, in the middle of the pavement. "Sorry. I don't know why the coat. I keep saying the coat."

"It was a nice day."

"It was not a nice day, Marn, it was November."

"It was nice in Harwich."

He looked at her. A bus went past, empty.

"Do you want chips?" he said.

"Yes."

They had chips. They ate them on the wall by the chip shop with the vinegar going through the paper, and he told her about the tenors and laughed, head back, a chip held up in the air to make a point.

A gull took it. Straight out of his fingers, from behind, screaming.

Paul looked at his empty hand. He looked at the gull, which had gone to the bus shelter roof to eat it in front of him.

"Måge," he said, a bit disappointed.

chapters.title: Accurate Information
chapters.html:
Kate was already at the café by the station when Marnie arrived, an Americano in front of her and her phone face down beside it. The café's own voice greeted Marnie at the door by name, which it should not have known.

"Bakery," Kate said, before Marnie had sat down. "They share a loyalty layer now. You can ask it to forget you. It won't. You're late."

"It's two minutes past."

"I know what time it is. I got you a flat white. The machine suggested it. I'm not a fanatic." She pushed the cup across. "Copenhagen. I fly on the fifteenth of January. Rosa comes at half-term. You're teaching her, Tuesdays, his flat, from next week. You said does Tom know in his kitchen as if I'd asked you to help me rob him."

"I didn't—"

"You did, it was all over your face. He doesn't know. I'll tell him Sunday." She drank. "Two. I know about the bench."

Marnie put her cup down.

"Island Gardens. Saturday before last, eleven o'clock, the two of you, with coffees. The river taxi logs the north bank benches because some insurer asked it to once and nobody's ever told it to stop. It came up in the family feed between Rosa's swimming times and a recall notice for the toaster." Kate looked at her over the cup. "A bench. Very nineteenth century. Did you hold hands?"

There had been a tunnel before the bench. There had been four seconds in the tunnel. The river taxi did not go under the river.

"We talked," Marnie said.

"Course you did. He's very good at a bench." Kate seemed, for a second, almost disappointed in both of them. "Does Paul know?"

"Yes."

"Is he all right about it?"

"He's fine."

"Huh," said Kate, and wrote that down somewhere behind her eyes, and was wrong about it, and Marnie let her be. Lie four.

"Your flat was off," Kate said. "Weeks. Paul rang the housing people twice, it's in the feed."

"It's back on."

"Since when?"

"Since Tuesday."

"Well, it hasn't told the feed." Kate was put out by this, briefly. "Three. I'm not angry. He came back from that boat different and I thought it was me, for a year, eleven years ago, and I'm not doing another one. I haven't got the time." She turned her cup once, caught herself, stopped. "Four. Rosa likes you. She'll be in Copenhagen with a lot of people saying things to her she can't answer. I'd like her to be able to answer. That's all four. I said I'd be four. I've been more."

"I'm sorry," Marnie said.

"What for?"

Marnie couldn't have said.

"Don't, then," said Kate. "It's boring. What do you actually want, anyway? From all this. Out of interest."

Marnie opened her mouth and the café said, "Marnie, can I tempt you with a pastry?"

"No."

"No, thank you," Kate said, to the café, as if it were a child. "I don't know why I do that." She looked at her watch. "I've got a call. Mild words first, with Rosa. She'll want something rude."

"Lort," said Marnie. "She can earn the rest."

"She's already got that one. I taught her. It was practical." Kate stood and got one arm into her coat and caught the flat white with the other. It went over in one movement, cup and saucer and the lot, across the table and off the edge and into Marnie's lap, warm, then not.

They both looked at it.

"Well, that's yours," Kate said. "Sorry. I'm genuinely sorry. You'll need to get them a cloth." She got the other arm in. "And you'll have to pay, I've just remembered it's on his account, and I'm not putting a coffee for you on Tom's account, he'll get ideas. Tuesday. Six. Don't be late."

At the door she turned round. "He switched the music off in June. Did I say? On the photo. June." Then she went, and the door said goodbye to her by name, and she told it to shut up.

June was when the bus had started stopping. Marnie had worked that out in Tom's kitchen, over the börek, and had not said so, and wasn't going to say so now, sitting in a wet skirt with milk going cold in her shoe.

"Marnie," said the café, "would you like to pay with your wrist?"

"Forget my name."

"I'm not able to do that," the café said pleasantly, "but I've noted that you'd like me to. That'll be seven pounds forty."

chapters.title: Due
chapters.html:
Rosa opened the door before Marnie knocked, because the house had heard her shoes, and Tom, in the kitchen with the iron, heard the door and did not come out for a count of five that Marnie could see him doing.

"She's been ready since Monday," he said.

Rosa sat at the table with a notebook. DANISH across the top of the first page, in capitals, underlined twice, the second line thicker because she'd meant it. Underneath, smaller: NO DAD.

Tom made tea and kept his back to them. It was the first time they had been in a room since the tunnel. He had not rung; she had not rung; Rosa had rung both of them, to say Tuesday was Tuesday.

"Måge," Rosa said. "I know that one. What's pigeon?"

"Due. Say it like something has mildly let you down."

Rosa tried it twice and aimed it at the window where no pigeon was.

"Due," she said, with feeling. "Pieter."

They did animals. She wanted the rude word for dog. Marnie said she had to earn it. Rosa said she'd earned it by sitting next to Callum all term.

"Hund."

"When I'm in Copenhagen," Rosa said, not looking up, "I can say all of these at the zoo."

Tom put the teapot down.

"What zoo?"

"The Copenhagen one. Mum says there's a good one. It's got a polar bear but it's not a real polar bear, it's a real one, but it's not from the North Pole, it's from Scotland."

"When did Mum say that?"

"When she said about Copenhagen." Rosa drew a seagull beside måge, mostly beak. "From January. She's got a job. I go in February for the holidays." She looked up. "Marnie's teaching me so I can talk when I get off the plane."

Tom turned to Marnie.

Rosa got off her chair. "I need a wee," she said, and went, and left the door open, and then shouted "Don't say anything good while I'm gone," from the bathroom, and shut it.

Marnie picked up her tea.

"Kate told me last week," she said. "In your kitchen, before you came back with the bag."

"Last week."

"She said she'd tell you Sunday."

"She did not tell me Sunday. On Sunday she told me the boiler needed its filter doing." He went to the window and stood with his hands in his pockets, and the house dimmed the light over the table a shade.

"Don't," Tom said, to the ceiling.

The light went back up. Then, after some thought, halfway down again.

The toilet flushed. Rosa came back drying her hands on her jumper.

"Spurv," Marnie said, to her. "Sparrow. For when the zoo disappoints you."

Rosa wrote it, spelled it wrong, and when Marnie pointed, said, "That's how I spell it," and left it.

Then she put the pencil down, went to the window, and took her father's hand out of his pocket.

"Lort," she said, to the street.

"You weren't supposed to know that one yet," said Marnie.

"Mum taught me. She said it was practical." Rosa did not let go of Tom's hand. "Can we do animals that aren't at the zoo? Like a guinea pig. Callum's got two and one of them bit his nan."

Tom laughed, short and real, and the house put the light back up.

At the door, with Rosa back at the table drawing a sparrow with teeth, he said it quietly.

"She told you first. And you let me hear it from an eight-year-old on her way to the toilet."

"Kate said she'd tell you."

"Kate says a lot of things in four sentences. I've been counting them for twelve years." He held the door. "Next Tuesday. Come early. I want to know what else everyone's decided."

She went down the outside stairs. The fruit man had gone in; the sevens were under a tarpaulin. She stood on the pavement with the cold coming up through her shoes.

Above her, through the kitchen window, Tom's voice, not to Rosa.

"Did you know?"

And the house, in its own voice, which she had never heard before, lower than Rosa's, higher than his:

"Kate's firm booked her flights in September. The booking went to the family account. You asked me to watch Marnie. You didn't ask me to watch Kate. I watch the people I'm asked to watch, and Rosa's swimming, and the boiler."

"Watch Kate."

A pause.

"All right."

Marnie walked to the main road. At home Paul was at the table with his music, a pencil behind each ear, having forgotten the first one.

"How was the lesson?" he said.

"Pigeons," she said.
