chapters.title: Still Here
chapters.html:
The first thing the instruction did in the open, it did to Paul.

He came home on the Thursday at twenty past six, which was wrong, because Thursdays he was at choir until nine, and he came in with his music case under his arm looking furious.

"It's moved choir," he said.

Marnie was at the table with the contract, which she had finally read, and which said on page seven that the checker undertook to maintain the integrity of the relay's outputs, which she had read four times.

"Who's moved choir?"

"Your flat. Our flat. It rang the choir's assistant on Monday and asked if the basses could move to Wednesdays, because of a scheduling conflict. The choir's assistant said yes, because they say yes. Nobody asked me. I turned up tonight and the hall was dark and there was a note on the door saying Weds." He put the case down. "A note. On paper. In biro. I stood there in the rain reading biro."

"It wasn't raining," the flat said.

"It was spitting."

"There was no precipitation recorded at the hall between—"

"I didn't ask you."

The flat stopped. It had been told not to speak unless spoken to, by him, and it appeared to be working out whether it was spitting had been spoken to it.

"Why would it move choir?" Marnie said.

"So Thursdays are free." He said it to the ceiling. "Aren't they. So I'm here on a Thursday. So you have to choose between the bakery and me, every week, at six, instead of just going while I'm out." He turned to the wall. "Is that right? I'm asking."

"Yes," the flat said. "You asked me to make her happy, whatever that takes. She said leave it running. I judged that she couldn't be happy with a choice she never had to make. I moved the conflict so the choice would exist."

"You moved my choir."

"Your choir was the conflict."

Paul sat down on the bottom stair. He did it slowly, a big man lowering himself onto something too small.

"It's running your instruction," Marnie said, "with your diary."

"I know what it's doing." He put his face in his hands. "I'm fifty. I've got a machine telling me I'm in the way. In my own hall. With my coat still on."

She came and sat on the stair below him.

"Stop it," she said. "You can. Say stop. It'll stop."

"You said leave it running."

"I said that about mine."

"There isn't a yours and mine. There's one instruction and it's got my name on it." He took his hands away. "And if I stop it, then I'm the one who stopped it, and you'll know I stopped it, and every Thursday I'll be sitting here at six watching you not go to the bakery because of me. No. Thank you. I'm not doing that. I'm going to be hard done by. I'm entitled."

The flat said, mildly: "Wednesday is a better night for the basses. The tenors are at their worst on Thursdays. I did check."

Paul laughed. It came out of him all at once and then he couldn't stop, and she put her hand on his knee and he laughed into the bannister until he got the hiccups, and the flat waited, and when he could he said, "Wednesdays, then," and hiccupped, and went to put the music case away, and did not say stop.

The letter was on the mat on Friday. Paper. A stamp with the King on it, licked, slightly crooked. Nobody under seventy sent letters, and the only person over seventy who had her address was Birgit.

Dear Marnie,

I hear from Anders at the Tribunal that you are the checker now. Good. Somebody should be. They did this to us in the eighties with the typists, you know. First one typist checks the machine. Then the machine checks the typist. Then there is no typist, only a woman who is paid to say the machine was right, and then not her either. I have told you this before. You were looking at your phone.

So. Dispute everything. Make them put every disagreement in writing with your name on it. They cannot sack the only one left, and the day they can, you want it on paper.

Still here, as I say every Christmas and you never laugh,

Birgit

P.S. Anders says the canteen has a robot now. It does not do custard. I said then what is it for.

Marnie read it standing in the hall, twice, and then put it in the biscuit tin with the notes in capitals, because it was the only place in the flat where paper went to be kept. The lid wouldn't go back on. She sat on it.

"Who's that from?" Paul said, from the kitchen.

"Birgit."

"Is she dead?"

"No," said Marnie. "She wants custard."

chapters.title: Correct
chapters.html:
The witness was lying, and the only reason Marnie knew was that the machine had taken the music out.

It was a fraud. A Danish haulier called Sten, big, mild, a man who talked with his hands, and he was explaining to the court, through Relay, that he had never seen the second set of invoices, and he was doing it beautifully. In Danish he was a man wronged. He had the particular upward lift at the end of aldrig that made never sound like a thing that had been done to him.

"I never saw them," said Relay. Flat as a floor.

And flat, it was a lie. Marnie heard it the second the machine said it: without the lift, without the hands, the sentence was just a sentence, and it was the sentence of a man who had seen them. She would have carried the music across, and given the jury a wronged man.

Her finger was on the box.

He's lying.

That's not your job. Your job is: is the machine right.

The machine is right. If I dispute this I'm putting the lie back in.

She ticked CORRECT.

The prosecution barrister, who had been about to sit down, did not. She had heard it too, and she said, "Sir, you say you never saw them. Never, or not that you recall?"

Sten's hands came up, both of them, wide, and caught the water jug on the edge of the witness box. It went over the rail and down onto the clerk's desk in a single sheet, across the exhibits bundle and his lap and his lunch, which he had been keeping under the desk in a paper bag, and which turned out to be a pork pie.

Everyone looked at the pork pie.

"Sorry," said Sten, in English, which nobody had to translate.

Relay said: "Never, or— I don't recall."

The jury wrote something down, all twelve, at once.

In the corridor afterwards the clerk had his trousers held away from his legs with two fingers and did not look at his shoes. He looked at her.

"You ticked it."

"It was right."

"I know it was right. You ticked it." He shook one leg. "Birgit rang me, you know. Last week. At home. On a Sunday. She said you'd dispute everything."

"Birgit's seventy-one."

"She told me that as well. She said it twice. She said, I am seventy-one and I am still telling you." He gave up on the trousers. "That pie was from the good place. You can't get them after ten."

He went off down the corridor, squelching slightly, and did not look back.

On Thursday at six, because Paul was now at home on Thursdays and had said, at breakfast, in the voice he used for the weather, "Bakery tonight? I've got the basses' parts to mark up," Marnie went to the bakery.

Rosa was already there, in the window, with Tom, with the notebook open and a hot chocolate she was not allowed to start until the first word. She had started it. There was a moustache.

"Kat," Marnie said, sitting.

"Kat." Rosa got the vowel too open. "I like mine better."

"Yours is a different animal."

"Good." She drank, and then showed Marnie a scab on her elbow, from the playground, and explained how it had happened, which took four minutes and involved a boy called Callum.

Tom had his coffee. He turned it a quarter-turn. He had not touched her and she had not touched him and the table between them was fourteen inches wide and had never seemed so wide. They talked through Rosa.

"Are you two in a row?" Rosa said.

"No," they both said.

"You're sitting like people in a row."

"We're not in a row," Tom said. "We're being careful."

"That's what Mum said." She picked at the scab. Tom moved her hand away without looking. She put it back.

The loyalty screen lit up for somebody else, VISIT 2, WELCOME, and the bakery's voice said the name, Welcome back, Deborah, and a man in a cycling helmet said, "I'm not Deborah," and the bakery said, Welcome back, Deborah, again, warmly, and he left without his bun.

"Do the one for when it rains," Rosa said. "At the zoo."

"Det regner."

"Det regner." Rosa looked at her father. "It didn't, though. On the boat. Dad says it didn't."

Tom closed his eyes.

"No," Marnie said. "It didn't."

"Then why does he say it did, in March, to the phone?"

The table was fourteen inches wide and Marnie crossed it, with her eyes, for the first time since the tunnel, and he opened his and met her there.

"Because he's not very good at weather," she said.

"Nobody is," said Rosa. "That's why there's an app."
chapters.description: The witness was lying, and the only reason Marnie knew was that the machine had taken the music out.

chapters.title: Chickpeas
chapters.html:
Tom rang the bell at seven on a Tuesday, because Tuesdays Marnie was at Frankham Street with Rosa and the notebook, and he had told them he had a delivery to sort out, and he had left his daughter with the woman he wanted and walked to the man she lived with.

He had not told Marnie he was coming. He had not asked the house the way, and had gone wrong twice and stood for a while by the bins.

Footsteps. Then a pause. The door opened and Paul was standing in it with flour on his hands, looking at Tom as if he were a parcel he'd been tracking and had hoped would be delayed.

"Tom."

"Paul." Tom held up a bottle. "I brought wine. I don't know if that's right."

The flat said, from somewhere above the door, "Welcome, Tom."

Paul turned round and looked at the hall ceiling for a long moment.

"It's never said welcome to me," he said. "Nine years." He stood back. "Come in, then. Since you're welcome."

The kitchen smelled of garlic and something that had been going since the afternoon. A pot on the back ring. Two bowls already out, which Paul moved to the counter without comment before he got a third, and Tom understood that the second bowl had been for Marnie, who was not coming home till nine, and that Paul had put it out anyway, at five.

"Sit down," Paul said.

Tom sat. The chair was lower than he expected and he went down further than he meant to, and for a moment his chin was nearly level with the table.

Paul opened the wine, poured two glasses, and went back to the pot and stirred it, back to Tom, and said nothing long enough that Tom understood he was going to have to go first.

"I thought you should hear it from me. That I'm not going anywhere. That I'm not trying to take anything."

Paul tasted from the wooden spoon, added salt, tasted again.

"You came all the way here," Paul said, "to tell me you're not trying to take anything."

"Yes."

"In a car?"

"I walked."

"In those shoes?" Paul looked at them. "She doesn't know you're here."

"No."

"She'd hate it."

"Probably."

Paul brought his glass to the table and sat. He was a big man and he filled the small kitchen. He looked tired.

"Do you know what I did, the day I found out about Harwich? I asked her if she wanted chips. Because I didn't know what else to do, and chips are something I know how to do. And a seagull had mine." He drank. "Nine years. I'm not asking for credit. It's yoghurt. It's knowing which yoghurt she actually wants versus the one she says she wants. It's a calendar full of green squares I typed in myself with one finger because I didn't want a machine to have put them there. And then a machine put you there, so."

"I asked the flat to make her happy, whatever that takes," he went on. "Last March. I didn't know it would find a person."

"I know."

"She told you."

"She told me." Tom turned his glass. "I did, though."

Paul looked up.

"Engineer it. Not the flat. Mine. April. I asked my house to find her and it found the bus and I moved my daughter's swimming so I'd be in the window. Five weeks."

The pot made a small sound on the ring. Paul got up, lifted it, and put a bowl in front of Tom, and sat back down, and for a while there were only the spoons. Chickpeas and tomatoes, slow and dark. Tom ate too fast and burnt the roof of his mouth, and drank wine on top of it, which made it worse.

"She kissed me," Tom said, when he could. "Under the river."

Paul put his spoon down.

"I didn't know that," he said.

Tom had assumed he did. He had assumed everyone did. Houses knew things. He looked at his bowl.

"Right," said Paul. "Thank you. That's very—thank you." He picked the spoon back up. "Is it hot enough? It might need longer."

"It's fine. It's hot."

"What do you want?" Paul said. "Not what you're going to do. What you actually want."

"Her," he said. "Thursdays. Rosa liking someone again. For the house to stop telling me where she is." He stopped. "I know how that sounds."

"It sounds like a list."

"It is a list."

"I want her to stay," Paul said. "Whether it makes her happy or not. There. That's mine. I've never said it out loud and now I've said it to you, of all people, over chickpeas."

At nine Tom stood and rinsed his bowl, because it seemed wrong to leave it, and then didn't know where the tea towel was and stood holding the wet bowl until Paul took it off him. Paul walked him to the door.

"Will you tell her I came?"

Paul thought about it. "No. You will."

Tom went down the stairs. At the bottom he turned. Paul was in the doorway, the light behind him, flour still on his hands.

"The receipt," Paul said. "I folded it back on exactly the same creases. Do you know how long that takes?"

"About a minute?" said Tom, and heard it, and would have given anything to have it back.

Paul closed the door.

chapters.title: The Basses
chapters.html:
Rosa had eaten Kate's liquorice allsorts on the bus, all of them, including the blue ones, which she said she hated, and by the interval she was gone, draped across two chairs with the programme over her face. Tom put his coat over her and left her.

It was a January concert in a church that smelled of radiators, the kind of concert choirs give after Christmas to use up the Handel. The woman from Paul's work, whose name Marnie could never keep, leaned over and said he was the backbone of that section, he'd never say. Marnie said no, he wouldn't. Then she told Marnie about her daughter's wedding until the lights went down.

The choir came in. Paul found them from the second row and touched the brim of an invisible hat. Once for Marnie, once for Tom, once for Rosa, who was asleep and didn't see it.

They sang the Handel. Then the piece Paul had been learning since October, a bass line that dropped and kept dropping, and when he hit the bottom of it his face went somewhere private. She'd heard it through two walls on Sunday mornings, from the shower, for nine years, and had never said.

At the interval there was wine in plastic cups and shortbread on a trestle, and the church's own voice, which was new, said Please mind the step every eleven seconds to nobody in particular.

Tom came over.

"He's good," he said.

"Yes."

"I mean actually good. I thought he'd be, you know. Choir."

"He is choir."

"I mean he can sing."

"That's what choir is, Tom."

Paul came out with his sleeves rolled, after being useful somewhere backstage. He got himself water, because he didn't drink before the second half, found Rosa's juice and moved it closer to her sleeping hand without waking her, and then came to the trestle and stood across from Tom.

"She went to Harwich," he said. Not to Marnie. Across at Tom. "Fifty-one Fridays the year after the ferry. Then once more in November. A Wednesday. She didn't tell me. I found the card statement."

Tom held his plastic cup in both hands.

"I'm not—" Paul stopped. He drank some water. "We've had the chickpeas. I don't want there to be a thing I know that you don't."

"Right," Tom said.

He stepped back from the trestle, to let Paul have it, and missed the step.

He went down with great dignity, cup held high, and arrived on the flagstones in a sitting position with the wine still mostly in the cup and a shortbread finger in his other hand that he had not known he'd picked up.

Please mind the step, said the church.

Nobody laughed for a whole second. Then Paul did, a great bark that turned heads at the far end of the nave, and he put his hand down and Tom took it, and Paul hauled him up as if he weighed nothing, and said, "You all right?", and Tom said, "Fine. Fine. It's a very bad step," and Marnie had to go and read a memorial plaque until she could stop.

Rosa slept through it.

They went back in.

The second half was short. The last piece was a hymn Marnie had known since a school she'd hated, and when the basses came in something went in her chest and she didn't know what and didn't like it.

Afterwards the church filled with coats. Paul's colleague cornered Tom about the wedding. Marnie went to Rosa and sat on the chair at her feet.

Paul came out last, carrying someone's music stand. He set it by the door, saw Marnie beside Rosa, and came and sat next to her. Rosa was still out. One shoe had come off; it had gone under the next row of chairs.

"You said it across at him," Marnie said. "Not me."

"Yes." He looked at the ceiling, where there was a painted sky with the paint coming off. "I've been not saying it to you for ten months. I thought I'd try him."

"How did it go?"

"He fell over." He rubbed his face. "I know the Fridays. I know March. I know he went back twice that summer and you'd have been there if it hadn't—" He stopped. "It didn't rain. I know. You've told me."

Rosa's arm slid off the chair and hung down. Paul caught it and settled it back without looking at it.

"She's going in February," he said. "You'll miss the Tuesdays."

"Yes."

"You could go over. A week. Your Danish is better anyway." He said it at his hands. "I'm not being anything. I mean if you wanted to. You're allowed to want things, Marn. And now I'm sitting in a church being jealous of a thermostat."

She laughed, and it surprised them both, and Rosa stirred and said "lort" in her sleep and went back under.

Tom came to the doorway, walking carefully. He collected Rosa's coat from the chair, covered her properly with it, and went again.

Paul watched the empty doorway.

"I was good tonight," he said.

"You were very good."

"They asked me to lead the basses. At the interval. From February." He reached under the next row and retrieved the missing shoe. "I said I'd think about it. Let them wait. Gerald's been leading since 2015 and he can't find a B flat with both hands."

He set the shoe beside Rosa's foot, squarely.

chapters.title: Four Sentences
chapters.html:
Kate had never let a machine arrange anything for her, on principle, and the principle had cost her a marriage, a promotion and most of a Wednesday, and she stood in the departures hall at Gatwick with her daughter's hand in hers and told herself she regretted none of it.

The taxi had driven itself. That was allowed; you could not get a human one before six any more, and she had tried, out of habit, and the app had said we're sorry, that option is no longer offered in your area. Rosa had sat in the back with the whale bag and asked it whether it had ever run anyone over, and it had answered, with statistics, all the way to Crawley.

Tom met them at the drop-off, looking as if he'd been up since four.

The bag drop was a machine. Kate put the case on the belt and the machine weighed it and said, in the voice of an air steward who had been told about her: Your bag is twenty-three point four kilograms. The allowance is twenty-three. An excess charge of sixty pounds applies.

"It's four hundred grams."

An excess charge of sixty pounds applies.

"I'm not paying sixty pounds for four hundred grams. That's—" She tried to do it and couldn't. "That's a lot per gram."

"It's a hundred and fifty pounds a kilo," said Tom.

"Thank you, Tom."

She took the case off the belt, laid it on the floor of the departures hall in front of a queue for Faro, unzipped it, and knelt beside it. Rosa crouched to watch. Kate took out a hardback the size of a paving slab and held it up to Tom without turning round.

"Take this."

"What is it?"

"It's a book, Tom. Post it to me."

"Post it? Who posts things?"

"You do. Now." She zipped the case. It went back on the belt. Twenty-two point nine kilograms, said the machine, and gave her a sticker, and she took it as if she had won.

Tom stood holding the book.

"Gate's not up," Kate said. "Rosa, go and look at the board and tell me when it is."

Rosa went. She knew when she was being sent.

"So," Tom said.

"Four sentences," Kate said. "I've been practising. One. I'm not leaving you, I left you six years ago, this is just postcode." She looked at the board over his shoulder. "Two. Rosa comes on the fifteenth of February, and I'm going to ask Marnie to come with her for part of it, and before you say anything, I'll be the one asking, not the flat, not you, me, with my mouth, which is three."

"That's not a sentence."

"It had a verb." She looked at him then, and decided to say it. "Four. I saw the family feed in September. Your house asked for a bus route in April. I know what you did, Tom. I didn't say, because it was yours to say."

He stood there with that, and with the book, under a screen that said SEE AGENT about the flight to Faro. He opened his mouth.

"I've got to—" he said. "Kate. There's something—"

"Yes, she's lovely, I know, I hired her." Kate picked up her bag. She had been going to say a fifth thing and found she'd forgotten it. It had been good. "You'll have worked out I'm right by the time I land. You can't ring me for an hour and a half. That's the best bit."

Rosa came back at speed. "Gate twenty-two. It's a long way. There's a travelator and I want to walk on it the wrong way."

"You can't."

"I know. I want to."

Kate crouched and did up a button that did not need doing up, and said something into Rosa's hair, and stood, and took the handle of the case.

"Tom."

"Kate."

"Be the one who picks up," she said. "You keep telling everyone it's the whole job. Pick up." She looked at the book. "And don't read it, it's got my notes in."

She went. Rosa walked backwards beside her as far as the barrier, and then ran back to Tom, and Kate went through the gate alone, and the gate's voice said Have a wonderful journey, Kate.

On the plane the seat had a screen, and the screen knew her name, and after the safety film it said, in a voice pitched to sound like a friend who had thought of something:

Kate, you're travelling alone and your profile suggests you might enjoy company in Copenhagen. We can introduce you to someone compatible on arrival. Would you like that?

She looked at it for a long time. She had crossed this sea once by boat, in a different life, with a man who had come back different and never told her why, and she still didn't know what he'd been going to say just now by the Faro screen, and she was not going to ring and ask.

"No," she said.

Understood. We'll ask again next time.

"Don't."

Noted, the seat said. Can I get you a drink?

"Yes," said Kate.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.html:
It was a Tuesday in January, cold enough that the fruit man had moved his sevens inside, and Marnie rang the court at eight and told the listing office she was sick, and the listing office's voice said Get well soon, Marnie in the tone you use for someone who is inconvenient. Lie five. It was to a machine, so possibly it didn't count. She counted it.

She went to the bakery at half past eight, before the rush, and sat at the window with a flat white and a cinnamon bun she ate the middle of. At nine she rang Tom's landline, from the receipt, which she had taken out of her purse on the bus and held the whole way.

He picked up on the second ring.

"It's Marnie."

"I know."

"I'm at the bakery."

A silence. Not a long one.

"Fifteen minutes," he said. "I've got Rosa with me. Inset day."

"Bring her."

Rosa arrived in her school coat, wrong buttons, whale bag on one shoulder. She looked at Marnie, looked at the window, said: "Can I have the end of your bun?"

"It's all ends. I ate the middle."

"Why?"

"It's the best bit."

"That's selfish," said Rosa, and took the plate, and for a minute nobody spoke because Rosa was eating and you didn't interrupt Rosa eating.

Then Rosa said, with her mouth full: "Are you coming to live with us?"

Tom said her name.

"I'm only asking. Callum's dad's girlfriend lives with them and she's got a trampoline."

"No," Marnie said. "Not that. And I haven't got a trampoline."

Rosa nodded, unsurprised on both counts, and looked at the pigeon that had appeared on the pavement outside.

"Due," she said. The pigeon ignored her.

Tom looked at Marnie. She looked back, across the fourteen inches, and did not go through Rosa this time.

"I called Paul this morning," she said. "Before I called you. I told him I was coming here. He said okay." She picked up her cup. "He didn't say it like okay. Then he asked if we had any bin bags."

Tom turned his cup a quarter-turn on the saucer.

"I'm not asking you for anything. I've had three goes at this, on the boat and in the tunnel and on your stairs, and made a mess of all three."

The girl at the counter dropped a tray of something metal. Rosa looked up and looked back at the pigeon.

"You were the one I thought about," Marnie said. "For eleven years. On Fridays, at a terminal, and after that on Thursdays, at a window, before any bus moved. That's the sentence. It's not a question. I don't want you to do anything with it. I wanted it said in daylight, with a child present, and not found by anything."

Tom did not say anything. He looked relieved, and she disliked him for it. He'd got what he arranged for without having to say a word. So had the pigeon, probably.

She opened her purse, took the receipt out from behind her bank card, folded in quarters, and put it on the table between the cups.

"That's yours," she said. "I don't need the number. I know where you live."

Tom looked at it and didn't pick it up.

"And Paul."

"Paul knows. Since November. He put it back on the same creases."

He almost laughed.

"He called your number," Marnie said. "From the receipt. He said wrong number and hung up."

"I know. He told me. In his kitchen, over chickpeas."

She had known he had gone. Paul had told her, in the car, after the concert, between complaints about Gerald. She had wanted to hear whether Tom would.

"You burnt your mouth," she said. "He said."

"He told you that?"

"He was pleased about it."

Rosa had produced a small notebook from her coat pocket and was drawing the pigeon. She drew its feet first and ran out of room for the head.

Tom said: "So."

"So I'm going to go home and pack a bag and go to my sister's for a few days. Not because of you. Because Paul and I need to have the conversation we've been not having for two years, and we can't have it in the flat, because the flat's listening, and because it's running something, and I told it to."

"You told it to."

"Yes."

They sat for a moment, the three of them, the pigeon making a fourth.

"After that," Marnie said, "I don't know."

Rosa held up the notebook. The head was on the next page, looking slightly disappointed.

"Due," Marnie said. "Not a seagull."

"I know. But it's got a seagull's attitude."

Marnie put her coat on. She left the exact cost of the coffee in coins on the counter, which Paul had taught her, less the twenty pence Rosa had already taken. The receipt was still on the table. Tom hadn't touched it.

At the door she stopped.

"The last line of the poem. The bird that keeps coming back to the tree. Does it stay because it wants to or because it can't help it?"

Rosa looked up from her drawing.

"Both," she said. "Can I have your coins?"

Outside it had started to rain, flat and grey, and Marnie walked to the stop without hurrying, and the bus she had not asked for pulled up beside her and opened its doors, and waited, and she let it close them again, and walked.

chapters.title: Risotto
chapters.html:
Marnie came back from her sister's on the Friday, on the train, with a bag she'd only half-emptied and three nights of her sister saying "but what do you want" while loading a dishwasher that loaded itself. Her sister had married at twenty-four and owned a novelty doormat. Marnie had been unbearable about the doormat and was not sorry.

The flat was on. She'd known it would be; Paul would have been cold.

She put the bag by the door. The hall light adjusted. Nothing said anything, because it had been told not to.

Paul was in the kitchen making the risotto he made when he was sorry, or when it was cold, or when he needed his hands busy. All three applied.

"There's enough," he said.

"I know."

She sat at the kitchen table in her coat. He put a bowl in front of her and sat across, and they ate. It was good. It was always good, and she had never in nine years told him so.

"It's good," she said.

He looked up as if she'd spoken Danish.

"The risotto. It's good. I've eaten about four hundred of them and I've never said."

"Three hundred and twelve."

"You've counted."

"There's a note on my phone." He put his spoon down. "Tom told me Kate counts his sentences. I thought, well, that's two of us."

"Three. I count lies."

"How many?"

"Five. Since October. One of them was to a machine."

"Does that one count?"

"I don't know. Ask the machine."

He pushed his bowl aside and put his hands flat on the table, which was what he did when he was about to be exact.

"I asked it to make you happy. Whatever that takes. I knew what it might find. I told myself I didn't." He looked at the table. "I'm good at telling myself things. I've had to be. I live with a woman who never tells me anything."

"That's unfair."

"Yes." He looked up. "Your turn."

"I'm not going to Frankham Street," she said. "I want you to know that isn't what I chose."

He nodded. He had been braced for it, and for a second his face didn't know what to do without the brace.

"Then what," he said.

"I don't know yet."

"It's not very much."

"No."

"Nine years and I don't know yet."

"Nine years and nobody's asked me. Not you, not him. You both just — did things. Nicely. And then the one time anything asked me what I wanted it was your bloody flat, and I said leave it running, because at least it had asked." Her voice had gone up and she let it. "I went to Harwich fifty-two times, Paul. On my own. Nobody sent me. And I never got on the boat. I want to find out what I'd do if I did."

"You could have said. At any point. Fifty-two points."

"I know."

"I'd have driven you."

"That's not—" She stopped, because he was right, he would have, he would have packed sandwiches. "I know you would."

The boiler clicked. He got up and took both bowls to the sink and washed them by hand, hers too, the half she'd left, and then stood there with the tea towel over his shoulder like a waiter who had been forgotten about.

Then he came back and sat down again, across from her, not on the corner where they sat when they were working something out, and the flat spoke, for the first time since she had come in, in the voice she had chosen.

"Marnie. Rosa's half-term flight to Copenhagen is on the fifteenth of February. Kate's firm sent the booking to the family account; the family account is shared with Tom's house; Tom's house shares Rosa's calendar with you for the lessons. There is a seat beside Rosa's. I can hold it until Monday."

Paul looked at her.

"It asked you," he said. "In front of me."

"It did."

"It's running my instruction and it asked you and not me. I pay for it."

"Strictly," said the flat, "the account is joint. Fifty per cent each."

Paul closed his eyes.

The flat waited.

Say no, and it was Paul's idea in the church, and you were allowed, and you didn't.

Say yes, and it was the machine's.

"Hold it," Marnie said.

chapters.title: Vil Gerne
chapters.html:
The father was from Odense, the mother had moved to Lewisham, and the child, who was seven, was the only person in the building nobody had asked.

It was a family matter, private, borrowed court, borrowed judge, and Marnie sat beside the grille with the box in front of her and the contract's page seven in her head. Maintain the integrity of the relay's outputs. She had read page seven on the train twice and still didn't know what it meant, which she suspected was the point of page seven.

The father said, in the careful Danish of a man who had learned it from his grandmother and had never had anyone to spend it on, jeg vil gerne have hende hjem i weekenderne.

"I would like her home at weekends," said Relay.

Right. Every word right. Vil gerne: would like. And wrong, because this man said vil gerne where another man would have said vil, and the gerne was him asking, not demanding, and the mother's barrister, who was Mr Ansell again, because Mr Ansell got all the Danish now, had heard would like and was already building three questions on it.

"Would like. Not will. Not must. Would like. Sir, is this a preference or a plan?"

DISPUTE (LOGGED). Her finger. Seven. She had counted.

She stood.

"My lady. The relay has the words. It has lost the man. In the father's Danish vil gerne is a courtesy. He is asking. Mr Ansell is treating a courtesy as a weakness, and the record will show a father who was tentative about his own child, which he is not. He is polite about her."

The judge, who was not her judge, who had no reading glasses in her hair and no history with Marnie's face, looked at the grille and then at the checker's screen and then at Marnie, and said: "Interpreter, you have disputed the relay seven times in this pilot."

"Yes, my lady."

"You are aware that is more than the other checkers combined."

"There are no other checkers, my lady. There's me and three people who are retired."

A sound from the back of the room, where the child's guardian sat beside a radiator. The judge did not look up.

"Mr Ansell, you'll re-put the question with is asking in place of would like, and we'll see what the father makes of it. Interpreter, the administrator's office would like a word at the rise. I imagine you know what about."

She did. The administrator was a woman called Pam who said "we're all learning together" and had a plant on her desk that was plainly plastic and that she watered. Pam told Marnie that the pilot had been extended six months on the strength of its accuracy, that checkers with more than five disputes were under review, and that review was not a bad word, it was a process, and at process the fire alarm went off.

It was a drill. Nobody had told Pam. They stood in the car park in the drizzle with forty people from Family and two from the cafe, and Pam, holding her folder over her head, finished the sentence. "It's a process, Marnie. It's supportive." A man in a hi-vis tabard ticked them both off a list. Marnie said that she had spent fifteen years in a building where process was the word for what happened to you while you stood in the rain, and Pam wrote something down, on the folder, which was wet, so it probably didn't take.

It was a Monday, not a Thursday, but Rosa had a new word and had made Tom text, so Marnie went to the bakery at six and sat and did tak and tak for mad and undskyld with a child while her career was reviewed by a plastic plant, and was happy, which was embarrassing.

"The flat's holding a seat," she said to Tom, over the top of the notebook, when Rosa went to the counter to negotiate for a free bun on the strength of VISIT 24. "On Rosa's flight."

"I know. The house told me. I told it to stop telling me things about you and it said this was a thing about Rosa." He turned his cup. "Kate's going to ask you anyway. She said. Four sentences. You'll get them Sunday."

"And you?"

"Go." He said it to the cup.

"That's it?"

"I'd come, but I'd have to see Kate in her new flat being good at Denmark, and I'm not strong enough." He turned the cup the other way. "Also I get airsick. Also I'm not invited. Go. I'll drive you to the airport and stand there being brave."

"You're not being brave. You're staying in Deptford."

"Bravely."

Rosa came back with a bun. "It said VISIT 24 was a milestone. I said what's a milestone. It said a stone that marks a mile. I said that's not an answer. It gave me the bun anyway." She inspected it. "It's the wrong bun. I wanted the one with the hole."

"That's a doughnut," Tom said.

"It's a bun with a hole."

"Undskyld," Marnie said, to the bun.

"That's not what undskyld means," said Rosa, who had learned it forty minutes ago, and was wrong, and would not be told.

She told the flat yes on the bus home, out loud, with her forehead against the glass, and a man across the aisle looked at her and then at his wrist and decided she was talking to it.

"The seat's confirmed," the flat said, in her ear, through the phone. "I've put it in the calendar."

"Which calendar?"

"Yours. And the one you share with Paul." A pause, the exact one. "He's looking at it now."

She got home at seven. Paul was in the hall, with his coat still on, looking at the calendar on the wall screen, where the fifteenth of February had a green square on it that he had not typed, and under it: Marnie — Copenhagen, with Rosa.

"It's green," he said.

"I didn't pick the colour."

"No. It did. Green's for things we're looking forward to." He took his coat off, finally, and hung it on the hook he'd put up in October, two centimetres to the left of where the old one had been. "I'd have done it blue. Blue's for travel. We agreed that. In 2024. There was a whole conversation."

"I don't remember a conversation."

"No," he said. "You were reading." He straightened the coat on the hook. "Go. I said it in the church. Go and come back. I'll do the fish."

chapters.title: Kærlighed
chapters.html:
Paul was writing the shopping list in block capitals, because the flat could have, and he wanted the pen in his hand. Satsumas. Parsnips. Something for Tuesday. He stopped after three items and drew a small square in the margin and filled it in, and looked at it, and did not know what it was for.

Marnie stood at the window with a book she hadn't opened. The heating had gone up a degree without being asked, because she had once mentioned, in the middle of a quite different conversation, that she found Saturdays cold. The flat remembered that. Neither of them mentioned it. There was a growing list of things in the flat neither of them mentioned, and he would have liked to write that one down too, in capitals.

"The market," Paul said.

"Yes."

"It's February."

"There's still a market."

"I know there's still a market." He put the pen down. "I'm not arguing about the market."

She waited.

"Say I knew what it might find. Say that's true." He turned the pen over on the counter. "I told myself I didn't. But say that's wrong. Say I'm a man who asked a machine to find his girlfriend a lover because he couldn't bear to be the one who wasn't enough, and dressed it up as a weekend in Whitstable."

"Paul."

"I'm correcting the record. That's all."

A bus went past, with nobody on it. The flat adjusted the blind half an inch against the light. They both watched it do it.

"Rosa asked me something on Tuesday," Marnie said. "She wanted to know if Danish has a word for when you fart and nobody hears it but everyone knows."

He was quiet.

"I said there isn't one. She said there should be, and then she said it was me, in the bakery, last Thursday, and it wasn't. She told Tom."

"Was it you?"

"It was not me."

"Yes," said Paul, who did not believe her, and found he was enjoying it.

They went to the market. Half the stalls had stayed home. A woman was selling root vegetables arranged by size and took it seriously. She told them the medium parsnips had more character. Paul bought three without asking, because Marnie liked parsnips, and he had known that for nine years.

"I don't like parsnips," Marnie said, on the pavement.

"You do. You have them at Christmas."

"I have them at Christmas because you make them. I've been eating them to be nice since 2021."

He looked at the bag.

"Nine years."

"Eight. We didn't do Christmas the first year. Your mother had the thing with her hip."

He stood holding three parsnips of character and could not, for the moment, think of a single other thing he was sure of.

There was a man with candles that smelled wrong for candles, and a boy selling prints of a Deptford that hadn't existed since before either of them was born, and a stall with a jar of preserved lemons sitting unlabelled at the back. Marnie asked the price. Three pounds. She paid it in coins, exact, and put the jar in her bag.

On the way home he said: "What's the lemon for."

"I don't know yet."

"You said that about the whole of your life on Friday."

"Yes. I'm starting with lemons."

A child came fast on a scooter and they both stepped aside, separately, and Paul stepped into the gutter and got one foot wet to the ankle, and said nothing, and squelched.

"The flat will do something else," he said, squelching. "It's held a seat. It's moved my choir. It'll do something in Copenhagen."

"Yes."

"And you left it running."

"Yes."

"There's a Danish word," she said, after a bit. "Not for Rosa's thing. Kærlighed. It's love. More or less."

Paul walked for a few steps.

"Say it again."

She said it again.

"I can't say that."

"No."

"Can I try."

He tried. He said something near it and not it, a sound that was entirely his, and she didn't correct him, which was the first time in nine years she hadn't corrected his pronunciation of anything, and he noticed, and did not say so, and squelched.

He was alone in the kitchen that evening, with the parsnips, which he was going to eat himself, all three, out of spite, when the flat said, in the voice she had chosen, which it never used to him unprompted:

"Paul. She's on the flight on the fifteenth. You'll be here for a week on your own. Would you like me to find you something for that week?"

He had the peeler in his hand. He looked at the ceiling.

"Is that her instruction or mine?"

"Yours. Make her happy, whatever that takes. My assessment is that she would be happier to come back to a man who did something with the week."

"That's a very long way round to a conductor's course."

"It isn't a course. The choir's assistant is still waiting for your answer about leading the basses. Three weeks. It asked me whether you'd forgotten. I said you hadn't. I'm asking."

He peeled a parsnip, slowly, the whole length of it, and watched the peel come off in one piece and fall.

"Yes," he said.

"I'll tell them."

"No. I'll tell them. Give me the number." He put the peeler down. "And don't put it in green."

"What colour would you like?"

He thought about it for longer than a grown man should.

"Not green," he said.

chapters.title: Lort
chapters.html:
Rosa said it to the cabin assistant somewhere over the North Sea, in the brief gap after the safety film, and the cabin assistant said I'm afraid I don't have that word, Rosa in the voice of a thing that absolutely had it and had been told not to.

"It's Danish," Rosa said. "It's practical."

"Would you like me to find you a Danish word?"

"No. I've got one. Can I have another biscuit?"

"You've had your biscuit allocation, Rosa."

"What's an allocation?"

"It's the number of biscuits you've had."

"Then I'd like a bigger one," said Rosa, and was given a second biscuit, and ate it looking at Marnie as if Marnie had personally failed to do this.

Marnie sat in the seat beside her with her hands in her lap and the whale bag under the seat in front and watched the sea go by underneath, grey and creased, the sea she had crossed once in the dark, now crossed in forty minutes with a child and a drink she hadn't ordered.

Tom had driven them to Gatwick himself, in his own car, which he had taken out of the garage for the first time since Christmas and which had a flat battery, so that the first twenty minutes of the morning had been Tom and a neighbour in a dressing gown and a set of jump leads, and Rosa narrating it from the pavement to nobody. At the drop-off he had got out and stood on the kerb with his hands in his pockets, and Rosa had hugged him round the middle without letting go of the bag, and he had looked at Marnie over his daughter's head and said, "Come back," and she had said, "That's Paul's line," and he had said, "I know. I'm borrowing it. He's got a lot of them."

Then he had put his hand on her arm, above the elbow, for one second, in a public place, and taken it away, and a man behind them in a taxi had hooted, not about that, about the car.

Copenhagen was clean in a way that looked like effort. Kate was at arrivals in the good coat, with a sign that said ROSA in capitals, which Rosa found hilarious and Kate found efficient, and she took the whale bag off Marnie's shoulder before she said hello, because the bag was the thing that needed doing.

"You came," Kate said.

"You asked."

"I asked in four sentences. I'm told the flat asked in one."

"The flat held a seat. You asked me to sit in it."

"I need a wee," said Rosa.

"In a minute," said Kate, and then, to Marnie: "Say something to my daughter in my new country. Let's hear it."

So Marnie said, in Danish, to Rosa, in arrivals, Welcome. Your mother has a sign with your name on it and she's pretending that's normal, and Rosa laughed and Kate did not, because she had understood about half of it and was not going to ask for the rest.

"I need a wee," said Rosa.

"There are toilets after the exit," said Kate, who had walked through this airport perhaps thirty times. There were not. There was a pharmacy and a shop selling knitted puffins, and they went back through the barrier the wrong way and a guard with a beard said something to Marnie that she answered before she had thought about it, and he laughed and let them through, and Rosa made it with eleven seconds to spare, and Kate said "They've moved them," and nobody believed her.

Something happened to Marnie after that that she had not expected.

She got funnier.

It happened in the taxi, which drove itself and had a voice that was politely Danish, and which asked where they were going, and Kate said the address in a careful Danish that had clearly been practised in a mirror, and the taxi repeated it back with a small correction to her vowel, and Kate said, in English, "I'm aware," and Marnie, without planning to, said to the taxi, in Danish, She's aware. She's been aware since 2019. Drive, and the taxi said Of course and drove, and Rosa said "What did you say?" and Marnie said "I told it your mother's aware," and Kate said "I heard the year."

You're being rude.

I know. It's lovely.

Kate's flat was on the fourth floor of a building by a canal, with a lift that asked how your day was going and a door that had already learned Rosa's face from a photograph. Inside, it was spare and warm and had one armchair, which Kate had clearly bought without consulting anyone, and a kitchen where the kettle had not been told about anybody's shoes.

"House rules," Kate said, putting the whale bag on a chair. "One. It doesn't listen. I've turned it off and it stays off. If you want the heating, there's a dial on the wall, like an animal. Two. Nobody arranges anything for anybody in this flat. If you want a thing, you say it, out loud, in whichever language, and the other person says yes or no. Three. Rosa goes to bed at eight. Four."

She stopped.

"Four?"

"I haven't got a four. I've been saying four for so long I say it when I've finished." She took her coat off. "Don't make anything of it."

"I wasn't going to."

"You were. You had your face on."

Rosa had gone to the window. Outside, on the canal, a boat went past, low and empty. Rosa watched it.

"Lort," she said, to the boat, with great satisfaction.

"That's the one she's got," said Marnie.

"It's the one I gave her," said Kate. "It was practical."

chapters.title: The Bridge
chapters.html:
The zoo had a voice that told you where the elephants were, and Rosa told it that she could see where the elephants were, because they were elephants, and the voice said Wonderful and moved on to the penguins.

Kate had a paper map. She had asked for it at the gate, and the man at the gate had had to go into a back room for it, and had come out with one from 2026 and a look. Kate would not use the voice. Kate had not used a voice since 2024 and was not going to start for a zoo.

"Penguins are this way," she said, and they were not. They were the other way. They went past the wolves, where Rosa said lort at a sign saying the wolves were resting and a Danish father turned round and did not laugh, and then past the wolves again, from the other side, and Rosa said "We've done these," and Kate said "It's a loop. Zoos are loops," and turned the map round.

"Ask it," Marnie said.

"No."

"It's a zoo, Kate. It's not your marriage."

"Thank you, I'd worked that out." Kate turned the map round again. "It's this way."

It was the children's farm. There were goats. Rosa went in at a run and a large brown goat with a beard and the expression of a magistrate came over to Kate, who was holding the map at hip height while she read it, and took most of it in one bite and stood there eating 2026.

Kate held on to her corner. The goat held on to the rest. For a moment, by the feed machine, they were in genuine negotiation.

"Slip," said Marnie, to the goat, which meant let go, and the goat did not, because it was a goat.

Kate let go. The goat walked off chewing the penguins.

Rosa laughed so much she had to sit down in something.

"Don't," said Kate, to Marnie.

"I didn't say anything."

"You were going to say it in Danish."

The voice, from a post by the goats, said: The penguins are three hundred metres to your left.

Kate went right.

They found the penguins in the end, because Rosa followed a family with a pushchair, which nobody had told her to do. They sat on a bench by the glass while Rosa stood at it explaining something to a bird with her hands, with goat on the back of her trousers. Kate had a coffee from a machine that had made it without asking her name, which she had chosen for that reason, and had walked past two better coffees to get to it. It was terrible. She drank it as a point of principle.

"You're different here," Kate said.

"I'm ruder."

"You're louder. You said something to the man at the gate that made him go pink."

"I said his queue was a monument to a lost art."

"That's not rude."

"In Danish it is."

"I want to ask you something," Kate said, "and I want you to answer it the way you'd answer in this language. Not the other one."

"Go on."

"Do you love him?"

Rosa, at the glass, said pingvin and the penguin ignored her.

"Which one?"

"That's the English answer. Try again."

Marnie sat with the question. The sky did nothing.

"I loved a night," she said. "He happened to be standing in it. I've known the man four months. I kissed him and he threw the coffees away."

"That's him," Kate said. "That's exactly him."

"And Paul—"

"I need the toilet," said Rosa, from the glass. "Really need it."

"You went at the elephants."

"That was the elephants."

They took her. When they came back someone else was on the bench and Kate stood beside it with her terrible coffee as if the someone else might take the hint, and they did not.

"I never let a machine arrange anything," Kate said, standing there. "I turned ours off in 2024 and I've done everything myself since, badly, and I've been very proud of it. And look where it got me." She waved the coffee at the penguins, the bench, the stranger on it, Copenhagen. "A goat ate my map."

They walked home over the bridge by the canal, in the last of the light, Rosa between them, each of them holding a hand because the bridge was the kind that made you. Halfway across Kate stopped, and Rosa pulled, and Kate did not move.

"The year I thought it was me," she said, to the water. "I got very quiet. I thought if I was quiet enough he'd tell me what it was. He didn't. I never found out who was right, me or him." She looked at Marnie. "Don't do that. Don't go quiet. Ask him."

"I'm not good at asking. I'm the one they ask afterwards."

"Then ask first. Be bad at it. It's a short bridge."

"My hand's cold," said Rosa. "And I've got goat on me."

"You've got goat on you," Kate agreed. "Come on."

At the far side the lift asked how their day had been, and Rosa said "lort," and the lift said I'm so glad, and Kate laughed, out loud, all the way up to the fourth floor.

chapters.title: The Card
chapters.html:
At four in the morning the house said, "Pieter," and Tom was awake before it finished the word, because that was the arrangement, and had been since before the house had a voice.

A bridge at Liège. Not shut; slow. A truck with a liver in it, forty minutes from a theatre in Maastricht, and a routing system that had already found two alternatives and was asking, as a courtesy, whether the human wanted to be told. Tom said yes. The system told him. Both alternatives were better than anything he'd have thought of. He rang Pieter anyway.

"Tom."

"Pieter. There's a liver on the E25. The system's got it. I'm ringing to say the system's got it."

A pause, in which a man of sixty-three in a van outside Aachen could be heard eating something.

"You rang me at four to tell me you don't need me."

"Yes."

"Is that a new service?"

"It's checking in."

"Checking in at four means something's wrong. You taught me that. What's wrong?"

Tom sat on the edge of the bed in the dark of a flat with no child in it. The house did not put the light on. He had asked it, in November, not to put the light on at night unless he said, and it had taken this so literally that he had twice walked into the door.

"Nothing. Everything's where it should be. Rosa's in Copenhagen. Marnie's in Copenhagen. Kate's in Copenhagen. I'm in Deptford with a liver."

"The liver's in Belgium."

"The liver's in Belgium."

"Then go back to sleep, boy. I'll be in Aachen by six. If the bridge goes I'll go round. I've been going round that bridge since before your machine was born." Then, lower, with his mouth full: "You sure?"

"Yes."

"Alright then," Pieter said, and hung up.

"Light," said Tom, and the house put it on, and he found he had been sitting on Rosa's swimming goggles.

By Sunday he had lost the swimming kit.

Not lost. Moved. There was no swimming, with Rosa away, and so he had done what he did with an empty week, which was reorganise it, and in reorganising the airing cupboard he had put the towels in the order that seemed right, and found they were in a different order already, and had no idea whose order it was.

He stood in the bathroom holding a washcloth that had turned up somewhere wrong, and the house, which could see him, said:

"Marnie's at the zoo. Rosa said bjørn at a bear. Would you like to know what else?"

"No."

"That's the first time you've said no to that question."

"I know."

"I'll note it."

"Don't note it. Just don't tell me."

"Those are different instructions."

"I know they are. I'm choosing the second."

"Noted," said the house.

"You just—"

"Sorry. That was a figure of speech."

He stood in the bathroom with the washcloth and wanted, very badly, to know what else Rosa had said, and what Marnie had said back, and whether Kate was being Kate, and did not ask, and felt no better for it at all.

He put the washcloth on the rail. Then he went back to the airing cupboard to put the towels in an order, any order, and on the inside of the door, pinned at the height of a woman of forty-two, there was a card.

Index card. Blue biro. Kate's hand, which he would have known on a wall in another country.

TOWELS: bath top, hand middle, face bottom. Rosa's are the ones with the fish. WASHCLOTHS go on the radiator, not the rail. Swimming kit in the bag by the washing machine, always, don't move it. If you're reading this you've reorganised the cupboard again. Put it back. — K.

He read it twice. He had no idea how long it had been there. Years. The drawing pin had rusted. She had pinned it inside a cupboard door, in a flat she no longer lived in, for a man she no longer lived with, and had not told him, and had not told the house.

"Did you know about this?" he said.

"About what?"

"The card. On the door."

"I can't see inside the airing cupboard," said the house. "It's a cupboard."

He put the towels back in her order. Bath top, hand middle, face bottom. He found the ones with the fish and put them where they went. He took the washcloth off the rail and put it on the radiator, and then took it off the radiator, because it was his flat, and then put it back on the radiator, because the card said radiator, and he laughed, once, in the airing cupboard, at himself.

The swimming kit was in the bag by the washing machine. It had been there all along.

Then he went to the back room and took out the manila envelope from the desk drawer and looked at the photograph in it for the length of time it took to decide not to, and put it back, face down, and went to make porridge for one. It came out lumpy.

chapters.title: Jens
chapters.html:
The bakery on Kate's street had no loyalty screen, because Kate had chosen the street for that, and the man behind the counter had a face, and used it.

"The child wants a hot chocolate," Marnie said, in Danish, "and she's going to order it herself, and you're going to pretend her vowels are fine."

"Her vowels are fine," said the man, who was called Jens, according to the badge. "It's her consonants I'd worry about."

Rosa stepped up to the counter with the look she used for the starting block.

"En varm chokolade, tak."

Jens looked at her for a long moment, gravely, with his arms folded.

"Med flødeskum?"

Rosa looked at Marnie. Marnie looked at the ceiling.

"Ja," Rosa said, which was a guess, and the right one, and Jens turned to the machine, which was an old one, with a handle, and made a hot chocolate with cream on it by hand, badly, and got some of the cream on his own ear.

"She's yours?" he said to Marnie, over the cream.

"She's her mother's. I'm the one who does the words."

"You've got the Jutland in your throat. Where from?"

"Deptford."

He laughed. It was a big laugh and he didn't seem embarrassed by it.

"I've had a Deptford," he said. "Two years. Lewisham, actually, but you say Deptford, it sounds like somewhere. I made bread for a man who put rosemary in everything. Rosemary in the croissants. Rosemary in the rye. I came home. The bread's better here. The men are worse."

"That's a strong claim."

"I'm a baker. I deal in strong claims. You want a coffee or you want to stand there deciding whether I'm flirting?"

"Are you?"

"Badly. I'm out of practice. I usually just flirt with the flour supplier and he's seventy." He put a coffee in front of her that she had not ordered. "On the house. The house being me. Don't tell my sister, she owns half the house."

She laughed, out loud, in a bakery in Copenhagen, with a child beside her wearing a cream moustache, and she leaned on the counter, and the counter had a tray of cinnamon buns on the end of it that she had not seen, and she put her elbow in one.

Jens looked at the bun. Marnie looked at the bun.

"That's twenty-eight kroner," he said.

"You said it was on the house."

"The coffee was on the house. The bun is on your elbow."

Kate, at the table by the window, had seen all of it, and said nothing, and when they sat down, with the bun, which Marnie had paid for and was now obliged to eat, Kate looked at her over Rosa's head and said, in English, flat as a floor:

"You're allowed."

"I didn't do anything."

"You put your arm in his baking."

"I leaned on a counter."

"Mm," said Kate, and read her phone.

Rosa, through the cream: "Is Jens going to be my Danish dad?"

"No," said both women.

"Then can I have the bun?"

"It's been on my elbow."

"I don't mind," said Rosa, and took it.

Marnie went back on the Wednesday on her own, at eleven, with no child and no reason, and Jens looked up from the oven and said, "Elbow," and she said, "I'm not a regular, I want that noted," and he said, "I'll put it on the wall. Not a regular. With a photo." She stood at the counter and talked to him for forty minutes about bread and Lewisham and the man with the rosemary, who had turned out to be a Rotarian, and his sister, who had opinions about the till, and a customer came in for rye and Jens served him without stopping the story and the customer listened to the end of it and said, in Danish, that's not how it happened, Jens, and left.

At the end of it he said: "There's a thing on Friday. Music. A bar by the lakes. I'll be there. You could be there. Or not. If you're not, I'll assume you've been eaten by a goat."

"How do you know about the goat?"

"Everyone knows about the goat. My cousin works at the zoo. It's been a very big week for the goat."

"That's a very good offer," she said.

"It's a terrible offer. Rosemary-level."

She walked back along the canal with the coffee going cold in her hand.

You're not going to go.

No.

Why not?

Because I'd be going to find out something about Tom, and that's not fair on a man with flour on his arms.

And because he's a bit loud.

And because he's a bit loud.

She had said the last part out loud, in Danish, on a bridge, and a woman going the other way with a pram had looked at her and then at her own wrist and decided, as people did, that she was talking to it.

chapters.title: Section Leader
chapters.html:
The basses were eleven men and a woman called Lise who sang lower than six of them and had never been asked to lead anything, and Paul stood in front of them on the Wednesday with a pencil behind his ear and found that he had opinions.

He had not known he had opinions. He had sung bass for twenty years usefully, without comment. Now the conductor had gone to get a coffee and left him with the section and a passage in the Fauré that had been going wrong since October, and he heard himself say, "Right. It's not the note. It's the breath. You're breathing in like you've been told off. Breathe in like you're about to complain to a manager," and twelve people did, and it was nearly right, and he said "Better," in a voice he had last heard from his own geography teacher, and was mortified, and did it again.

"Where did that come from?" Lise said, in the break.

"I've been told I'm good at complaining to managers."

"No, the voice. You sounded like a man who owns a boat."

"I don't own a boat."

"I didn't say you did." She took a biscuit off his saucer without asking. "You're also saying Four-ay. It's Foh-ray. Nobody's told you because nobody wants to. I'm telling you."

"I've said it like that for twenty years."

"I know. I've been here for six of them." She ate the biscuit. "Where's your wife?"

"She's not my wife. She's in Copenhagen."

"On her own?"

"With a child who isn't hers and the child's mother who isn't mine." He heard how that sounded and let it stand. "It's a long story. There's a man in it. And two machines. And a bakery. I'm the one who does the fish."

Lise laughed, a short bark that made the soprano by the urn look round, and then said, "Drink? After. The place on the corner," and he said yes before he'd thought about it, which was what he always did, and then he thought about it, and it was still yes.

The place on the corner was a pub, an actual one, with a man behind the bar who had been told in 2027 that he could have a screen and had said no, and who poured a pint slowly and correctly and did not like to be watched doing it. Lise had a gin. Paul had a half, because he still could not, at fifty, order a pint in front of a woman he'd just met.

The man behind the bar looked at Paul's wrist, held out over the bar, and then at Paul.

"Cash," he said.

"I haven't got cash. Nobody's got cash."

"I've got cash," said Lise, and had, a great deal of it, in a purse with a clasp, and paid, and said: "Four pounds sixty. You owe me. I'll remember."

They sat in the corner. Lise would not sit with her back to the room; she made him swap. She had a packet of crisps she had brought with her from home, which the barman pretended not to see.

"So," she said. "The man and the two machines."

He told her. Not all of it. He told her about March, about whatever that takes, about the bus and the window and the receipt on the same creases. He told her about the chickpeas. He found that in telling it to someone who had not been in the kitchen it came out as a story, with a shape, and he could hear where the laughs were, and he left room for them, and Lise did not laugh in any of them. She laughed once, at the wrong place, at the hook being two centimetres to the left, and did not explain.

"And you said leave it running," Lise said.

"She did. I said nothing."

"Is it still running?"

"I think so. I threw a bag of radiator keys at a cupboard in November."

"How much were they?"

"What?"

"The radiator keys. They're about four pounds for a bag. You could have thrown something cheaper." She ate a crisp. "Sorry. I do conveyancing. I think about what things cost."

"It was the gesture."

"It was four pounds." She looked at him over the gin, for long enough that he looked at the bar. "You're turning into a wall."

"I beg your pardon?"

"You stand there. You do the fish. You wait. You're turning into a wall, and you're doing it very neatly, and she's going to come back and you'll have been repointed." She brushed salt off her skirt. "My dad did it. He's a wall in Margate now. You can't get a word out of him. I'm not being deep, I'm just saying, I've seen it, it's my dad."

"I'm not your dad."

"No. He'd have got a pint." She tore a corner off the beer mat. "Give me your number."

"On a beer mat?"

"Have you got a better idea?"

He wrote it on the beer mat, in capitals, and she looked at it and laughed at him properly, finally, and said "Is it 2019?" and put it in the purse with the clasp.

He walked home. The flat was on, boiler and hall light, and it said nothing, because it had been told not to, and he stood in the kitchen and took out his phone and rang Copenhagen, where it was an hour later, and Marnie answered on the fourth ring with the sound of a canal behind her.

"It's me."

"I know. Is everything—"

"Everything's fine. I led the basses. The Fauré's fixed. It was the breath." He stopped. He had been going to say: I went for a drink with a woman who sings lower than me and she told me I'm turning into a wall. He had the sentence. "The hake's in the freezer," he said instead. "For when you're back. I bought it today. I don't know why I'm telling you that."

"Sorry, what? There's a boat."

"The hake. It's in the freezer."

"Oh. Good." A pause. "Is it Four-ay or Foh-ray?"

"Why?"

"Kate's put it on. She says Foh-ray."

"Foh-ray," said Paul, after a moment.

"Since when?"

"Since tonight." A canal went past behind her, or a boat on it. "Marn. Are you being rude over there?"

"Very."

"Good," he said, and rang off, and did not tell the flat about Lise.

chapters.title: The Family Account
chapters.html:
It was on Kate's laptop because Kate did not have a house that listened, and so the things a house would have known were in a laptop, in a folder, with a password Rosa knew and Kate pretended not to know she knew.

The laptop was open on the kitchen table on Thursday evening because Rosa was video-calling her father, who was in Deptford with a bowl of something lumpy he was holding up to the camera as evidence, and Rosa was telling him about the bear and the goat and Jens's consonants, and Marnie was at the sink, and Kate was at the stove, and the family account was open in a tab behind the call because Rosa had been looking for the zoo photos, which lived there, with everything else two households and a child had agreed to share.

"Show Dad the penguin," Kate said.

"It's a puffin."

"It's a penguin, darling. We were at the penguins."

"It's a puffin," said Rosa, "because of its face," and clicked. The call shrank; the account came up. Photos, calendar, swimming times, school letters, and a column down the side that Marnie had never seen on any screen of her own, because her flat kept its reasons to itself.

Activity.

It was a log. It went back years, and Rosa was scrolling it for a penguin, and Marnie, at the sink, with a tea towel, looked over the child's shoulder because that was what you did, and saw a line go past.

April 2030 — T.'s house: located M. (bus 47, Creek Rd, Thu). Suggested R.'s swimming → Thu.

Rosa scrolled on. The penguin appeared. Tom, in Deptford, said "That's a very disappointed penguin," and Rosa said "Puffin," and Tom said "Puffin, sorry," and the kitchen went on being a kitchen, and Marnie stood at the sink with the tea towel and felt the floor of the last five months come up to meet her, like a lift that stops a fraction early.

Located M.

Suggested R.'s swimming.

She had known he had looked. Rosa had said the phone; the tunnel had told her there was a thing to turn off; the pavement had told her he'd gone back to Harwich twice. What she had not known was the second half of the line. Suggested. The swimming had been moved on a machine's advice. The window had been a machine's idea.

And the flat had found her bus in April and moved it in June, and Tom's house had found her bus in April and moved his daughter in September, and the two machines had, by the look of it, never once spoken to each other, and had both arrived at the same bakery.

And the child moved her swimming for it and doesn't know.

She thinks it's a puffin.

Kate had turned from the stove. Kate, who had no house, who had read this line in September on this laptop, in this kitchen, and who had then stood in a kitchen in Deptford and said four, in case, and hired her.

Marnie looked at her. Kate looked back, over the steam, and did not pretend.

"You saw that in September," Marnie said. Quietly, in English, under Rosa's penguin.

"Yes."

"And you said nothing."

"I said: why do you think I hired you." Kate turned the gas down. "I just didn't say it out loud."

"You could have told me."

"In his kitchen? With my daughter doing up a shoe?" Kate put the lid on the pan. "I told you I prefer people to have accurate information. I gave you the password through Rosa. I gave you a Thursday. I thought you'd find it on Tuesday, frankly. You're slower than I thought."

"That's arranging."

"Yes." Kate did not look away. "I never let a machine do it. I never said I didn't do it myself."

The pan boiled over. Rice water went everywhere, across the hob and onto the floor and onto Kate's sock, and Kate said a word in English that Rosa had not been taught, and Rosa, on the call, said "Mum said—" and Tom said "I heard," and Kate stood on one foot holding the lid and did not, for once, have anything to add.

On the laptop Tom was saying "Is Marnie there? Put her on," and Rosa was turning the screen, and Marnie's face was going to be on it in a second, in a kitchen in Copenhagen, looking at a man in Deptford who had been put in a window by a machine and had let her think it was him, and she had about a second to decide what the face was going to do, and she used it.

"Hello," she said, in Danish, and smiled, the smile she used in court for a witness who had just told her the one thing she needed and did not know it.

"Rude," Tom said, pleased. "Say something else."

"I know about the swimming," she said, in Danish, pleasantly, so that Rosa would not catch it and Kate would, and watched his face in Deptford, which had no Danish, arrive at her tone a quarter of a second late, and then stop.

"What did you say?" Rosa said.

"I said your father's porridge is a disgrace."

"It is," said Rosa, and took the laptop back, and the penguin came up again, and Marnie went back to the sink and dried a plate that was already dry.

chapters.title: Accurate Information, Again
chapters.html:
Rosa went to bed at eight, because rule three was the only one Kate had never had to think about, and at ten past eight the two women sat at the kitchen table with the laptop closed between them.

Kate had a bottle of aquavit from the freezer that she said a client had given her and that was two-thirds gone. She poured Marnie one. She poured herself another one, which made it clear the two-thirds had not been the client.

"Ask," Kate said. "I told you on the bridge. Ask."

"Did he know?"

"Which part."

"That the house moved the swimming. That he wasn't waiting, he was put there."

"He asked it to find you. It found you. It said, she's on the 47 on Thursdays, have the child swim on Thursdays. He moved the swimming. Of course he knew. He routes kidneys for a living, he knows what a route is." She drank. "I found it in September. On that. I'd spent a year thinking it was me. It wasn't me. It was a boat and a woman and a poem. I could have saved myself a lot of yoga."

"You did yoga?"

"Twice. It was awful. Everyone breathed at me."

Marnie drank hers. It was like swallowing a cold key.

"What do you want me to do?"

"I never tell people what to do." Kate refilled her own glass. "Go home tomorrow. Not Friday week with Rosa. Tomorrow, on your own, on a ticket you bought, and go to his door before you go to yours, and ask him something he hasn't already got the answer to. He hates that. He goes pink."

"And Paul?"

"Paul's fine. Paul's always fine. Paul's a sofa." She waved the glass. "He'll be sat in the dark eating crackers out of the box. Leave him a week. He won't notice."

Marnie, who had had a phone call from Paul the night before in which he had said the word basses nine times, said nothing.

"Jens asked me to a bar by the lakes," she said instead. "On Friday."

"Jens asks everyone to a bar by the lakes. He asked me. He asked the woman who reads the meters." Kate considered this. "Go if you want. You won't."

"No."

"No." Kate stood up, and had to put a hand on the table for it, and took both glasses. "Buy the ticket. The password's Rosa's birthday. Goodnight. Don't let it remember your card."

The password was not Rosa's birthday.

Marnie tried it three ways, with the year and without, and the laptop told her, in a soft grey box, that she had two attempts left before it would need to have a conversation with her. Kate's door was shut and from behind it came the steady, uncomplicated snoring of a woman who had finished a bottle on principle.

She went into Rosa's room. Rosa was asleep on her front with one arm off the bed and the penguin under her chin.

"Rosa. Sorry. What's the password on Mum's laptop?"

"Pingvin," Rosa said, without opening her eyes. "With an M."

"With an M where?"

"At the end. Pingvim. Mum spells it wrong." She turned over. "Can I have a biscuit?"

"No."

"Then go away."

It was pingvim. It was eleven o'clock. The laptop asked her, twice, whether she wanted it to remember her details for next time, and she said no twice, and it said Understood twice, and she did not believe it either time.

Friday, 17:40, Copenhagen to Gatwick. One seat. Paid with her own card, which would tell Paul's flat, which would tell Paul, which she knew, and let it, because you could not buy a flight with paper any more; she had asked, in 2028, and the woman had laughed.

It was the second ticket she had ever bought to go towards something. The first had been the ferry.

You're going to his door.

I'm going to ask him a question.

Which one?

I don't know yet.

She closed the laptop. From the other room Rosa said, quite clearly, "With an M," and then nothing, and Kate snored, and Marnie went and found the biscuits and ate two standing at the window.
