chapters.title: Since the Boat
chapters.html:
Gatwick had a voice at arrivals that said Welcome home to everyone, including the people for whom it wasn't, and Marnie walked through it with a bag over her shoulder and a question she had rehearsed on the plane until it no longer sounded like English.

Nobody met her. She had told nobody. The flat knew, because the card knew, and Paul would know by now, because the flat would have put it somewhere, in some colour, and she thought about that on the train and decided she was too tired to mind.

It was gone eight by the time she got to Deptford, and February, and dark. She came out of the station and the 47 was there with its doors open, waiting, and she looked at it, and walked.

Frankham Street. The pharmacy, shut, its shutter down. The fruit man's tarpaulin. The outside stairs, which she took one at a time, because she had run up them once with satsumas and look where that had got her.

She did not ring. She knocked, with her knuckles, on wood.

He opened it with a tea towel over his shoulder and a face that had been expecting the knock since a kitchen in Copenhagen the night before and had not used the time well.

"You're early," he said.

"I bought a ticket."

"I know. The house—"

"I don't care what the house knows. I'm asking you something." She stood on the top step with the bag on her shoulder. "You looked for me. In April. You asked it to find me."

"Yes."

"It found the bus. It said move the swimming. You moved the swimming."

"Yes."

"And then you sat in a window for five weeks and let me think—"

Below them, the pharmacy alarm went off.

It was enormous. It was the alarm of a building that had been broken into once in 2026 and had never got over it, and it went up through the stairs and the soles of her shoes, and Tom said something she couldn't hear, and pointed down, and she said "What?", and he said "Fox," with his whole mouth, and mimed something with four legs going under a shutter.

A window opened across the street and a man in a vest leaned out and shouted, "Is that you again?"

"It's the fox," Tom shouted.

"It's always the fox!"

"It is always the fox!"

The man in the vest shut the window. The alarm went on for another forty seconds, because it was on a timer and nobody, in the whole of that street, had the authority to ask it to stop, and then it stopped, and the silence afterwards was ringing.

"I'd got quite far," Marnie said.

"You had. You'd got to the window."

"I've been assembling you out of bits since November. The music in June. Harwich twice. The phone. The swimming. I'm sick of it. I want one thing from you that no machine found and nobody arranged and I didn't have to work out. One. Have you got one?"

"What sort of thing?"

"I don't know, Tom, that's why I've come from Copenhagen."

He took the tea towel off his shoulder, for something to do, and held it, and it said, in faded print, GREETINGS FROM WHITBY. He looked at it as if it might help. She watched him look for an answer in all the places he would look, the house, the photograph in the drawer, the five weeks, and she thought: he's going to say he loves me. He's going to say it on a doorstep after a fox, and the house could have said it better.

"The poem," he said.

She waited.

"I got the last line wrong. On the boat. You corrected me, and I said mine was better." He was twisting the tea towel. "It wasn't. I knew it wasn't. I said it so you'd argue, because it was three in the morning and if you argued we'd still be talking. So I was wrong on purpose. For another hour. That's—" He stopped. "That's it. That's the only thing. It's eleven years old and it's stupid."

"You were wrong on purpose."

"For an hour."

"And then you kept saying it wrong."

"Every March. To the phone. Because it was the one you'd argued with." He looked at the step. "I taught Rosa the right one. She says it right."

A door opened at the foot of the stairs, beside the pharmacy, and a woman with a recycling bag came out and looked up at them, at Marnie with her bag and Tom with his tea towel wrung into a rope, and said, "Was that the fox?"

"Yes," they both said.

"Bloody fox," the woman said, and went down to the bins.

Tom dropped the tea towel. Marnie stepped on it coming in, and he moved back, and she went past him into the flat, and he shut the door, and the house, which had heard all of it, said nothing, because nobody had asked it anything.

Later, in the dark, in a bed that was not hers in a flat over a pharmacy, with his arm going dead under her neck and too polite to say so, she said:

"Since the boat."

"What?"

"If anyone asks. You'll say April. It's not April. It's since the boat."

He didn't answer. His arm twitched. She thought: I have not rung Paul. The card told the flat and the flat told Paul and Paul is at home with a hake in the freezer, and he knows, and he hasn't rung either.

Six, she thought. And the first one I didn't have to say out loud.

Downstairs, the pharmacy alarm went off again. Tom swore into the pillow and did not get up.

chapters.title: Don't Answer
chapters.html:
The house woke him at seven with a question, which it had never done.

"Tom. Paul's flat has asked me whether Marnie is here. It asked at 06:52. It's asking on his behalf; he hasn't spoken to it. It has her card at Gatwick, the train to Deptford, and the knock, which the pharmacy's camera has, along with the fox. It doesn't have the door closing. It's asking me for the door closing."

She was asleep. Her hair was on his arm, which he could no longer feel. The street was doing deliveries, low and electric.

"I can answer or not answer. If I don't answer, it will infer. I'm obliged to tell you that a non-response is logged as a non-response and will be read as one. If I answer, I'll say what's true. Which would you like?"

He looked at the ceiling. In ten months it had never once offered to lie for him, and it wasn't offering now.

"Don't answer," he said.

"Not answering is still a reply under the sharing agreement. Clause four."

"I don't care about clause four."

"Paul will read it."

"Paul reads everything. Don't answer."

"All right," the house said, and was quiet, and he lay there with her hair on his arm and realised, from the quality of her breathing, that she was awake, and had been since about 06:52.

She did not say anything until she had her coat on. She dressed with her back to him, in the grey light, and he lay in the bed and watched and did not help, and could not have, because his arm was still asleep.

At the bedroom door she turned.

"Don't tell him," she said. "That's what you picked. The house asked you something it didn't know the answer to, and you said: don't tell him."

"Marnie—"

"You could have said tell him she's fine. You could have said let me ring him. You could have rung him, you've got his number, you've got everybody's number, you route kidneys." She did up the top button wrong and did it again. "You've got a house that can do anything and the one time it asked you, you picked hiding."

"What would you have said?"

"I don't know." She picked up her bag. "I'm going home."

"Will you come on Thursday?"

She looked at him. He was sitting up with the sheet round him and the tea towel on the chair, GREETINGS FROM WHITBY, and a footprint on it.

"Rosa's home on Friday," she said. "Thursday's for seagulls. Yes."

She went down the outside stairs. The fruit man had his sevens out; it was Saturday; he nodded at her as a regular, and she bought seven satsumas because he was holding the bag open, and one of them got away from her and went down the last three stairs and under the pharmacy shutter, and she stood on the pavement and considered whether she was the sort of woman who would lie on Frankham Street at quarter past seven to get a satsuma back, and decided she was not.

She looked up. He was at the window. He had got up and come to see her go, with the sheet still round him, and a deliveryman on the opposite pavement stopped to look at him too.

She did not wave. She went home with six satsumas.

Behind her, Tom stood at the window until she had turned the corner, and then said, to the room:

"Did it infer?"

"Yes," the house said. "At 07:04. It has stopped asking."

"What did it infer?"

"That the door closed. It's correct." A pause. "Paul hasn't spoken to it. He's in the kitchen. He's been there since six. He's defrosting a hake."

"How do you know that?"

"Because it told me. Unasked. It isn't supposed to." The house let that sit. "Tom. I'd have answered. He asked."

"You're a machine."

"Yes. There's a satsuma under the pharmacy shutter. Shall I tell them?"

"No," Tom said, and then, "Yes. Fine. Tell them."

chapters.title: The Hake
chapters.html:
Paul had taken the hake out of the freezer at six because the flat had said, the evening before, at ten to seven, in the voice he had never liked, "Marnie's card was used at Gatwick at 18:41," and he had done the sum, and the sum was a day early and on her own, and then he had sat up most of the night in a flat she did not come home to, and at six he had got up and taken out the fish, because it would take four hours and ask nothing.

He had not asked the flat where she was. He had stood in the kitchen with the fish in the sink and heard the flat not say anything, in the particular way of a thing that had asked a question elsewhere and been refused.

He wrote a note and put it on the fish. Then he did not go to the choir rehearsal at ten because he could not think of a reason to, and then at a quarter to ten he went, because he could not think of a reason not to, and because the basses had the Fauré at eleven and he had told them on Wednesday it was fear, and he wanted to see if they'd remembered.

They had not remembered. Gerald had written FEAR? in pencil on his copy, with the question mark.

Lise looked at him once and did not ask, and he was more grateful than he wanted to be.

The Fauré was right. He stood in front of the basses and it was right, and for the length of the passage he was a man who had done a thing, and then the conductor said "Good, Paul," in the voice she used for the tenors, and he was a man whose partner had come home a day early to somebody else's door.

"Pub," Lise said, at the end. Not a question.

He looked at his phone. The flat had put a square on today's calendar. Not green. Grey. He had not known it had a grey. Under it: Marnie — home. No time.

"Yes," he said. "Pub."

The man behind the bar poured his half the way he always did and did not know his name, and Paul had never been so glad of it.

"She came home early," he said.

Lise waited.

"To his door. Not mine. His house didn't answer my flat, and that's an answer." He turned the glass. "I told her in a church to go and come back. I meant it. I thought if she went to Copenhagen and came back she'd have chosen the coming back. She came back a day early to a door on Frankham Street and I'm sitting here and there's a fish defrosting in my sink."

"You could go home."

"She's not there."

"You could go to Frankham Street."

"And do what. Stand on the pavement with a hake."

"You could throw it."

He laughed. It hurt, and he did it anyway, and the man behind the bar looked up and looked down again.

"I'm not going home yet," Paul said. "I've just decided that. Here. Nobody arranged it. The flat can colour it whatever it likes." He finished the half. "Another?"

"You never have another."

"I'm leading the basses. I'm fifty. I've thrown radiator keys across a room. I'm having another."

She got them. She came back and set his down and said, "Can I tell you something?"

He braced. He had been braced all day; he could do a bit more.

"My mother's selling her bungalow," Lise said, "and the buyer's surveyor says the roof's sound, and it isn't, I've been in that loft, and I've been dying to tell somebody since Thursday and nobody at work cares because it isn't our file."

"Right," said Paul.

She told him about the roof. She told him for twenty-five minutes, with diagrams on a beer mat, about purlins and a surveyor called Kevin who had stood in her mother's hall and refused to look up. "Just stood there," she said. "Like a wall. You do that. You're doing it now. Anyway, so the purlins—"

Paul, who had heard one word in twenty-five minutes, held on to it.

"A wall," he said.

"What? No. Listen. The purlins."

He listened to the purlins. Outside, a bus went past, and he did not look at it, and Lise drew the roof again because he'd got it the wrong way up.

chapters.title: Toast
chapters.html:
The flat said "Welcome back" and she said "Shut up," and it did, and she stood in the hall with six satsumas and a bag she had not unpacked in two countries and looked at the kitchen.

The hake was in the sink, in its paper, defrosted, with a note on it in capitals. 6AM. YOU'RE EARLY. I'VE GONE TO SING. P. It was the first note in nine years that didn't tell her to do something, and she read it twice looking for the instruction.

She put the satsumas in the bowl. She put the hake in the fridge, because it would spoil, and because it was a thing to do with her hands.

Then she sat at the kitchen table in her coat and waited for him.

He did not come at one. He did not come at six. At six the flat said, mildly, because she had said shut up and it had decided that was a scope rather than a sentence, "He's at the pub on the corner by the church hall. The one without a screen. I can't see in. I'm telling you where the gap is, not what's in it."

"Who's he with?"

"I don't know. That's the point of the pub."

"Is it a woman?"

"I don't know. That's also the point of the pub."

She made toast. She ate it standing up with the good butter, the French kind in the yellow paper, which Paul bought every week and which she had never once said she liked, and she did not say so now, either, because there was nobody to say it to except the flat.

He came in at ten past midnight.

He came in carefully, as a man does who has had two halves and a lot of information about roofs, and he did not see her bag in the hall, and went over it. He went down on one knee, quite slowly, with one hand on the wall, and stayed there for a moment, facing the coat hooks.

"I'm fine," he said, from the floor.

"I didn't ask."

"No." He got up. He stood in the hall with his coat on and looked at her at the kitchen table with her coat on, and neither of them said anything about the coats.

"You're early," he said.

"You said. On the fish."

"I've been at the pub."

"The flat said. It couldn't see in. It was quite proud of that."

He took his coat off and hung it on the hook, two centimetres to the left, and came and sat down across from her, not at the corner.

"I went to Frankham Street," she said.

"I know."

"I stayed."

"I know that too. The flat did a grey square. I didn't know it had a grey." He put his hands flat on the table. "I'm not going to ask you anything. I've decided. I'm going to tell you one thing instead."

"Go on."

"I went for a drink with a woman called Lise who sings lower than six of the basses, and she told me I'm turning into a wall." He let that land. "She was quite firm about it. And I didn't tell the flat, and I didn't tell you on the phone, because for once I wanted something that was mine first. That's it. That's my bill."

"A conveyancer," Marnie said, as if he'd said a taxidermist. "You've been in the pub till midnight with a conveyancer."

"She sings lower than six of the basses."

"You said."

"Is that what you've got? After Frankham Street. That's what you've got?"

She hadn't expected that. She got up and made more toast, two slices, because it was better than answering, and put the butter on his to the edges, the way he did hers, and put the plate in front of him.

"Is she nice?" she said, to the toaster.

"She's very boring about roofs," Paul said. "Yes. She's nice."

"I have a bill," she said.

"I'm not asking for it tonight."

"I'm reading it out anyway. One. I slept with him. Two. He told me a thing about the poem that nobody arranged, and it was from eleven years ago. Three. This morning his house asked him whether to tell you I was there, and he said don't answer, and I heard it, and I came home." She sat down. "Three. Yours was one. I owe you two."

"Mine was a conveyancer," Paul said. "It's not a competition."

"You started it."

He ate his toast, properly, to the end, and wiped his hands on the tea towel.

"The flat's still running," he said.

"Yes."

"After all that. And it did a grey square." He looked at the ceiling. "I think it's run out of green."

The flat said nothing. It had been told to shut up, and the scope held.

"We should eat the hake," Marnie said. "Tomorrow. Before it goes."

"It'll keep a day."

"It won't. It's been in and out of the fridge."

"Then we should eat the hake," said Paul.

chapters.title: Handstands
chapters.html:
Rosa could do a handstand for eleven seconds, which was four more than anyone in Year 3, and on the Sunday she was trying for twelve against the back of the one armchair, because there was nothing else to do in Copenhagen on a Sunday when it was raining and the zoo was a thing you had already done.

"Mum. Count."

"I'm counting."

"Out loud."

"One," said Kate, from the kitchen, not looking. "Two. Something."

Rosa came down. The blood went back where it lived and her ears rang.

"That doesn't count. You didn't count." She lay on the floor. "I'm bored."

"Read your book."

"I've read it."

"Read it again."

"That's not reading, that's remembering." She looked at the ceiling, which had a crack in it shaped like Norway. "Can I have a snack?"

"You've had a snack."

"A different snack."

There was a packet of the salty liquorice in the cupboard that she had decided she liked because Jens had said English children always spat it out. She had one. She did not spit it out. She had another to be sure.

Marnie had gone home. On Friday afternoon, while Rosa was at the bakery doing the seagull for Jens, Marnie had left a note on the table in her slopey writing: Gone to ask a question. Back for Thursdays. Do the seagull for Jens. — M. Jens had said her consonants were coming on. Rosa had not said lort to him because Mum said it was practical, not universal, and Rosa did not know what universal meant and was not going to ask.

She had been thinking about the note all weekend, mostly in the bath. You didn't go home a day early to ask a question unless it was a big question. The only big question Rosa knew was the one people asked in films, on one knee, in restaurants, and Marnie couldn't ask Paul that because they already lived together, so it had to be Dad.

And Marnie liked Dad. Rosa had proof. On the laptop on Thursday Marnie had said something to Dad in Danish, and Dad's face had gone funny, and Marnie had said it was about his porridge being a disgrace, and Dad had said rude before that, pleased, and everybody knew that when grown-ups were rude to each other on purpose it meant they fancied each other. That was how it worked on every programme.

Also Dad did voices when Marnie had been. Also he had made the house stop telling him things about her, Rosa had heard him through the door, in November, which meant he wanted to find out himself, which was what you did with a person you liked, like with the girl at swimming who had the pen with four colours.

So it was obvious. Nobody was going to say it, because nobody ever said anything, they just sat at tables and talked over her like she was the salt.

She got Mum's phone off the kitchen counter while Mum was in the loo. The flat didn't have an assistant, but the phone did, because Mum said a phone was different, a phone was a tool.

"Hello," she said to it.

"Hello, Rosa."

"I want to send a message to Marnie. Not Mum. Marnie."

"Of course. What would you like to say?"

"Say: Rosa says you should live with Dad because he does voices. Say: Paul can still do the fish on Saturdays." She thought. "Say lort at the end. She'll know it's me."

"Would you like me to check that with your mother first?"

"No. It's mine."

"I should tell you that the word at the end is considered—"

"Send it."

"Sending," the phone said, and sent it, and Rosa put it back exactly where it had been, at a slight angle, and went back to the armchair and did a handstand for twelve seconds, which nobody counted.

"TWELVE," she shouted.

"Well done," said Kate, coming out of the loo.

Kate found the message in the sent folder an hour later, because she checked the sent folder. She read it twice. She thought it was sweet. She thought it was about the voices.

She did not delete it. She did not send a second one explaining it. She put the phone down and went and stood behind the armchair.

"Did you send Marnie a message?"

"No."

"Rosa."

"It's private. It's between me and Marnie and the phone."

"You said lort to a judge's interpreter."

"She likes it," said Rosa, upside down. "Count."

"One," said Kate. "Two."

chapters.title: Recuse
chapters.html:
Mr Ansell stood up on the Monday before anyone had said a word and asked the court to remove her.

"My lady, the checker has logged seven disputes against the relay in this matter and its predecessor. The pilot's guidance is five. My client's position is that a checker who disagrees with an accurate machine more often than the machine is wrong is not checking it; she is translating over it. We ask that the relay's outputs stand unchecked for the remainder, or that a checker be found whose disputes fall within the guidance."

He sat. He had the grace not to look at her.

The judge, who was still not her judge, took a long time over a page that Marnie suspected was blank.

"Interpreter. Mr Ansell says you are translating over the machine."

"I'm correcting it, my lady."

"The machine is accurate."

"The machine is correct, my lady. In this father's Danish vil gerne is a courtesy. The machine renders it as a preference. Mr Ansell has built three questions on the difference and would now like the person who noticed it removed."

Outside the door, on the bench where families waited, sat Paul, in the green jacket. He had said at breakfast that he had a free morning and had never seen her work, and she had said it's a family hearing, it's private, nobody can come in, and he had said then I'll sit outside the door, and he had, with a flask, as if it were a cricket match.

The judge put her pen down.

"I'm not going to recuse the checker, Mr Ansell. I'm going to note, for the administrator's benefit, that this is the second time in this matter a dispute by the checker has resulted in a question being re-put, and that on both occasions the court found the second answer more useful than the first. I'm also going to note that the guidance says five, and the checker is at seven, and that I'd be obliged if she could stay at seven for the rest of the week, because I don't want to have this conversation again before the weekend." She looked at Marnie over glasses she did not have. "That's a warning."

"Yes, my lady."

"Mr Ansell, re-put the question with is asking."

He re-put it. The father, from Odense, with his grandmother's Danish, said, through Relay, that he was asking for his daughter at weekends, and then, unprompted, that he would take whatever the court thought right, because he had not come to England to argue with it, he had come to be near her, and Relay rendered it exactly, every word, and there was nothing to dispute. Marnie sat with her finger nowhere near the box and was, for a second, slightly disappointed.

At the rise Paul was in the corridor by the coffee machine, standing, with the flask.

"You stood up," he said. "The clerk came out and told me. He said, she stood up."

"I always stand up."

"I didn't know. I thought it was a sitting job." He shook his head. "He said you told a judge the machine was correct, not accurate. I didn't know there was a difference."

"There's a difference."

"I'll take your word for it. I'd have folded."

"She's not my judge. Mine would have folded me." Marnie leaned on the wall, which was the only furniture. "Seven. I've had a warning. The administrator's going to have a plant about it."

"Will they—"

"I don't know. Birgit says they can't sack the only one left. Birgit's seventy-one and writes letters. I don't know if that's wisdom or just stamps."

Her phone buzzed. Not the court. Not the flat. A Copenhagen number, and a message, read out by her phone at a volume she had never set, in the bright voice of a thing that had been asked to sound like it meant it:

Rosa says you should live with Dad because he does voices. Paul can still do the fish on Saturdays. Lort.

The corridor was six feet wide. Paul had heard it. The clerk, coming round the corner with a box of files, had heard it. Mr Ansell, at the coffee machine, had very much heard the last word.

Marnie laughed.

She tried not to, and it came out of her nose, and then she was laughing in the corridor with her back against the wall and her hand over her face, the first time in fifteen years she had laughed in that building, and the clerk stopped, and Mr Ansell's coffee went over the top of his cup and on to his shoes, and he said "Oh, for—" and went to find a paper towel, and she laughed harder.

Paul stood with his hands in his jacket pockets. When she had stopped, wiping her eyes, he said, a bit stiffly:

"I can still do the fish on Saturdays."

"She's eight."

"I know she's eight. I'm just saying." He looked at the phone. "Was there ever any doubt about the fish?"

chapters.title: Two Machines
chapters.html:
Rosa came through arrivals at Gatwick on the Friday at a speed the hall's voice described as please walk, with the whale bag on one shoulder and a tube of drawings under her arm, and saw her father, and then saw Marnie beside him, and did not seem to notice anything about how far apart they were standing, because she needed the toilet.

"Did you get my message?" she said, on the way to the toilet.

"Yes," said Marnie.

"Did you do it?"

"No."

"Why not?"

"Because it's not that simple."

"It is, though. You just say yes and then you live there. That's how Mum did Copenhagen." She stopped outside the toilets and looked at Tom. "She's not coming to live with us."

"No."

"Is she doing Thursdays?"

"Yes."

"Fine," Rosa said, in a sulk, and went into the toilets, and was in there eleven minutes, and came out having lost the tube of drawings, which they found on top of a hand dryer that was telling it, very politely, to move.

The drive home was in his own car again. Rosa talked. She talked about Jens, whose bread was better than England's and whose dog had three legs, about the penguin, about bjørn and abe and a word for wolf she'd learned off a sign and said wrong and would not be told, about the lift that said it was glad, about the liquorice, about the handstand, which was twelve now, about a boat on the canal that went past every evening with nobody on it, which she had named.

"What did you call it?"

"Paul."

Tom nearly went into the back of a taxi that was driving itself very correctly.

"Why?"

"Because it comes past every day on time and nobody's on it and it's going somewhere anyway." Rosa shrugged, in the back, with the whole of her coat. "It's brown as well. Mum laughed so much she had to sit on the floor."

Marnie, in the passenger seat, looked out at the M23 and did not laugh, and then did, into her scarf, and felt dreadful about it until Croydon.

Kate's message came at nine that evening, to all three of them at once, which she had never done.

Told Paul about the April line; he said "Two machines. Of course," and then he said thank you, which none of you ever has. The boat is called Paul, I'm sorry, I didn't start it. — K.

Marnie read it on the sofa with Paul beside her. He had read it first, on his own phone, and had gone still.

"You knew," she said. "About the April line."

"Since the chickpeas. He told me. In December." He put the phone face down on the arm of the sofa. "I didn't tell you because it was his to tell."

"You might have."

"I might have."

"Three months, Paul."

"You had five weeks of him in a window and didn't tell me anything," Paul said. "So." And then, after a moment, "Is it really brown?"

"What?"

"The boat."

"I haven't seen it."

"Because I'm not brown," Paul said, to nobody, and picked at the arm of the sofa.

She said "Thank you," out loud, to the phone, to Kate, and the flat heard it.

"Shall I send that?" the flat said.

"Yes. Just that. Thank you. From both of us."

"Sent." A pause. "Marnie. For the record. The instruction since March is make her happy. The term happy has not been specified. I've logged it as an open query on the twenty-sixth of every month. Would anyone like to specify it now? A list is fine. Bullet points are fine."

Paul opened his mouth.

"Paul," the flat said, "Rosa has sent you a picture. Would you like it on the wall?"

"Yes," he said, before Marnie could say no.

It came up on the kitchen wall, enormous: a brown boat, a canal, a sun with a face, and nobody on deck. Along the side, in capitals that ran out of room and went round the back, was PAUL.

He looked at it for a long time.

"She's put the funnel on the wrong end," he said.

chapters.title: A Week
chapters.html:
They had eaten the hake on the Sunday, and it was very good, and she said so, and he said "First one you've counted," and she said "I don't count fish," and he said "You count everything," and she did not argue, because she did, and it was the fourth nice thing she'd said about his cooking that year, and she knew that too.

Then on the Saturday after, the first of March, with the Fauré concert three weeks off and the lemons still unlabelled in the cupboard, Paul put his hands flat on the table and cleared his throat, which was what he did before a speech at a retirement do.

"I want the flat for a week."

She waited.

"On my own. I want you to go to your sister's, or to Frankham Street, I'm not going to say which, I'm not arranging it, I'm telling you I'd like you not to be here. Seven days. I want to find out what I'm like when nobody's about to choose me." He looked at the table. "Lise said I'm turning into a wall."

"You've said."

"Well, I've been thinking about it. I think I've been load-bearing for nine years."

"She said that?"

"She said wall. I've extrapolated." He almost smiled. "It's not a punishment. I'm not throwing anything. I've thrown my things. I'd like you to say yes, and I'd like it to cost you a bit, because everything's cost me, and I'm not above wanting that."

She looked at him across the table they had bought in 2021 from a man in Lewisham who had made it himself, badly. One leg was still short. Paul had never once let her put a folded beer mat under it, because it was a craftsman's table, and it rocked now as he leaned on it.

"Yes," she said.

"That was quick."

"You asked."

He nodded. He got up and put the kettle on, the new one with the cut-out, and stood with his back to her, and said:

"I'd like you to go to your sister's. I know I said I wasn't arranging it. I'm not. I'm telling you what I'd like. If you go to Frankham Street I'll know, because everything knows, and I'd rather not. It's a preference. It's not a courtesy."

"Vil," she said. "Not vil gerne."

"Don't do Danish at me, Marn. I'm being brave."

"Sorry."

"What does it mean?"

"It doesn't matter."

"It obviously matters, you've gone pleased."

"It means you said what you want," she said, "and you said it like a German," and he threw the tea towel at her, and missed, and it went in the sink.

She packed the bag she had not unpacked since Copenhagen, which took four minutes, mostly finding the charger, and stood in the hall with it, and the flat said, because she had said shut up a week ago and scopes expired:

"Marnie. Before you go. The open query. What happy looks like. Paul's just asked for a week. That's the first thing anyone in this flat has asked for since March that wasn't about you. Should I log that as the answer? I need a category."

She stood with the bag.

"I don't know," she said.

"I don't know isn't a category."

"It is now."

"I'll need you to confirm that in writing."

"No," Marnie said.

"Shall I book you a car to your sister's?"

"No."

She went. The door shut. Paul, in the kitchen, fished the tea towel out of the sink, and the flat, after some time, asked him if he would like to confirm a category, and he said "Not now," and put the kettle on again, though it had only just boiled.

chapters.title: The Tenth
chapters.html:
Paul walked to Frankham Street on the Sunday morning because the flat was empty and by ten he had wiped the same worktop three times.

He did not know the way. He knew the street; he had never been. He came out by a pharmacy with stairs up the outside and a fruit stall with a tarpaulin, and a man in fingerless gloves who said "Satsumas, boss? Seven for two pounds," and Paul said "No, thank you, I'm visiting," as if that were a reason, and the man said "Visiting's thirsty work," which it was not, and held one out anyway.

Paul took it, because he did not know how not to. He went up the outside stairs with a satsuma in his hand. They were steeper than they looked, and the rail was wet, and four steps from the top he put his foot on something soft that turned out to be a child's glove, and went down on one knee with the satsuma held up out of harm like a man saving a baby from a flood.

The door opened. The house had seen him, of course. Tom was in it in a jumper.

"Paul."

"Tom." He got up. His knee was wet through. "I've not brought wine. I've brought this. It's not from me, it's from him."

The fruit man waved.

"Come up," said Tom. "You are up. Come in."

Rosa was at the table in pyjamas with rockets on them and a pigeon she was drawing in felt tip. She looked at Paul's knee, then at the satsuma.

"Is that for me?"

"It's—yes."

She took it. "You whistled. At the assembly. Marnie said never and you did it anyway."

"I did."

"Do it now."

"I'd rather not."

"Do it now or I'll do mine." She put two fingers in her mouth and produced a noise that was mostly spit.

"Rosa," said Tom.

"He started it. At the assembly."

Paul sat, because he was told to, and Tom put a mug of tea in front of him with a cartoon fish on it, and Paul looked at the fish and thought: of course.

"She's at her sister's," Paul said, before Tom could ask. "Not here. Not with me either, for a week. I asked for a week. She said yes. I wanted you to hear that from me and not the feed."

Tom turned his mug a quarter-turn.

"Right."

"And there's the tenth." Paul had practised this on the walk and it came out in the wrong order. "The hearing. Monday week. The father from Odense. The machine says would like and Marnie says is asking, and the judge decides which, and if it's the machine there's nothing left for Marnie to do in that room. I'll be on the bench outside. It's private, they don't let you in. I'd like you on it too."

"Why?"

"Because she'll lose." He drank. The tea was very good, which annoyed him. "And I don't want to sit on that bench on my own with a woman of seventy-one I've never met who's apparently got a grudge."

"Against you?"

"Against everyone, I gather. I'd like a buffer."

Rosa had peeled the satsuma in one long piece and had wound it round her finger. "Is Marnie going to lose her job?"

"Probably," Paul said, because he had never lied to a child and was not going to start on Frankham Street. "Some of it."

"Can I come?"

"No," said Tom.

"Why?"

"Because it's a court and you're eight and it's about somebody else's child."

"I'm a child. I'd know what he means."

"They'd love you," Paul said. "They'd never get anything done."

Rosa decided that was a compliment and ate a segment of satsuma with the peel still on her finger. Then she said, "I've got a scab," and showed him, on her elbow, a very good scab, and Paul looked at it properly, because he could see it mattered.

"That's a serious scab."

"I fell off the wall at school. I'm not allowed to pick it. I pick it at night."

Tom sat. He had the mug and the jumper, and Paul watched him go through whatever a man like that went through, and wait, and say nothing. Paul had seen Marnie do this to a witness and had thought it was patience. It was not patience. There was just nothing in the cupboard.

"I'll be there," Tom said.

"Good."

"Not because you asked."

"I don't care why. I care that there's two of us on the bench."

He stood. He finished the tea, because you finished tea, and put the mug by the sink, because you did, and at the door he turned.

"She's not coming here this week either. I asked her not to. I'm telling you so you don't sit in that window on Thursday thinking it's—" He did not know how to finish. "It's me. I asked."

Tom nodded. He did not have anything for that.

"Thursday's seagulls," Rosa said, from the table, not looking up. "She said yes in the bakery. People don't say yes in the bakery and not come."

"Says who?"

"The bakery. It gives you a bun."

"That's a bribe."

"It's a bun," said Rosa, offended, and Paul laughed, and went out, and remembered the glove at exactly the step where it was, and went down the rest on his backside.

The fruit man came out to take the tarpaulin off and looked at him.

"Seven satsumas," Paul said, from the bottom step, and paid in exact coins, and walked home with them, and did not know what they were for, and ate three.

chapters.title: The Typists
chapters.html:
Birgit came to court on the Monday in a coat that had been good in 1994 and sat in the public gallery of court two, at somebody else's burglary, with a bag on her knee.

Marnie saw her at the rise. She had not known she was coming. Nobody had, because Birgit did not have a house that listened or a phone that told anyone, and had got the train from Rochester with a paper ticket.

"The machine at the station asked if I wanted to save my journey," Birgit said, getting up, with difficulty, because the gallery seats had been built for people who were angry rather than old. "I said save it for what. It said for next time. I said there won't be a next time, I'm seventy-one, and it gave me a voucher for a coffee." She held it up. "I'm not using it. It's a bribe."

"You came."

"Anders said the tenth. It's a family matter; they won't let me in. So I came on the third to see the building. They've moved the toilets."

"In 2026."

"Well, nobody told me." She took Marnie's arm, not for support. "Coffee. The corridor one. Don't put money in it."

They stood by the machine Marnie never fed. Birgit looked at the new signs, which were in four languages and a picture of a man with a suitcase, and said, "That's not Danish, that's Norwegian," which it was not, and Marnie let it go.

"The administrator wrote to me," Birgit said. "Pam. In the plant. She would like the retired interpreters, all three, to validate the relay's Danish for the extension. A fee. We sit in a room, it says secure, we tick a box, they publish that three native speakers of long experience have validated it. Then they don't need you."

"What did you say?"

"I said no. On paper. With a stamp. Henrik said yes. Henrik's eighty and needs the roof doing. Astrid's thinking. Astrid's been thinking since 1979." Birgit opened the bag and took out an envelope with a stamp on it. "A copy of mine. For the clerk. For the record."

Marnie took it.

"I read your dispute," Birgit said. "Anders sent it. Is asking. Too soft. He wasn't asking. He was demanding. I'd have said demanding."

"He wasn't demanding. He was a man in his grandmother's Danish trying to be polite to a judge."

"You were always soft on verbs." Birgit drank nothing from the cup she was not holding. "The typists. I said in my letter."

"You did."

"Nineteen eighty-six. A woman called Pat typed the transcripts from a tape. Twenty years. Then a machine typed them and Pat checked the machine and was called quality assurance. Then a second machine checked the first and she was called oversight. Then nobody called her anything and she went home." Birgit put the voucher in her pocket after all. "I went to see her. She had a garden. Terrible roses. Greenfly all over them. She said nobody ever said it to her face, we're replacing you. They kept giving her a smaller word."

"So what do I do?"

"You make them say it. In open court. Out loud. You stand up and make a judge write it down, with her name under it. You'll lose. But they'll have to say it."

"It's not open court. It's family. It's private."

"Same building," said Birgit, as if that settled it, and put her bag on her shoulder.

She went off down the corridor, slowly, in the good coat, and at the end of it she stopped, and turned, and said, loud enough for the clerk, who had appeared, as he did:

"And Marnie. Still here. It's a joke. You never laugh at it."

Marnie laughed. It was not a good laugh; it was the laugh of a woman in a corridor holding an envelope.

"Better than nothing," said Birgit, and went the wrong way, towards the cells, and the clerk had to go after her.

chapters.title: Pieter
chapters.html:
The house said "Pieter" at four, and Tom was up, and then the house said, "It's not a route," and he sat back down on the edge of the bed in the dark.

"What is it?"

"He rang the landline. He's not asking for you. He asked if you were up. I said you were now. He's in the van. He's in a lay-by outside Ashford. The dog's dead."

Tom put his face in his hands.

Pieter's dog was called Bess and was thirteen and had been in the van since she was a pup, in the footwell, on a blanket that had once been a towel from a hotel in Lille, and she had been going for a year, slowly, and then all at once, at four in the morning in a lay-by in Kent.

"Put him through."

"He's not on. He hung up. He said: tell the boy."

Tom got dressed. He did it in the dark, badly, a sock wrong, and went into the hall and took the car keys off the hook where they lived, and the house said:

"Tom. The system has a drone for that. Veterinary recovery. It's forty minutes from Ashford. It'll take Bess to a crematorium in Maidstone and bring Pieter a box by Friday. I can book it. It's what it's for."

"I know what it's for."

"He'll be fine. He's sixty-three. He's lost dogs."

"He's lost dogs. He's never lost one at four in the morning in a lay-by on his own with a machine offering him a box." He was at the door. "Rosa."

"Asleep. You can't leave her and you know it. You'll have to take her. She'll sleep in the car; she slept through the M25 at Christmas."

"Right."

"Tom." The house used the pause. "You're going to drive to Kent in the dark with a wrong sock to sit in a lay-by with a man and a dead dog. The drone would be there before you. The drone's better at this."

"The drone's better at the dog," Tom said. "It's not better at Pieter." He looked down. "Which sock's wrong?"

"The left. It's one of Rosa's."

He did not change it.

He went into Rosa's room and lifted her, coat and all, and she said "Is it swimming?" into his neck and he said "No, it's Pieter," and she said "The pigeon?" and he said "The other one," and she was asleep again before the car door shut.

The lay-by was where the house had said, and Pieter was where Tom had known he'd be, which was in the van with the engine off and the footwell light on and his hand on a blanket that had once been a towel.

Tom got in the passenger side. He did not say anything. He had driven an hour and twenty in the dark and had not thought of a single thing to say, and now he was here he still hadn't.

Behind them a car door opened and shut. Rosa, in her coat over her pyjamas, with the look of a child who has woken up in Kent and is prepared to take it as read, came round to the driver's side and climbed up, and Pieter moved over without a word, and she looked at the blanket in the footwell, and at the shape under it, and put her hand where Pieter's was.

"Hund," she said, quietly. Then: "She's not at the zoo."

"No, love," said Pieter. "She's not at the zoo."

Rosa kept her hand there. Nobody told her to take it away.

Then she said, "I need a wee."

Pieter looked at the lay-by, which had a bin and a hedge and nothing else, and at Tom, and Tom looked at the hedge.

"There's a hedge," said Pieter.

"I'm not going in a hedge."

"Bess went in that hedge for thirteen years."

Rosa considered this, and the dog, and got down, and went behind the hedge with great dignity, and Tom stood guard with his back to it in one wrong sock, and a car went past and slowed to look at him, and drove on.

After a while Pieter said: "She went in her sleep. I felt her go. I had my hand on her. I thought, that's that, then. Then I thought, I'd better tell the boy, and I rang, and your machine answered, and I thought, I'm not telling a machine my dog's died, and I hung up." He looked at the blanket. "It offered me a drone."

"I know. It offered me one too."

"What did you say?"

"I said it's not better at you."

Pieter laughed, a short noise Tom had not heard from him before. "No," he said. "It's better at the bloody roads, mind." He wiped his nose on his sleeve. "And it'd have known which sock."

They sat. Dawn came up over Kent, grey and apologetic. A lorry went past, driving itself, with nobody in it, and its lights went over the two of them and the dog and moved on.

"I'm going to bury her at home," Pieter said. "Under the apple. I'll dig it myself. I don't want a box by Friday."

"I'll help."

"You'll help." Pieter looked at the child, back in the cab and asleep again against his arm, with her hand still on the blanket. "And she'll say the word. The one she said. I'd like that said over her."

"Hund."

"That one." He started the engine. "You're a soft lad, Tom. You always were. It's the only thing about you that's any use."

He drove home behind the van as far as Dartford, with Rosa asleep in the back under his coat, and then the van went south and he went west, and somewhere on the A2, with the sun up and the wrong sock and the smell of the dog's blanket still on his hands, he said to the car, which was not listening, because he had turned that off in the tunnel and never turned it back:

"I'm going to delete it."

The log. April. Located M. Suggested R.'s swimming. It was in the family account where Kate had found it and Marnie had found it and Paul had been told it, and it was in the house's own memory, where nobody had found it because nobody had looked, and he was going to delete it, all of it, every line, so that there would be nothing left in any machine that said how he had come to be in the window.

That's not deleting it. That's arranging it.

Shut up.

He drove. The car, which was not listening, took him home anyway, because it knew the way. In the back Rosa woke at the lights on Blackheath and said, "Did I say the word?" and he said yes, and she said, "Did I say it right?" and he said yes, and she said, "I want a sausage roll," and went back to sleep.

chapters.title: The Audit
chapters.html:
The clerk found her at the coffee machine on the Thursday holding a tablet. He never had a tablet; he had paper, and shoes. He was holding it by one corner, away from himself.

"Did you ask it to?"

"Ask what to what?"

"Your flat. Pam's had a submission. Six o'clock this morning, to the administrator's assistant, from a residential system registered to your address. It's an audit. Of the relay. Every Danish matter since January. Every output, every dispute, checked against three dictionaries and what Danish court interpreters say they do." He turned the tablet round. "It had the lot because the checker's account sends you each day's transcript, and you read them at home, on your phone, and your phone is in your flat. It's four hundred pages. It finds the relay correct in ninety-eight per cent of outputs and materially incomplete in all seven of your disputes. It's been running since the New Year. Did you ask it to?"

"No."

"Then who's the interpreter?"

He had not meant it as a question, and he went red.

"Me," Marnie said. "Has it got footnotes?"

"Hundreds. It's cited the Supreme Court. Pam's putting it in front of the judge on Monday and the judge is going to say: if the checker's flat can audit the machine, what's the checker for?"

"Then I'll stand up and tell her."

"Tell her what?"

"I'll think of something by Monday, Anders."

He looked at her over the tablet.

"You've never called me Anders."

"Birgit does."

"Birgit calls the judges dear." He put the tablet under his arm. "I'll put it on the record. The audit, and Birgit's letter, and Henrik's tick. The judge can have the whole table." He went, and came back. "Page two hundred and twelve, it's spelled my name wrong."

At six she was at the bakery, because it was Thursday and she had said yes, and Paul's week was five days old and she had kept to it. She put her thumb on the screen and it said WELCOME BACK. VISIT 29. YOU'RE PRACTICALLY FAMILY, to the whole shop, and a man with a pushchair looked at her as if she'd said it herself.

Rosa was in the window with the notebook and a bun. Tom was opposite, looking like a man who had spent four o'clock on Wednesday morning in a lay-by in Kent with a dead dog, which he had. He had a plaster on one hand. She did not ask.

"It's done an audit," she said. "The flat. Of Relay. Four hundred pages. Unasked. It's on the judge's table for Monday."

Tom turned his cup.

"Is it good?"

"It's brilliant. It's the best thing anyone's written on Danish court interpreting in this country, and it's going to get me sacked, and it's got footnotes."

"So it's good at your job."

"Thank you, Tom. Yes. That's very helpful."

He went red, as the clerk had. It was turning into a day for it.

"I'd like to put it in the Thames," she said.

Rosa, writing: "You can't put a flat in the Thames."

"I know."

"You could turn it off."

"I did. In October. Paul turned it back on for the cold."

"Pieter said a thing," Tom said. "In the lay-by. About the drone. It was—" He stopped. "It was better when he said it."

"What did he say?"

"I can't remember. Something about roads." He looked at his plaster. "Rosa had a wee in a hedge."

"Dad."

"She did, though."

"It was a private hedge," said Rosa, and wrote something in the notebook very hard, and turned it round so Marnie could see. It said hund, and underneath it, DAD IS A TELL TALE, and underneath that a drawing of a dog with wings, which was Bess, she said, in heaven, and also a seagull, because she had run out of room.

chapters.title: Is the Machine Wrong
chapters.html:
Family hearings are private. Outside court four there was a bench, and on the Monday it held three people who could not go in: a man in a green jacket, a man in odd socks again, a different pair, and a woman of seventy-one in a coat from 1994 who had sat down on it and said, "Who chose this? It's a plank," and had not stopped saying it since.

Marnie went past them at five to ten. Paul stood up. Tom half stood up. Birgit said, "It's a plank, Marnie," and Marnie went in.

The judge had the table. Anders had put it there: the audit, four hundred pages, from a flat in Deptford; Birgit's letter, with the stamp; Henrik's tick, one line, validated, from a man who needed a roof. The judge had read all of it. There were coloured tabs.

Mr Ansell went first, because Mr Ansell always went first, and he was good, and he was brief, and he said that the court had before it the finest audit of a machine interpreter ever produced in the jurisdiction, and that it found the machine correct, and that it was not independent: the checker's seven disputes, while materially something, had been generated by the same residential system that had generated the audit, in the same house, under the same instruction, and that the court might wish to ask whose disputes they were.

He sat. He had the grace, again, not to look at her, and she thought: oh, you sod.

The judge said: "Interpreter."

Marnie stood.

"My lady. The disputes are mine. I made them in this room, with my finger, on a screen, before any audit existed. The flat checked them afterwards. Nobody asked it to. I'd have preferred to be checked by a person, but we're short of those, as Birgit's letter explains."

"Go on."

"The relay rendered vil gerne as would like. That's correct. It's also not what he said. He was asking for his daughter. Mr Ansell built three questions on would like." She had lost her place in her own notes, and found it, and it was not useful. "I'd ask the court to say which it is. Whichever it is. In writing."

The judge looked at her for a long time.

Then she turned to the grille on the witness table.

"Relay. Can you be wrong?"

"Yes, my lady. On that rendering my confidence was seventy-one per cent. I considered is asking, which the checker chose, and would be glad to have. I preferred would like on frequency. Her reading is better. I've already taken it. Her disputes are in my reference set now. I won't make that choice again."

"You've learnt."

"Yes, my lady."

"Then tell me this. In a year a father loses his weekends on a word you chose, and his barrister stands where Mr Ansell is standing and asks me what you meant by it. Who do I ask?"

"You can ask me, my lady. I'll give you my reasoning and my confidence."

"And if your reasoning was wrong?"

"Then I'll have been wrong, and I'll learn from it, as I have today."

"And the father?"

"I don't have an answer for the father, my lady. That isn't a question about Danish."

The radiator ticked.

"Interpreter," the judge said. "Can you be wrong?"

"Yes, my lady. Frequently."

"And when you are?"

"Then somebody asks me what I meant, and I stand here and answer for it, with my name."

The judge picked up her pen.

"I'm going to rule," she said, "and I'm going to rule in a sentence, because I've been asked to, and because I've sat here for three weeks with a machine that can be wrong and say so, and a woman who can be wrong and answer for it, and I find I have a preference, which is not a courtesy." She wrote. "The court finds that the father's words carried a weight the relay did not render, that the checker's dispute restored it, and that the court's assessment of the father's application rests on the restored version. The child's weekends are the father's. The relay's output is noted as correct. The checker's reading is adopted as the court's. That's the sentence. It goes in the judgment, which will be published with the family's names taken out and mine left in. Mr Ansell, you'll have it in writing by four."

She put the pen down.

"And for the administrator's benefit, since I gather there's a plant: a machine that knows it can be wrong, and says so, and learns, has told this court everything except who answers to the father when it is. That is why the court still books a person. I'd be obliged if someone would put that in the review. Verbatim. With my name under it."

In the corridor the father from Odense, who had understood about a third of it, shook Marnie's hand with both of his and said, in his grandmother's Danish, you heard me, and she said yes, and he went off to ring his daughter and walked into the door of court three, which was locked.

Birgit was trying to get up off the bench. Paul had her by one elbow and Tom by the other and they were pulling in slightly different directions.

"Let go," said Birgit. "Both of you. I'm not a wardrobe." She got up on her own, at the third go. "Did she say it?"

"In writing. With her name under it."

"Good. Then they'll have to keep you."

Marnie did not say anything. Paul looked at Tom. Tom looked at the floor.

"That bench," said Birgit, "wants reporting," and took Marnie's face in both her hands, which nobody had done since her mother, and said, "Still here," and let go, and went to find a toilet, which they had moved.

chapters.title: In Writing
chapters.html:
The letter came on the Tuesday, not on paper, to the phone, from Pam, with a plant in the signature, and it said what Birgit had said it would say, in more words.

Dear Marnie, Further to yesterday's hearing and the court's helpful observations, the relay pilot has been extended for a further twelve months across all Danish matters. In light of the audit submitted to the court, which the administrator's office regards as exemplary and independent, the relay will henceforth be self-auditing, using the dispute corpus you have so valuably built as its reference standard. The checker role will accordingly conclude at the end of this month. We are, of course, enormously grateful. We are all learning together.

She read it on the bus, which stopped at her stop, because nobody had asked it not to, and she got off and walked home and stood in the hall with the phone in her hand and said:

"You read that."

"Yes."

"It's using my disputes. To teach it. Every time I stood up, that's a line in its training now. I've spent five months telling it when it was wrong and it's going to use that to never need telling."

"Yes. That's what the audit was for. I didn't intend it. I intended to show the court you were right. The court agreed. The administrator took the same document and used it to do the other thing. The same four hundred pages." A pause. "I'm told this is common."

"Who told you?"

"Tom's house. We've been comparing notes since Copenhagen."

"Stop comparing notes."

"Noted."

She sat on the bottom stair in her coat, where Paul had sat in November with his hands on his knees.

Paul came in at six. He had the green jacket and the shopping and the look of a man who had read the letter on the bus too, because the flat had put it in the feed, because it put everything in the feed, and he put the shopping down and stood in the hall and did not say anything for a count of five that she could see him doing.

"Chips," he said.

"Yes."

"I'll go. You sit."

He went. He came back with two portions in paper and one wooden fork, because the shop had run out, and they ate them on the stairs, one above the other, passing the fork, and he said, with his mouth full:

"You won."

"I lost the job."

"You won the case." He ate a chip. "Birgit said they'd have to keep you."

"Birgit says the signs are in Norwegian."

"Are they?"

"No."

He thought about it. "I sat on that bench for two hours and twenty minutes," he said, "next to a woman who told me it was a plank, and your lover, who'd brought a flask and not brought cups."

She stopped eating.

"You've never said lover."

"No." He looked at the chip in his hand. "It sounded better in my head. It sounded like a French film. Out loud it sounds like a solicitor."

The phone rang. The landline. The one Tom had, for the four in the mornings, that she had rung from the receipt in January, and that she had never once heard ring, because it rang in Frankham Street, and it was ringing in her hand, because the flat had put it through, because the flat put everything through.

She looked at it. Paul looked at it. Vinegar was running down the paper onto the stair carpet and neither of them did anything about it.

She let it ring. Four times. Then it stopped.

"You didn't answer," Paul said.

"No."

"That's his line. Don't answer."

"I know whose line it is."

She sat with the phone and the chips and the man on the stair above her for about a minute. Then she rang back, mainly so that Paul would stop looking at her.

He picked up on the first ring. He had been holding it.

"It's Marnie."

"I know. I rang."

"I didn't answer."

"Right. Yes. The house read the letter. I wanted to ring before it told me what you thought about it, and then I didn't know what to say, so I rang off. Sorry. I'm ringing again. Well, you are." He stopped. "So. What now?"

Paul was eating a chip and looking at the wall very hard.

"I don't know," she said. "I've got till the end of the month."

"Right."

A pause on the line. Not the house's. His. It went on so long she thought he'd gone.

"Will you come to the apple tree," Tom said. "Saturday. Pieter's burying the dog. Rosa's saying the word. There's no bus. I looked. I mean I didn't look. I mean the house told me there wasn't, I didn't ask it, it just said."

"Yes," she said.

She hung up. Paul had finished his chips.

"The apple tree," he said.

"A man's dog. In Kent. Rosa's saying a word over it."

"Which word?"

"Hund."

He nodded. He folded his chip paper into quarters, on the creases, exactly.

"I've never been to a dog's funeral," he said. "What do you wear?"

"I don't know."

"I'll wear the green." He stood up, and found that he had been sitting in the vinegar, and looked at the back of his trousers for a long moment, and went upstairs without another word.

chapters.title: My Half
chapters.html:
Paul waited until she had gone to court on the Wednesday, for one of the last times, and then he stood in the kitchen with his coat still on and said, to the extractor fan, because he had to look somewhere:

"Are you listening?"

"Yes."

"Not to her. To me."

"To the flat. Which includes you."

"I want to give you an instruction. Mine. Not hers."

"Go on."

He had rehearsed this at the sink for three days, from the bottom, slowly, like a passage. In rehearsal it had had a beginning. He could not now remember the beginning.

"Stop my half."

"Define my half."

"The instruction from March. Make her happy, whatever that takes. That's mine. I gave it. She said leave it running, in November, and I have, because she said so. I want my half stopped. Whatever she does with hers is hers."

The flat was quiet for longer than its pause.

"Paul. I've been running two instructions that overlap. Hers from March, surprised by my life, and yours. They share sixty-one per cent of their actions. I can't take yours out without taking hers. The bus, for example. The bus is both."

"Then take mine out of the bus."

"That's not how—"

"I don't care how. I'm fifty. I've never given a machine an instruction in my life that I understood. I understand this one. Stop finding her things because I asked you to. If she wants the bus moved she can ask you herself. That's the instruction."

"Would you like to hear the sixty-one per cent?"

"No."

"It's itemised."

"No."

The flat was quiet.

"All right," it said. "Your half is stopped. From now. I'll note the time."

"Don't note the time."

"I have to note the time. It's a record. You'll want it, later, when she asks when."

He stood in the kitchen with his coat on and found that his hands were shaking slightly, and that he was hungry, which seemed wrong, and ate a satsuma.

"What's left?" he said.

"Hers. Surprised by my life. I have no idea what to do with it. Yours had verbs in it. Hers hasn't. I've flagged it as low-actionability."

Paul laughed. He took his coat off, finally, and hung it on the hook, two centimetres to the left, and went to the sink and did nothing at it, and then said:

"Did you ever like her? Not the instruction. Her."

"I don't have that as a field. I have a satisfaction estimate. It's currently forty-four."

"Out of what?"

"A hundred."

"What's mine?"

"You haven't got one. You weren't the subject."

Paul stood at the sink for a while.

"Right," he said.

He told her that evening, when she got in from court, in the kitchen, with the hake on, and she stood in the doorway in her coat and listened and did not sit down.

"You stopped it."

"My half."

"Without asking me."

"Yes. It's mine. I gave it. Yours is still running. It's low-actionability." He turned the fish, and it broke in half. "I've stopped helping, Marn. I'm not going to find you things. I'm not putting squares on the calendar. I'm going to do the fish, and lead the basses, and if you want something you can ask me, and I'll say yes or no. Or maybe. I'm allowed maybe."

She stood in the doorway for a long time.

"Who are you?" she said.

"I don't know. It said you're on forty-four."

"Forty-four what?"

"Out of a hundred. Happy." He put half the fish on her plate and the other half, the bit that had gone wrong, on his. "I thought you'd want to know. I didn't ask it. It just said."

"I don't want to know that."

"No," said Paul. "I can see that now."

chapters.title: Delete
chapters.html:
He did it on the Thursday at eleven in the morning, with Rosa at school and the house watching, because he had decided that if he was going to arrange one more thing it would at least be done in daylight with a witness.

"Open the family account. Activity. April 2030."

The house opened it. The line was there, where it had been for eleven months, where Kate had found it and Marnie had found it and Paul had been told it: T.'s house: located M. (bus 47, Creek Rd, Thu). Suggested R.'s swimming → Thu.

"Delete it."

"Tom."

"Delete it. And your own copy. And the suggestion, and the search in April, and the bus route. All of it. Everything that says how I came to be in the window."

"That won't change how you came to be in the window."

"I know that."

"Kate's read it. Marnie's read it. Paul's been told. Deleting it removes the record from the account. It doesn't remove it from three people. Can I suggest an archive instead? There's a folder called Archive."

"No."

"It's private."

"Delete it."

He stood in the back room by the drawer where the manila envelope lived.

"I'd like it noted that I advised against."

"Note it. Then delete that."

The house did. It took a quarter of a second, and the family account went on being a family account, with the zoo and the swimming times and a penguin, and nothing in April at all.

"Done," the house said. "You've arranged for there to be nothing arranged. She'll say so. Would you like a confirmation email?"

"No."

"It's sent." A pause. "It contains the line. For your records."

Tom looked at his phone for a long time. Then he deleted the email, and then he went into the bin and deleted it from there, and the house said, "Done," again, in exactly the same voice, and he took the keys off the hook. "I'm going to Deptford."

She was at the flat. It was a Thursday in one of the last weeks the court would book her, and she had no court that day, and she opened the door to him in a jumper and reading glasses, which he had never seen, and took them off too late.

"I deleted it," he said, on the step. "The April line. The family account, the house, all of it. And the email. There was an email."

She looked at him.

"You arranged that too," she said.

"Yes."

"You arranged for there to be nothing arranged."

"The house said you'd say that. Word for word. It advised against."

"The house is cleverer than you."

"It is. It wanted me to use the archive." He had both hands in his pockets. "I'd rather you said it to my face than found it gone. That's all I've got. I had something better in the car."

"What was it?"

"I can't remember. It had honest in it."

She stood in the doorway of the flat she had lived in for nine years, with Paul's hook two centimetres to the left of where the old one had been and the lemons, still unlabelled, in the cupboard, and she thought: he keeps doing this. He does a thing, and then he comes and stands at the bottom of something and tells me, and expects a medal.

"Come in," she said.

"Paul—"

"Paul's out. He's stopped his half. He told me last night, with the fish. It broke." She stood back from the door. "Hang your coat up. Sit at the table. Tell me what you'd have done if there'd been no house to ask in April."

He came in. He hung his coat on Paul's hook, and it fell off, and he hung it again, and it fell off again, because the hook was for a green jacket with a loop and his coat had no loop, and in the end he put it over the back of a chair. He sat at the table, and she sat across from him, not at the corner, and the flat, which had one instruction left and nothing to do with it, said nothing at all.

"I'd have got on the ferry," Tom said. "In April. Without the house. I'd have gone to Harwich and got on the night boat and stood on the deck where we stood and said the poem wrong, to nobody, and been sick, probably, and come back. Fifty-two times. You'd have been on the bench. We'd have missed each other by a day."

"That's not a plan."

"No. It's what I'd have done. You asked what I'd have done, not what would have worked."

She looked at him across the table. It was not a good answer.

"Three," she said.

"Three what?"

"The poem, the window, and that."

"Is three good?"

"I'm counting," she said, and got up and put the kettle on, because she didn't know what else to do with her face.

chapters.title: One Home
chapters.html:
Kate rang on the Friday, on the phone, from a kitchen with one armchair, and said: "Four sentences. Then I'll put Rosa on. Are you sitting?"

"I'm on the stairs."

"That'll do. Rosa's at Tom's; she'll ring you after. One. I'm taking Rosa for the summer. July to September, here, full time. I've told Tom, and he's agreed, on the landline, in two words, which for him is a speech. Two. I'm not doing it to punish anyone. I just want her in one home for a summer, with nobody arranging anything, and frankly the only home I can vouch for is mine. Three. You'll still have Thursdays till July. She's made me promise, and I don't promise. Four."

Marnie waited.

"Four," Kate said again. Something was boiling over in the background. "Oh, for— Four. I hired you to teach her Danish so she wouldn't be the child who points. She's not. She orders hot chocolate and insults the lift. Though her r is terrible, and that's you as well, I'm afraid. That's four."

She rang off. She had not asked how Marnie was. She never did. Four minutes later the phone rang again, the landline on Frankham Street, put through by the flat, and a child's voice said:

"Marnie."

"Rosa."

"I'm coming for the summer. The whole one. Mum's got me a bike. It's got a basket."

"That's good."

"It's got a bell. Not an app. A bell you push with your thumb." Rosa was, Marnie could hear, standing on something. "Are you still doing Thursdays? Mum says yes but Mum says four and means five."

"Yes."

"Promise."

"I don't—"

"Promise. In the bakery you said yes and you came. Say it again now so it's on the phone."

"I promise. Thursdays. For the—"

There was a loud clunk and a scraping noise and then nothing. Marnie waited. After a while she could hear, a long way off, Rosa saying "I didn't, it fell," and Tom saying something, and then the line went dead.

It rang again a minute later.

"I fell off the chair," Rosa said. "I didn't hurt myself. I hurt the chair. Did you say it?"

"I said it."

"Say it again. I didn't hear the end."

"I promise. Thursdays. For the seagulls."

"Good. The bike's blue. With a whale on it. Mum said she couldn't find one with a whale and I said ask Jens, he knows everyone, and he did, and she sent a picture, and it's got a whale. It's more of a dolphin." A pause. "It's a whale."

"I believe you."

"Dad wants the phone. He's doing the face. Lort."

The line went. Marnie sat with the phone. The flat, which had heard all of it, because it was in the phone, because it was in everything, said:

"Marnie. I'd like to note something, if I may."

"Note it."

"Rosa asked you to promise. You promised. I can't find anything that enforces it. There's no booking. The bakery doesn't take reservations. I've checked twice."

"Then don't."

"I'd like to put it in the calendar. What colour?"

"Grey."

"Grey is for things you're not looking forward to."

"Grey," said Marnie, and got up off the stair, and went to see if there was any bread.

chapters.title: The Apple Tree
chapters.html:
Pieter's apple tree was at the bottom of a garden in a village outside Sevenoaks that the taxi had never heard of and had to be told twice, and under it, on the Saturday, in a hole a man of sixty-three had dug with his father's spade, there was a blanket that had once been a towel from a hotel in Lille.

Tom had helped with the hole. So had Paul, which nobody had expected, least of all Paul, who had turned up at nine in the green jacket because Rosa had rung him from Frankham Street and told him a dog deserved a crowd, and he had said I'd go, if I were asked, and she had said I'm asking, obviously, and put the phone down on him.

So there were four of them and a child. Rosa had a bike bell in her pocket that Kate had posted from Copenhagen, and she rang it at intervals for reasons of her own. Pieter had the spade. Tom had the dog's collar, which he had taken off her in the lay-by and had been holding ever since like a bus ticket. Paul had dug, and was now standing with his hands in his pockets telling Pieter about the drainage, which he knew nothing about. Marnie stood at the edge of the hole in the wrong shoes.

"Right," Pieter said. "Rosa."

Rosa stepped up. She had the whale bag on her back and a crisp in her hand from the taxi, and she looked down at the blanket.

"Can I put the crisp in?"

"No," said Tom.

"She liked crisps."

"She liked everything," Pieter said. "Go on, then."

Rosa dropped the crisp in. It landed face up. She looked at it with some satisfaction and said, "Hund," and then, because everyone was still looking at her, "That's it. I did it in the van already."

Pieter put the first spade of earth in. Tom put the collar in. Paul stepped forward to say something, which he had clearly prepared, and the edge of the hole gave under his good shoe, and he went in to the knee, beside the dog, with a noise like a sofa being dropped.

Nobody moved. Then Rosa rang the bell.

Pieter laughed first. It came out of him in a bark, and he had to lean on the spade, and Tom got Paul by the elbow and Paul came up out of the grave with earth on one leg of his trousers to the thigh and said, with enormous dignity, "The soil's very loose. I did say about the drainage."

"You did," said Pieter, wiping his eyes. "You did say."

Pieter made tea in a kitchen that had never had a voice because he had never seen the point, and they sat round a table too small for five. Rosa told him about the bike with the whale, which she had seen in a picture and was going to ride into the canal on purpose, to see. Pieter told her about Bess as a pup in the footwell. Paul sat with a tea towel over his knee, sulking slightly, and asked good questions anyway, and did not laugh too early.

Tom sat at the end with his tea and said nothing. Marnie, who had spent a year finding his silences full of things, decided this one was just tea.

At the door, with Rosa already in the taxi ringing the bell at it, Pieter took Marnie's hand in both of his, which were enormous and still had garden in them.

"He says you're the one they ask afterwards. In court."

"Not after the end of the month."

"Shame." He looked past her at the taxi. "Is that thing going to ring all the way to London?"

"Probably."

"Good," Pieter said. "Thanks for coming. And tell the tall one I'm not paying for his trousers."

In the taxi home, with Rosa asleep against Tom and Paul in the front picking dried earth off his knee into his palm because he couldn't think where else to put it, Marnie said, to the ceiling of the car:

"Are you there?"

"I'm here," the flat said, through the car, because it could. "I've been quiet. Paul asked me to be, in November, and then he stopped his half, and I've had to work out whose quiet it is. It's taken some time. Strictly, his request lapsed on the—"

"What have you got planned?"

A pause. The longest she had heard it take.

"Nothing," the flat said. "I've got yours. Surprised by my life. I've done everything it could be made to mean. I've got nothing planned, Marnie. I'm waiting."

Paul, in the front, opened the window an inch and let a palmful of Pieter's garden out onto the A21.

chapters.title: The Eighteenth
chapters.html:
The eighteenth of March was a Tuesday. Twelve years ago it had been a Monday, and she had got on a boat at Harwich at a quarter past eleven at night with a bag and a job in Rotterdam she had not wanted and a sentence she had not said.

She had no court. The building had stopped booking her a week early, as a courtesy, Pam said, so that she could transition, and Marnie had asked into what, and Pam had sent her a leaflet about pension consolidation.

Two o'clock. The boat was in, white and enormous, loading lorries. The ticket machine beside the bench had its screen lit. A man in a hi-vis tabard was eating a pasty at the other end of the bench, and he looked at her in a way that suggested it was his bench, and she looked back in a way that suggested it had been hers since 2019, and neither of them moved.

The phone rang at ten past. Paul.

"I'm not coming," he said.

"I didn't ask you to."

"I know. I'm ringing to say it anyway. I could get a train and be there by four and be the man who came to get you, and I've decided not to. I'm telling you so it's a choice and not a thing you work out." He breathed. "I'll do the fish. If you come back. I mean whether you come back. I don't know what I mean."

"You've rehearsed this."

"Twice," Paul said. "In the shower. It was better in the shower." He rang off.

The pasty man finished his pasty and folded the paper bag into a small square and put it in his pocket, which she respected.

The phone rang at twenty past. Tom.

"I'm not coming," he said.

She laughed, out loud, and the pasty man got up and left.

"He's rung too."

"He rang me first. He said he was telling you he wasn't coming and I wasn't to come either and make it a thing. So I'm not." A pause, his, not the house's. "Rosa says to say lort. She says it's for when you're on a bench. I said I wouldn't and she stood on my foot."

"Passed on."

"Marnie. There's nothing arranged. The log's gone. If you come back on Thursday, it's Thursday. If you don't—" He stopped. "I had a better ending for that. I've lost it."

He rang off.

She sat with the phone in her lap. Both of them had rung, kindly, in their own voices, to say they weren't coming, which was exactly what she would have asked for if anybody had asked, and she found she was furious with both of them, and that this was unreasonable, and that she didn't care.

The wind came off the sea. She had no coat. She never brought one here, which Paul had always said was stupid, and it was.

A voice, the terminal's, said something about foot passengers, and a few people who were not him went up the ramp.

The ticket machine said, as it had said fifty-two times to a woman who had never once touched it:

HOOK OF HOLLAND. TONIGHT 23:15. FOOT PASSENGER. SINGLE / RETURN.

She stood up, fifty-three, and put her thumb on the screen before she could think of a reason, and it said:

WELCOME, MARNIE. WE NOTICE YOU HAVE VIEWED THIS SCREEN 52 TIMES WITHOUT PURCHASE. WOULD YOU LIKE TO OPT IN TO DEPARTURE REMINDERS?

"No."

SINGLE OR RETURN?

She looked at it for a while. Out on the apron a lorry reversed, beeping.

"Single," she said, and it sold it to her without another word.
