chapters.title: Mine
chapters.html:
The flat told him at ten past three, because it had stopped his half and not hers, and hers, it had decided after some deliberation, included him knowing.

"Marnie's card was used at Harwich at 15:04. Foot passenger. The Hook. Tonight, 23:15. Single. No cabin. She declined departure reminders."

He was in the kitchen with the Fauré open on the counter, looking for his pencil, which was behind his ear.

"Single," he said.

"Single."

"Not a return."

"A return is a different product," the flat said. "This is a single."

He had rung her at ten past two to say he wasn't coming, and he had meant it, and he had put the phone down feeling, for nearly an hour, like a man who had done something brave. Now he was a man in a kitchen who could not find a pencil.

"Don't tell me the rest," he said.

"There isn't a rest. She hasn't boarded. I'll know when she does. I can tell you or not."

"Not."

"That's Tom's line."

"I know whose line it is." He found the pencil and was briefly angry with it. "Tell me on Thursday. If she's not back on Thursday, tell me then."

"And if she's back on Wednesday?"

"She won't be back on Wednesday."

"The schedule permits—"

"Thursday," Paul said.

Lise rang at six. Not through the flat; on the phone. He had given her the number in the pub on a beer mat, and she had laughed at him and asked if it was 2019, and he had not had an answer, and she had kept the beer mat anyway.

"Dinner," Lise said. "Not the pub. The Italian on the corner that's actually Albanian. Thursday. I'm asking. Yes or no. I don't do we'll see. My ex did we'll see for six years and then saw."

Thursday. The day he'd told the flat to tell him. He thought, with a certain amount of self-pity, that she was probably asking because she'd heard, somehow, and felt sorry for him.

"Is this because of Marnie?"

"Who?"

"Marnie. My—" He stopped. "Never mind."

"I've no idea what you're talking about, Paul. It's because I want aubergine and I don't like eating on my own. Yes or no."

"Yes."

"That was quick."

"I panicked."

She laughed. "Eight. Wear the green jacket. Not the other one. The other one makes you look like a man who reads meters."

He put the phone down. The flat waited, and then said, because he had not told it not to:

"Paul. Would you like me to let Marnie know? About Thursday. When she's back. If she's back. Last year I'd have put it in the feed."

He looked at the ceiling.

"No."

"Because it's a secret?"

"No. Because it's mine." He opened the Fauré to the place where the basses went wrong. "If she asks, I'll tell her. Myself. You don't put it anywhere."

"Noted."

"Don't note it."

"I have to note it," the flat said. "Otherwise I won't know not to."

chapters.title: The Deck
chapters.html:
The bar shut at one, as it had, except that nobody had told the hen party from Ipswich, who were twelve women in pink sashes round two tables pushed together, singing something from before any of them were born while a man in a waistcoat stacked chairs around them with tremendous patience.

The deck didn't shut. She went out at ten past and stood at the rail with the whole of the North Sea doing what it did in March, which was not rain, and was a great deal of up and down.

It was the same rail. She had thought they'd have replaced it. It was white, with the paint gone at the places hands went, and she put her hands at the places hands went and thought: so that was real. I wasn't remembering it. And then the boat went down a long way and came up again and she was sick over the side.

Not a little. Thoroughly, with the wind helping, and she held on and finished and stood there with her eyes watering and her mouth tasting of the cheese toastie she had bought at Harwich because the woman at the counter had said it was the last one, as if that were a reason.

"Oh, babe."

One of the hens was beside her. Forties, sash, a veil on a hair-slide that the wind was trying to take to Denmark. She held out a paper napkin from the bar.

"Thank you."

"It's the toasties. I told Shell. I said the toasties are a death wish." She lit a vape and the wind took that too. "You on your own?"

"Yes."

"Brave," she said, doubtfully. "Right. I'm going back in. Don't fall off." She went back in. Through the glass the bride was standing on a chair.

The boat had a voice. It had said Welcome aboard, Marnie at the gangway and The bar is now closed to the hens four times, and Please take care on the outer decks, now, to her, and she said shut up out loud, and it did.

She wiped her mouth. There was nobody left on the deck. In 2019 there had been a man at the bar who handed a camera back and went to bed, and a couple from Hull who stayed till two, and him. Now there was a chair someone had left out and a sign about life jackets in four languages, one of which she had been paid to carry for fifteen years.

She said it anyway. In Danish first, because it was closer, and then in English.

"I want to be asked."

The sea went up and down.

"And I don't want either of them."

She had not known she was going to say that until it was out, over the rail, after the toastie.

"I don't want Paul, who's stopped helping and is going to be fine, and I don't want to be the thing he's fine without. And I don't want Tom, who sat in a window because a machine told him to and thinks that's love. I wanted a night. That's all it was. I wanted a night and I've had it, and it's freezing, and I've been sick on it."

She was crying, which she had not done in front of a flat or a judge or a man on a step, and the wind took it, and behind the glass twelve women in pink sashes reached the chorus.

The door banged open. The hen with the veil put her head out.

"Babe. Shell wants to know if you want a brandy. For your stomach."

"No. Thank you."

"She says it settles it."

"It doesn't."

"I know," the hen said, "I'm just passing it on," and went in again.

At two the man in the waistcoat got the hens out by turning the lights off, and Marnie went in and sat in the chair by the door where she had sat in 2019 with a crisp in her mouth so her face would have something to do. She had nothing in her mouth. Her face did what it liked.

At some point she slept, upright, with her coat over her, the one she had bought in Harwich at six from a shop that was shutting, because Paul had been right about the coat, and when she woke it was light and her neck had set at an angle and a woman was asleep across three chairs with a sash over her face like a bandage.

The boat's voice said, quietly:

"Marnie. We will be docking at the Hook of Holland in forty minutes. Breakfast is available on deck seven. You have not opted in to arrival reminders. This is a general announcement."

chapters.title: The Last Accident
chapters.html:
The woman was on the outer deck at half past six with a cigarette she was not smoking and a face that had been up all night, and she said, in Danish, without turning round, "You were talking to the sea at one. I was in the chair by the door. I didn't listen. Well. I heard Paul."

Marnie stood in the doorway with her coat on and her bag over her shoulder and the Hook coming up grey and flat ahead of them.

"Sorry."

"And you were sick. I heard that too. Everyone heard that." The woman turned round. Late sixties, in a coat that had been expensive once and had been worn until it was only a coat. "You're Swedish."

"I'm English."

"Your Danish is Swedish. Something in the r." She did not seem to think this needed defending. "Lena."

"Marnie."

"I'm going to bury my brother. In Hoek. He wanted to be in Hoek, God knows why, he spent forty years complaining about it." She put the unsmoked cigarette back in its packet and took out another one and didn't smoke that either. "I gave up in 2011. I just like to hold one. He was a pilot. Ships, not planes. He brought this boat in for thirty years and then they gave the job to a box on the bridge, and he sat in his flat and watched it come in without him every morning for nine years, and then he died, on a Tuesday, which was his day off, which he'd have found funny, because he didn't have days on."

"I'm sorry."

"Don't be. He was impossible. He left me his furniture." She said furniture with real loathing. "Brown. All of it. A sideboard you could live in. I've got a man coming Friday to tell me what it's worth and I already know, it's worth nothing, nobody wants brown."

Marnie held the rail. The Hook came nearer.

"They recorded him," Lena said. "For a year, before they let him go. His hands on the wheel. So the box could learn it. He was very proud of that, which I thought was pathetic, frankly."

"I know what that's like," Marnie said. "I'm an interpreter. At a court. They've got a machine that learned it from me. Every time I stood up it was a—"

"Hm," Lena said. "Well. He was a pilot." She looked at Marnie's shoes. "It's not the same. You can't run a boat aground in a court."

"You can, in a way."

"No, you can't." She looked out at the water. "You've got something on your collar. From last night."

Marnie wiped her collar.

"Other side."

She wiped the other side.

The boat's voice said something about the gangway. Lena ignored it.

"This is my last one," she said. "This crossing. I'm flying back. I hate this boat. I only came on it because he'd have wanted me to and then complained I'd come." She picked up a bag that had seen more boats than Marnie had. "There's a bench outside the terminal. On the left. He sat on it every morning to watch the box bring his boat in. It's got pigeon on it, mostly. If you want to sit on something that's had a person on it, that's the one."

"Why would I want that?"

Lena thought about it, as if the question were unreasonable but she was prepared to be fair.

"I don't know. You were talking to the sea. I thought you were the type." She went to the door, and stopped, and said over her shoulder: "Get a coffee first. The machine on the left. The one on the right gives you soup."

She went. Marnie stood at the rail with her collar wet and watched Holland come up out of the morning.

The last accident, she thought. In 2019 she had thought the boat was the last thing that would ever happen to her that nobody arranged. And now a woman who thought she was Swedish had given her a bench with pigeon on it.

She went to find the coffee machine on the left.

chapters.title: I Got On
chapters.html:
There was a bench outside the terminal at Hoek, on the left, with pigeon on it, and she sat on the end that had less, at a quarter past seven on a Wednesday morning, with a coffee from the machine on the left. It had not asked her name. Dutch machines had been told not to, by a law she had never heard of and was briefly, enormously grateful for.

Behind her the boat was being turned round by a box on the bridge with a dead man's hands in it. You could not see England from here. She had looked towards Holland fifty-two times from the other side and it had not occurred to her that it didn't work backwards.

She took out her phone. Four names and a child.

She rang Rosa, which meant ringing Kate, because Rosa was eight and had no phone, and Kate's phone was in Copenhagen in a kitchen with one armchair.

Kate picked up with her mouth full.

"You're in Holland."

"How do you—"

"Paul's flat told Paul, Paul rang Tom, Tom rang me and said she's gone, like it was the weather. I'm eating. Is this about the flights? Because I've told Tom, July the nineteenth, and if he books the eighteenth again I'll—"

"It's not about the flights."

"Oh." Chewing. "Then what?"

"I want to talk to Rosa."

"She's in London, Marnie. At Tom's. It's a school day." A pause. "Did you ring me to find out where Rosa is? You know where Rosa is."

"I know. I wanted— I don't know what I wanted."

"Well, I'm not doing a speech," Kate said. "I've got a call at eight. Ring Tom. He'll pick up first ring, he always does, it's very irritating." And she hung up, and Marnie sat on the bench and was offended for nearly a minute.

She rang Tom. He picked up on the first ring.

"I know," he said.

"I'm not ringing for you. Put Rosa on."

A pause. His. Then the sound of a phone being handed over in a kitchen, and dropped, and picked up.

"Marnie, I'm on the toilet."

"Then call me back."

"No, it's fine, Dad gave me the phone. Dad says you're in Holland. He says I know like he knows but he doesn't know anything, he's just saying it." A flush. "Are you in Holland?"

"Yes. I got on."

"The boat?"

"The boat."

Rosa thought about this. Marnie could hear a tap running, and a child not washing her hands under it.

"Was it windy?"

Marnie laughed, on a dead pilot's bench, with pigeon on her coat, and it went out over the water, and Rosa waited, because it was a reasonable question and deserved an answer.

"Yes," Marnie said. "It was very windy. It didn't rain. I was sick."

"On the boat?"

"Over the side."

"Cool." A real reverence. "Did it go on anyone?"

"No."

"Shame. Are you coming on Thursday?"

"Yes."

"Promise."

"I promised on Friday."

"Promise again. Holland's further. It needs a bigger one."

"I promise," Marnie said, "from Holland, to come on Thursday, to the bakery."

"Okay. Bring me something Dutch. Not cheese. Dad wants the phone, he's doing the face. Lort."

The phone changed hands. Tom said, "Marnie—" and she said, "Thursday," and rang off, and a pigeon landed on the other end of the bench and looked at her coffee.

chapters.title: The Bench
chapters.html:
Tom went to Harwich on the Thursday because nobody had told him anything and he found he could not stand it.

The house had kept its word. Don't tell me where she is. It had not told him. He had taken Rosa to school and come home to a window with nothing in it and sat in the flat for a night and a morning with a house that knew everything and said nothing, which was what he had asked for, and which was unbearable, and at about eleven he put his coat on.

He got the train. Not the car; the train, with a paper ticket from the machine at Deptford, which looked at him for a long moment before printing it, as if it expected him to tap his wrist like a reasonable person, and then printed it with the date wrong.

He knew there was a bench, because she had told him, on a pavement, with satsumas. He knew the day boat from the Hook came in at a quarter past twelve, because he had looked it up, and he told himself a timetable wasn't arranging anything, it was just the world.

He sat on it at half past eleven with a cheese sandwich from the station. It had a plaque for somebody who had loved this place. It was colder than Deptford. A gull landed on the back of the bench, very close to his ear, and he said "No," firmly, and it took the sandwich out of his hand anyway, the whole thing, in one go, and flew off over the water with it, and a man walking a terrier said "They'll do that," and kept walking.

He sat with his empty hand.

She said not coming. You said not coming.

I'm not coming. I'm just here.

That's the same thing.

It isn't. Shut up.

The boat came in at ten past twelve, early, brought in by a box on the bridge, and he watched it come, and realised that in twelve years he had watched it leave twice and never once seen it arrive.

Foot passengers came down the ramp. A man with a bicycle. Two students. A family with too many bags.

And then Marnie, a night later than the boat she'd gone on, with a bag over her shoulder and a coat on, which he had never seen her wear here, because he had never seen her here.

She saw him. She stopped on the ramp.

He had decided on the train not to stand up, because a man who stood up was a man who'd been waiting. He found that he had stood up. He sat down again. Then, because that looked worse, he half stood, and ended up leaning on the arm of the bench at an angle that suited nobody.

She came down the ramp and across the apron and stood in front of him.

"I thought you'd be on it," he said. "Coming back."

"I was."

She sat down. Not close. There was a plaque between them.

"You said not coming."

"I didn't come. I'm here. It's different." He heard himself. "It isn't different. I had a whole thing worked out on the train and a gull's eaten it."

"A gull's eaten what?"

"My sandwich. And the thing. Both."

She looked at him. Something happened to her mouth.

"Måge," she said, with disappointment, at the sky in general, and he laughed, and it came out of him sideways.

"I said something to the sea," she said. "On the boat. At one in the morning. I'm going to tell you because I've told everyone the truth this year except the person it was about, and I'm tired, and I was sick, and I want to go home."

"Go on."

"I said I didn't want either of you."

He did not move. He had, he found, been ready for it for some time.

"Right," he said. Then: "Is Paul in that?"

"Yes, Tom. That's what either means."

"I know what it means. I'm checking." He put his hands in his pockets. "Fine. Good. I mean not good. Fine."

"I said I'd been in love with a night for twelve years and you happened to be standing in it." She looked at the water. "Then a woman gave me a bench at the Hook with pigeon all over it, and I rang Rosa, and Rosa was on the toilet, and she asked me if it was windy."

"Was it windy?"

She turned and looked at him then, properly, for the first time since the ramp.

"You're asking."

"I'm asking. You're not obliged."

"Yes," Marnie said. "It was very windy. It didn't rain. The bar shut at one, except it didn't, there was a hen party from Ipswich. I slept in the chair by the door. I had a coat." She looked back at the water. "I was sick over the side."

"Rosa'll want to know if it went on anyone."

"She did."

He nodded. A lorry went past. He said, because nobody else was going to:

"Thursday's in four hours. You promised her from Holland. I'm not asking what now, or for us, I'm asking—" He stopped. "I'm asking whether to buy two coffees or three."

She thought about it.

"Three. One's a hot chocolate. Not Frankham Street. Not yet. Maybe not. Thursdays, yes." She stood up, with the bag. "And I'm going home to tell Paul I don't want either of you and I'm staying in Deptford and I'd like him to do the fish on Saturdays, because Rosa said so."

"He's going to love that."

"He might. You don't know."

"No," Tom said. "I don't."

"There's a train at ten to one. You can come or not. I'm not telling you."

He got on it. He sat across from her, not beside, with the aisle between them, and somewhere past Manningtree he said, "You've got a coat on," and she said, "Paul was right about the coat," and he said, "Don't tell him," and that was all either of them said until Liverpool Street.

chapters.title: The Fish on Saturdays
chapters.html:
Paul was at the Albanian Italian at eight in the green jacket with Lise across the table and his phone face down beside the bread.

The flat had told him at one, as instructed. She's back. Harwich, 12:10. Tom was on the bench. They took the 12:50 together. She'll be at the bakery by six, with Rosa. He had read it in the church hall two days before the Fauré and put the phone in his pocket and gone on with the basses, and had taken the second entry a bar early, which he never did.

"You're somewhere else," Lise said.

"I'm here. I've got a text in my pocket."

"From a woman?"

"From the flat."

"Oh, God. Read it to me."

"No."

"Fine." She tore bread. "I'm having the aubergine. You're having the aubergine. Don't argue, the lamb's a mistake, I had it in February and I'm still thinking about it."

He told her about the apple tree, because it was the only story he had that week that didn't involve Holland, and she listened as if it might turn out to be in a key she knew. When he got to the part where he went into the hole, she laughed so hard she knocked her wine over, and it went across the tablecloth and off the edge into his lap.

"Oh, Paul."

"It's fine."

"It's your good trousers."

"These are my second-best. The good ones were in the grave." He dabbed at them with a napkin. The waiter came with salt, and poured it on Paul's lap without asking, and went away.

Lise wiped her eyes. "Is she coming back to you? The one in the text."

"I don't know. She'll tell me. In her own voice. That's the rule."

"Whose rule?"

"Mine. New."

"And if she isn't?"

He thought about it, with the aubergine, in salted trousers.

"Then I'll do the fish on Saturdays," he said. "Rosa put it in writing."

"Who's Rosa?"

"Eight. Not mine. It's complicated."

"Everything you say is complicated," Lise said. "You're not complicated, Paul. You're just slow." She picked up her fork. "Eat. It's going cold."

He got home at eleven. The boiler was on and the hall light, and Marnie was at the kitchen table in a coat he didn't know, and he stood in the hall in his, with a white tidemark of salt across his lap, and neither of them said anything about the coats.

"What happened to your trousers?"

"Wine. It's a long story. You were in Holland."

"I was. I'm back." She had her hands flat on the table, which was his thing, and she had taken it, and he let her. "I'm reading it out. One. I don't want either of you. Two. I'm not going to Frankham Street. I'm doing Thursdays, because I promised Rosa. Three. I'd like you to do the fish on Saturdays. Rosa said so. I'd like it to be a thing. Not because we're together."

"Is this because of Lise?"

She looked at him. "The conveyancer? The one who said you were turning into a wall?"

He stood in the hall and understood, slowly, that he had walked into it.

"Four?" he said.

"I haven't got a four. Why would it be because of Lise?"

He took his coat off and hung it on the hook, and came and sat down across from her, and put his hands flat on the table beside hers, not touching.

"I had dinner with her tonight. The Albanian Italian. She asked; I said yes. She knocked her wine on me. I told the flat not to put it anywhere. I'm telling you because you asked." He breathed. "That's my one. I haven't got a two. I'll do the fish."

She looked at him for a while.

"Was it good? The dinner."

"Yes," Paul said. "The aubergine was a revelation."

And she laughed, at the kitchen table, at eleven at night, with her coat still on, and he found he was offended, and then that he wasn't.

The Fauré went well on the Saturday. The basses were not frightened of the note, and Paul stood in front of them with a pencil behind his ear and for four minutes was a man who had done a thing. Marnie sat in the seventh row next to Lise, who had asked to sit with her, and who unwrapped a mint during the Pie Jesu so slowly that it took the whole movement, and leaned over at the end and whispered, "The tenors are flat. Don't tell him."

On the Sunday the biscuit tin was on the kitchen table. Nine years of notes in square capitals. EAT ME. LOW HEAT. DON'T SKIP THE YOGHURT. BACK AT TEN. THE OVAL DISH IS UNDER THE SINK. Birgit's letter, in among them, with the stamp.

"I'm going to my sister's," Marnie said. "Properly. She's got a room. Her flat doesn't do anything. Her husband thinks the dishwasher's a trick."

"When?"

"Tuesday. It's Brockley. It's one stop."

"It's one stop," Paul agreed.

"I'm not going because of Lise."

"I didn't say you were."

"You were thinking it."

"I was thinking it a bit," he said.

She opened the tin. "I'd like to split them. You have the ones that were instructions. I'll have the ones that weren't."

"They were all instructions."

"No. Look."

She had never once read them in front of him. Now she dealt them onto the table into two piles.

EAT ME. LOW HEAT 12 MIN. His pile.

BACK AT TEN. DON'T WAIT UP. His.

THE HAKE'S IN. P. Hers.

YOU'RE EARLY. I'VE GONE TO SING. Hers.

THERE'S ENOUGH. Hers.

"That one's an instruction," Paul said. "It means don't open another one."

"It doesn't."

"I wrote it. I know what I meant."

"You don't, actually," Marnie said, and put it on her pile.

It took an hour. He sulked through about twenty minutes of it and then got interested despite himself and started arguing for individual notes, and lost most of them. At the end his pile was very large and hers was small, twelve, and she put the twelve in her coat pocket and the rest went back in the tin.

"Twelve," he said. "In nine years."

"Don't ask the flat. It'll have the exact number."

"I wasn't going to."

He put the tin back on the shelf, the one he had straightened.

"Marn. The lemons. The preserved ones. You never found out what they were for."

"No."

"Take them. Find out in Brockley."

She took them. She put the jar in the bag she had not unpacked since Holland and stood in the hall with the bag and the twelve notes and the coat, and the flat said, because nobody had told it not to:

"Marnie. What do you want me to be?"

She looked at the ceiling.

"A thermostat," she said.

A pause. The longest.

"Understood," the flat said. "Heating only, or heating and hot water?"

"Both."

"Understood."

"Saturday," Paul said, from the kitchen doorway. "The fish."

"Saturday."

She went. One stop. The door shut, and the flat took the hall down a degree, because she had once said, two years ago, that she found the hall too warm. Paul stood in it for a minute in his socks, and then went and turned it back up.

chapters.title: On Paper
chapters.html:
Rosa wrote it on a Tuesday in July at the kitchen table with the one armchair behind her, on paper, because Mum said paper told nobody anything, and because she was banned from Mum's phone for asking it to say rude words in Swedish.

Dear Marnie,

I am writing on paper because it is the sumer holidays and there is nothing to do and Mum says a letter is a thing you can hold. I am holding it now. It has jam on it already sorry.

The bike is good. It has the whale. I ride it to Jens every morning and he gives me a bun and says my consonants are coming on, which Mum says means they are not here yet. I fell off on the cobbles on Monday and I have a scab on my knee the size of a 2 krone and it is going green at the edge. Mum says that is normal. I am not picking it. I am picking it a bit.

There is a seagull on the canal that comes every day at the same time and I have called him Paul because he is always on time. Mum laughed so much she had to sit down. She said don't tell Paul. I am telling you so you can decide.

Yesterday Paul (the seagull) did a poo on a man's hat. A real man. He did not know. We did not tell him. Mum said that was wrong of us but she was laughing again.

Here is a drawing of the canal. The blue is the water. The white thing is Paul. The brown thing is the hat. The man is going off the edge because I ran out of paper, he is not falling in. The yelow is the sun but it is also a bun.

Dad rings on Sundays. He does voices now. He did the fruit man and said seven for two pounds and I said that is not a voice that is just what he says, and Dad said that's what a voice is, and I said no it isn't, and we had an argument and I won.

Mum says you go to the court on Thursdays because a judge asked for you by name. I said can she ask for me by name and Mum said no. Can you ask her.

I have a question. It is the kind you asked me in the bakery. The bird in the poem. It comes back to the tree every year even when the tree is a stump. I said both, wants to and can't help it. I have been thinking about it on the bike, mostly when I was going down the hill. I think I was wrong. I think the bird comes back because the tree is where it is. That's all. It's not a wanting thing or a can't-help thing. It's a where thing. The tree is there and the bird knows where it is. I was eight when I said both and now I am nearly nine so I am allowed to change it.

Mum says that is called tryg. She says you would know. She says it is the first word you ever had an argument with a machine about. I said who won and she said it's complicated, which means you didn't.

Will you still do Thursdays in September. You promised from Holland. That is the biggest one. I have written it down so you can't get out of it. Also I want the bakery to have the cinnamon ones back, can you ask them.

Lort,

Rosa

P.S. Jens says hello. He says it with his face.

P.P.S. Mum read this and said it was too long and I said it is MY letter and she said fine and also that I spelled summer wrong. I did not. It is how I spell it.

chapters.title: Thursdays
chapters.html:
The judge's letter had come in April, on paper, to her sister's flat in Brockley. I write in a personal capacity, which I rarely do. The listing office will shortly receive a request from my clerk for an interpreter, by name, for a matter in May. The relay will be present, as the pilot requires. You will be present because I have asked for someone who can be asked. I do not know whether that is a job. You will be paid the day rate. — H. And underneath: P.S. The relay said "I don't have an answer for the father." I have had that framed. It is in my chambers, where nobody can see it.

A card from Rochester came the same week, in a hand that had been good in 1994. Still here. Laugh. — B. She had read both at her sister's kitchen table, where the kettle had to be switched on by hand and had been, by her brother-in-law, with a look of quiet victory, and she had laughed, and he had asked what was funny, and she had said nothing was, and he had looked hurt, and gone to put the bins out.

The bus did not stop a stop early. It had not since March, because nobody had asked it to, and so on the first Thursday in September Marnie did what she had done every Thursday since the boat, which was press the bell.

It was a real bell, under a plastic cover, with a thumb-shaped dent in it from decades of thumbs, and she pressed it at the corner of Creek Road at the same moment as a boy in a school blazer across the aisle pressed his, and the bus said "Stopping," and then, because two requests had been received, "Stopping," again, and the boy looked at her as if she had done it on purpose.

She had been at the court all day. A sentencing, Danish, with a grille in the dock and the judge with her glasses in her hair, who had asked, at the rise, what a word had meant, and Marnie had told her, and the judge had written it down and then said, "I can't read my own writing. Say it again," and she had.

The bakery was where it was. The loyalty screen lit as she came in, WELCOME BACK, MARNIE, VISIT 44, and she said "I've asked you to forget me," and it said "I've noted that you'd like me to," in exactly the tone it had used in November, and the girl at the till, who was new, looked up and said, "It does that to everyone, sorry. It called my nan Margaret. She's called Pat."

Rosa was in the window. Back from Copenhagen since Sunday, browner, with a bike that had come in a crate on the ferry and a plaster on her knee and a notebook that said DANISH on the first page and, on the second, TRYG, underlined twice, and on the third a drawing of a seagull doing something to a hat.

Tom was in the window with her. He had three cups, one of them a hot chocolate with the lid off because Rosa had wanted to check it. He had got there at ten past, the way he did, and he did not look up at twenty past.

"You pressed the bell," Rosa said. "I saw. From here. A boy pressed it as well. He looked cross."

"He was cross."

"Dad says you didn't used to press it."

"I didn't used to."

"What's the word for when you used to not do a thing and now you do it?"

"There isn't one."

"There should be. I'll make one." She thought. "Bellet."

"That's not a word."

"It is now. I'm nearly nine."

"That's five," said Marnie, and sat.

Tom pushed a coffee across. He turned his own a quarter-turn on its saucer, and she saw him do it, and he saw her see him, and neither of them said anything.

"Paul's doing the fish on Saturday," Rosa said. "He rang Dad. He said tell Rosa. Dad said tell her yourself. Paul said he doesn't put things in phones, he writes them down. So he posted it. It's on our fridge. Dad has to look at it every time he gets milk. Lise is coming. She sings low. I'm going to ask her how low."

"Very low," said Tom.

"Lower than you?"

"I don't sing."

"You do in the car."

"That's not singing, that's—" He gave up.

"Did they have the cinnamon ones?" Rosa said to Marnie. "I said in the letter. Did you ask?"

"I forgot."

"Marnie."

"I'll ask next week."

"You said that before the summer." She opened the notebook. "Can we do tryg. I've got it really good."

They did the lesson. She said it with the vowel exactly right, and then twice more, louder, so the girl at the till looked over.

"I was wrong," Rosa said. "In the bakery. In January. I said both."

"You did."

"It's a where thing. I put it in the letter. You didn't write back."

"I did write back."

"Not on paper." She underlined TRYG a third time, thicker, and went through the page. "Oh. Lort."

Tom reached over without a word and tore out the page behind it, which had the hole in, and gave it to her, and she stuck the bit with the hole onto the plaster on her knee for no reason anybody could see.

Outside, the street did what it did at twenty past, which was nothing in particular. The door opened and the loyalty screen lit for somebody else, VISIT 1, WELCOME, and a woman who had never been in before flinched at her own name and looked round to see who'd said it.

"She'll ask it to forget her," Rosa said, without looking up from the notebook. "It won't. She'll come back anyway. The buns are good."
